Committee confirms monthly meeting cadence during setup (Months 0–4 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-02-08). Document all approvals and decisions.

Responsible Body/Role: Heat Response Steering Committee (majority vote, Chair has tie-breaker; quorum 4 of 6 members including Chair or Vice-Chair).

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1.3 (2026-11-17); allow 1 week for scheduling after membership confirmed.

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Steering Committee meeting minutes with formal approvals
  • Signed alert-declaration delegation letter
  • Approved GDPR legal-review scope and budget authorization
  • Approved procurement route and authority matrix
  • Distribution of decisions to all stakeholders and departments

Dependencies:

  • Steering Committee membership confirmed and first meeting scheduled
  • Alert thresholds and delegation drafted for approval
  • GDPR legal review initiated

10. Partner-liaison officer identifies and initiates formal engagement with ≥4 key intermediary partners: housing associations, social services, NGOs and pharmacy chains. Send introductory letters explaining the program, data-protection model (intermediary-held lists, no personal data to city), expected roles (outreach via their existing contacts, daily call-logging, partner training) and timeline. Request designation of a partner contact person for each organization. Schedule individual scoping meetings to understand partner capacity, existing data systems, and any data-governance constraints.

Responsible Body/Role: Partner-liaison officer (incident commander until this role is hired; then designated Partner-liaison Officer within Heat Response Operations Team).

Suggested Timeframe: Introductory letters sent by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01); scoping meetings held by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Written introductory letters to ≥4 partners
  • Scoping-meeting notes for each partner (capacity, data systems, constraints)
  • Designated partner contact person and escalation contact for each organization
  • Summary of preliminary partner feedback and risks

Dependencies:

  • Partner-liaison officer designated or interim role assigned
  • Program governance and data-protection model finalized

11. Cooling-center Operations Lead (or interim coordinator) identifies all potential refuge sites (target 10, range 8–12): libraries, community centers, parish halls, sports halls, malls. Confirm facility ownership/management, current heating/cooling systems, accessibility status, available space for people and supplies, liability insurance, and facility-manager contact. Request provisional facility-use agreements from each site for the 5-month season (June–October, Months 6.8–11.8 = 2027-04-23 to 2027-09-30). Conduct preliminary accessibility audit checklist at each site.

Responsible Body/Role: Cooling-center Operations Lead (external candidate or interim coordinator from civil protection or public works) with support from municipal facilities/real-estate office.

Suggested Timeframe: By Month 1.2 (2026-11-14); provisional agreements signed by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • List of 10 proposed cooling-center sites with location maps
  • Preliminary facility-use agreements (draft or signed) with each site
  • Accessibility audit checklist results for each site
  • Summary of required fit-out work and estimated costs per site

Dependencies:

  • Cooling-center Operations Lead designated or interim role established
  • Steering Committee approved governance and alert model

12. GDPR legal lead and counsel finalize all template data-processing agreements and MOUs based on counsel's legal opinion (Month 1 = 2026-11-08). Make revisions per counsel advice. Prepare separate versions if needed for different partner types (housing associations may have different data-handling capacity than NGOs). Include: data scope, lawful basis, contact frequency, escalation rules, breach notification (≤48 hours), data deletion schedule (season end), staff confidentiality and training requirements. Distribute finalized DPAs to all identified partners by end of Month 1.3 (2026-11-17) with 2-week review/sign-off target (deadline Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23).

Responsible Body/Role: GDPR specialist legal counsel (external) and municipal legal lead (0.5 FTE), with input from incident commander and partner-liaison officer.

Suggested Timeframe: Finalized DPAs ready for partner distribution by Month 1.3 (2026-11-17); sign-off deadline Month 1.5 (2026-11-23).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Finalized template DPAs incorporating counsel's legal opinion
  • Version control and change-log for each DPA
  • Covering letter explaining DPA to each partner
  • DPA sign-off checklist and tracking log

Dependencies:

  • GDPR counsel's legal opinion received (Month 1 = 2026-11-08)
  • Partners identified and contact persons confirmed

13. HR coordinator conducts second-round interviews and makes job offers to selected candidates for Cooling Center Operations Lead, Outreach and Enrollment Lead, Transport Lead / Dispatch Coordinator, Home Kit Lead / Installation Coordinator, and Legal and GDPR Lead. Obtain signed offer letters and employment contracts. Agree start dates (target 50% by Month 1.8 = 2026-12-02, remainder by Month 2 = 2026-12-08). Conduct background checks, occupational health clearance and compliance documentation as required.

Responsible Body/Role: HR coordinator (0.5 FTE) and municipal HR director.

Suggested Timeframe: Offers made and accepted by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); contracts signed by Month 1.7 (2026-11-29); start dates confirmed.

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Signed employment contracts or service agreements (5 lead roles)
  • Background-check clearance confirmations
  • Occupational health clearance or pre-employment health assessments
  • Confirmed start dates and onboarding schedule

Dependencies:

  • Recruitment interviews completed (Month 1.3–1.5 = 2026-11-17 to 2026-11-30)
  • Budget authorization for salaries confirmed

14. Incident commander and partner-liaison officer conduct individual scoping meetings with each of the ≥4 identified intermediary partners. Agenda: (1) review partner's existing resident/client contact database and data-protection practices; (2) explain heat-response program goals and the intermediary-held list model (no city access to personal data); (3) present the data-processing agreement template and explain lawful basis for contact (public task / consent hybrid); (4) confirm partner's capacity to conduct phone outreach (call-list, staff, availability); (5) discuss escalation rules and partner feedback mechanism; (6) agree on pilot call targets and schedule for Month 2 (2026-12-08) mock-drill testing. Document all partner commitments and concerns.

Responsible Body/Role: Partner-liaison officer (newly hired, or interim coordinator if not yet in post) with incident commander.

Suggested Timeframe: Meetings held by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); documented summaries by Month 1.7 (2026-11-29).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Partner-scoping meeting notes (1 per partner)
  • Partner capacity assessment and call-target agreement
  • Escalation protocol and feedback mechanism agreed
  • Partner sign-off on data-processing agreement (or issues flagged for resolution)

Dependencies:

  • Introductory partner engagement completed (Month 0.8–1.2 = 2026-11-01 to 2026-11-14)
  • DPA templates finalized and ready for partner review

15. Procurement specialist issues formal procurement notices for kits, handyperson services, and transport infrastructure. For fast-track items (kits, installation, phone systems), use framework call-offs or below-threshold purchasing routes per the approved procurement plan. Issue specification documents, evaluation criteria, and submission deadlines (target: bids due by Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23 for Month 1.7 = 2026-11-29 decision). For taxi/accessible-transport retainer, issue a small competitive RFQ or invite negotiation from 2–3 pre-qualified operators; aim to sign contract by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14) to lock in standby rates before summer demand.

Responsible Body/Role: Procurement specialist (0.5 FTE) with incident commander and relevant lead roles.

Suggested Timeframe: Notices issued by Month 1.3 (2026-11-17); bids received by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); awards by Month 1.7 (2026-11-29).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Procurement notices for kits, handyperson and phone-system items
  • RFQ or invitation for transport retainer contract
  • Bid evaluation reports and selection rationale
  • Purchase orders or contract awards (pending final signatures)

Dependencies:

  • Procurement specifications finalized (Month 0.8 = 2026-11-01)
  • Budget allocation confirmed
  • Steering Committee approval of procurement route

16. First operational meeting of the Heat Response Operations Team: Incident commander convenes public-health deputy, operations lead (civil protection), communications lead and partner-liaison officer (interim or newly hired). Agenda: (1) review alert thresholds and incident-command delegation; (2) confirm SITREP and briefing schedule (08:30 and 09:30 on alert days); (3) review public-communications plan and messaging templates; (4) review partner and cooling-center status; (5) establish daily decision-log and escalation hotline; (6) plan for Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness-gate drills (phone line, outreach mock-calls). Publish operations team charter and meeting schedule to all staff and partners.

Responsible Body/Role: Incident commander (chair), with public-health deputy, operations lead, communications lead and partner-liaison officer.

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1.5 (2026-11-23).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Heat Response Operations Team charter and ToR
  • Standing meeting schedule (daily SITREP and 09:30 briefing on alert days, weekly on non-alert)
  • Decision-log template and escalation protocol
  • Communications-cadence and messaging templates (draft)

Dependencies:

  • Incident commander and operations leads designated
  • Alert thresholds and delegation finalized
  • Steering Committee's first meeting held and decisions documented

17. All governance bodies now formally established submit their initial meeting minutes and charter documents to the Steering Committee. Legal lead conducts a compliance check: confirm all roles are filled (or interim assignments documented), all DPAs are signed or in final review, all procurement orders are placed, and all operational teams have published charters and meeting schedules. Incident commander submits a project-status dashboard showing: (1) governance bodies operational; (2) staffing progress (% of positions filled); (3) procurement status; (4) partner engagement status; (5) risks and corrective actions. This consolidated status report is reviewed at the Steering Committee's Month 2 (2026-12-08) meeting as part of the readiness-gate assessment.

Responsible Body/Role: Legal and GDPR Lead (0.5–1 FTE) with incident commander and PMO coordinator.

Suggested Timeframe: Compliance check completed by Month 1.8 (2026-12-02); status dashboard finalized by Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness-gate meeting.

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Consolidated governance-body charter and ToR document (all bodies, 1 summary)
  • Governance compliance checklist (roles filled, DPAs signed, procurement placed, operational charters published)
  • Project-status dashboard (staffing %, procurement %, partner % engaged, risks and corrective actions)
  • Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness-gate evidence summary (centers ready, transport signed, phone line live, training completed, procurement ≥90% ordered)

Dependencies:

  • All governance-body leads hired and in post or interim-assigned
  • DPAs signed with all partners
  • All procurement orders placed
  • All governance bodies' first meetings held and documented

18. Cooling-center Operations Lead finalizes facility-use agreements with all 10 sites. Conduct a detailed accessibility audit at each site using a standardized checklist (wheelchair access, toilet facilities, water points, quiet/low-stimulus rooms, parking, emergency exits, first-aid kit availability, AED locations). Categorize sites as 'fully accessible' (no remediation needed) or 'minor modifications required' (≤€10k, ≤4 weeks). Issue remediation cost estimates and timelines for each site. Prioritize 5–6 fully accessible sites to open by June 1 (Month 6.8 = 2027-05-02). For sites requiring remediation, develop a schedule and budget authorization for work to complete by May 31.

Responsible Body/Role: Cooling-center Operations Lead with an accessibility consultant or municipal disability-access officer (advisory role).

Suggested Timeframe: Accessibility audit completed by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); remediation plans finalized by Month 2 (2026-12-08).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Detailed accessibility audit report for each of 10 sites
  • Categorization of sites (fully accessible, minor remediation, unsuitable)
  • Remediation cost estimates and timelines per site
  • Site prioritization: 5–6 priority sites for June opening with no or minor work
  • Approved remediation budget and schedule

Dependencies:

  • Cooling-center Operations Lead hired and in post
  • Provisional facility-use agreements signed (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23)
  • Accessibility consultant or municipal accessibility office engaged

19. Transport Lead (Dispatch Coordinator) begins volunteer-driver recruitment campaign targeting retirees, charity staff, faith-group members and community volunteers. Partner with NGOs, faith organizations, municipal community centers and local media to advertise. Accept applications from October through January (Months 0–3 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08). Conduct vetting in monthly cohorts (background check, driving history, safeguarding screening, insurance verification). Target: 40 volunteer drivers (range 30–50), with ≥20 fully vetted and trained by Month 2 (2026-12-08), remainder by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Provide each volunteer with orientation on heat response, center locations, transport-request protocols, passenger safety and incident reporting.

Responsible Body/Role: Transport Lead / Dispatch Coordinator (external hire or interim coordinator from civil protection) with occupational health and volunteer-coordinator support.

Suggested Timeframe: Recruitment launched Month 0 (2026-10-08); applications accepted through January; vetting in batches (monthly cohorts beginning Month 1 = 2026-11-08); ≥20 fully trained by Month 2 (2026-12-08), remainder by Month 3 (2027-01-08).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Volunteer-recruitment campaign flyers and social-media posts
  • Volunteer application form and vetting checklist
  • Batch 1 vetting results (background checks passed/failed) by Month 1.8 (2026-12-02)
  • Volunteer driver insurance certificates and agreements
  • Volunteer orientation and training schedule
  • Volunteer roster with contact details and vehicle information

Dependencies:

  • Transport Lead hired or interim role assigned
  • Budget for volunteer expenses (mileage, fuel) and insurance confirmed

20. Outreach and Enrollment Lead develops heat-response outreach scripts (3–5 minute call format with escalation rules). Scripts should include: greeting and program introduction; identification of the resident's heat risk; description of cooling centers and transport support; consent confirmation for future contact; escalation triggers (signs of heat illness, social crisis, homelessness). Draft scripts in Spanish and test with focus groups of older residents (target: 10–15 participants) by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) to confirm clarity, cultural appropriateness and acceptability. Incorporate feedback and finalize scripts by Month 1.8 (2026-12-02). Translate core scripts into 4–6 identified non-official languages by Month 2 (2026-12-08) and conduct language-group focus testing.

Responsible Body/Role: Outreach and Enrollment Lead (external hire or interim coordinator) with partner-liaison officer, public-health nurse adviser and community language ambassadors (as they are recruited).

Suggested Timeframe: Draft scripts Month 1 (2026-11-08); focus-group testing Month 1.3–1.5 (2026-11-17 to 2026-11-30); revisions and translations Month 1.5–2 (2026-11-30 to 2026-12-08).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Heat-response call script (Spanish, v1.0)
  • Focus-group testing notes and feedback
  • Revised script incorporating feedback (v1.1)
  • Escalation decision-tree and escalation script (when to call EMS, when to refer to nurse line)
  • Scripts translated into 4–6 languages (draft versions for partner review)

Dependencies:

  • Outreach and Enrollment Lead hired or interim role assigned
  • GDPR legal review completed so scripts comply with consent and data-handling rules
  • Community partners (focus groups) identified

21. Home Kit Lead develops a household-targeting rubric to identify homes eligible for the 2,000-kit program. Rubric scoring (0–100 points): top-floor or poor insulation = 30 points; age ≥75 (or 65+ with self-declared chronic condition) = 25 points; living alone = 20 points; built before 1980 = 15 points; no air-conditioning = 10 points. Eligibility threshold = ≥60 points. Validate rubric against a sample of 50–100 enrolled high-risk residents from partner contact lists to confirm sensitivity and specificity. Assess GDPR compliance (ensure rubric does not infer protected health data beyond what residents have consented to share). Finalize rubric by Month 1.8 (2026-12-02) and pilot the targeting process on a sample of 200 households by Month 2 (2026-12-08).

Responsible Body/Role: Home Kit Lead / Installation Coordinator (external hire or interim coordinator) with Outreach and Enrollment Lead and an equity analyst or data coordinator.

Suggested Timeframe: Draft rubric Month 1 (2026-11-08); validation and GDPR check Month 1.3–1.5 (2026-11-17 to 2026-11-30); finalized rubric Month 1.8 (2026-12-02); pilot targeting Month 2 (2026-12-08).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Household-targeting rubric (scoring methodology, point weights, threshold)
  • GDPR compliance assessment for rubric
  • Validation-test results (sample of 50–100 households)
  • Pilot-targeting report (200 households scored and prioritized)

Dependencies:

  • Home Kit Lead hired or interim role assigned
  • Enrolled high-risk resident data from outreach partners available
  • GDPR legal review confirms data-handling scope

22. Incident commander and public-health deputy finalize the emergency-management operational structure in writing. Document: (1) alert-declaration process (forecast data receipt, threshold evaluation, decision authority, notification sequence); (2) daily SITREP and briefing schedule on alert days; (3) stand-down criteria and procedures (alert ends when forecast no longer meets thresholds and actual temperatures normal for 48 hours); (4) escalation hotline and incident-log procedures; (5) mutual-aid triggers with hospitals and EMS (e.g., notify at ≥1.5× historical average heat-related call volume); (6) handover coverage for multi-day events (backup incident commander, rotation of SITREP leads). Publish this as an operational playbook chapter. Conduct a tabletop scenario drill with the Operations Team (2 hours, Month 2 = 2026-12-08) to validate the process and identify gaps.

Responsible Body/Role: Incident commander with public-health deputy and operations lead (civil protection), supported by PMO coordinator.

Suggested Timeframe: Operational procedures documented by Month 1.8 (2026-12-02); tabletop drill conducted Month 2 (2026-12-08).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Alert-declaration and operational procedures document (SOP, flowchart, decision tree)
  • SITREP and briefing templates with sample data
  • Stand-down criteria and notification procedure
  • Mutual-aid trigger matrix (EMS/hospital notification thresholds)
  • Tabletop scenario drill after-action report with lessons and corrective actions

Dependencies:

  • Incident commander and operations leads designated
  • Alert thresholds set and approved by Steering Committee
  • Operations Team established and first meeting held

23. Procurement specialist places the first batch of purchase orders (30–40% of total kit volume, ≈600–800 kits) for cooling supplies (shading, fans, thermometers, hygrometers). Negotiate expedited delivery for February (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) to allow ≥6 weeks for installations before the first summer heat days (target June 1 = Month 6.8 = 2027-05-02). Lock in transport standby-retainer contract terms with taxi/accessible-transport operator if not already signed. Identify 2–3 backup suppliers for each kit category to mitigate supply-chain risk. Arrange secure interim storage (municipal facility or supply partner warehouse) for kits arriving in February–March.

Responsible Body/Role: Procurement specialist (0.5 FTE) with Home Kit Lead (once hired) and project coordinator.

Suggested Timeframe: First call-off orders placed by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14); transport contract signed by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14); backup suppliers identified by Month 1 (2026-11-08); storage arrangement confirmed by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Purchase orders for first kit batch (30–40% of 2,000 kits)
  • Signed transport/taxi standby-retainer contract with pricing and performance terms
  • Backup supplier contact list and pre-qualification documentation
  • Storage facility agreement and inventory-management protocol

Dependencies:

  • Procurement specs finalized and RFQs issued (Month 0.8–1 = 2026-11-01 to 2026-11-08)
  • Supplier bids evaluated and awards recommended (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23)
  • Budget authorization for purchase orders confirmed

24. Conduct a formal, comprehensive Steering Committee meeting (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) to review and make a go/no-go decision on the Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate. Gate criteria: (1) ≥8 of 10 cooling-center sites signed with named managers; (2) ≥50% of places in fully accessible sites; (3) transport retainer contract signed; (4) ≥20 volunteer drivers vetted; (5) heat helpline live (08:00–22:00 daily, 24-hour at Level 3) with a successful mock drill (5–8 simulated calls, ≥3 escalations handled correctly); (6) outreach training delivered to 50–80 partner and street-contact staff with ≥80% attendance and pass score; (7) 100% of tranche-1 procurement orders placed. Incident commander presents evidence for each criterion. Committee votes to pass, pass-with-conditions or fail, and approves any corrective actions if gate is not fully passed. Document decision.

Responsible Body/Role: Heat Response Steering Committee (majority vote, quorum 4 of 6 including Chair or Vice-Chair), with incident commander and lead-role representatives presenting evidence.

Suggested Timeframe: Month 2 (2026-12-08), scheduled 1 week in advance.

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Readiness-gate evidence summary (1-pager per criterion with supporting data)
  • Heat helpline mock-drill after-action report
  • Outreach training attendance and assessment results
  • Procurement status and order-confirmation list
  • Steering Committee decision minutes with formal vote
  • Go/no-go approval for proceeding to Month 4 (2027-02-08) scale gate and full operations

Dependencies:

  • All governance bodies operational and reporting metrics
  • Cooling centers, transport, phone line and outreach staff in place
  • Mock drills and training completed
  • Procurement ≥90% ordered

25. Immediately after Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate (whether passed or conditional), Evaluation Lead and university evaluation partner finalize the evaluation design and pre-register the analysis plan. Specify: baseline heat-related EMS and ED counts (obtained from hospitals by Month 1 = 2026-11-08, quality audited by Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23); comparison methodology (pilot vs. matched districts and prior years, aggregate counts only, no identifiable records); temperature-adjustment method; confidence-interval reporting; and plain-language statement of attribution limits. Data-processing agreement with hospitals, EMS and primary care is finalized; daily aggregate-count delivery test (validation pilot) scheduled for April (Month 6 = 2027-04-08). University partner publishes the pre-registered protocol on a registry (e.g., OSF) by Month 3 (2027-01-08).

Responsible Body/Role: Evaluation Lead (0.5–1 FTE, municipal or partner) and university evaluation partner (external, ≈€50k–80k contract).

Suggested Timeframe: Evaluation design finalized by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23); pre-registered protocol published by Month 3 (2027-01-08).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Finalized evaluation design document (comparison groups, statistical methods, attribution approach)
  • Data-processing agreement with hospitals/EMS/primary care
  • Pre-registered analysis plan (published on OSF or registry)
  • Baseline data-quality report and any limitations or caveats
  • Data-sharing infrastructure test plan (validation pilot for April)

Dependencies:

  • Baseline EMS and ED data obtained and quality-audited (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08)
  • University evaluation partner contracted and data-processing agreement signed
  • Steering Committee approved the evaluation scope

26. Recruit, vet and begin training 8–12 community-language ambassadors from identified migrant associations and communities. Ambassadors will be paid part-time staff (≈10–15 hours/week during alert season) responsible for: translating and culturally adapting materials; co-delivering phone-line interpretation support; accompanying door-knock teams in their own languages; staffing cooling-center welcome desks; and conducting focus-group testing of heat messages. Launch recruitment by Month 1 (2026-11-08) with a target start date of Month 1.8 (2026-12-02). Conduct vetting (background check, reference checks) and onboarding by Month 2 (2026-12-08). Provide ambassadors with a 2-day orientation on heat illness, program goals, escalation rules and confidentiality by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23).

Responsible Body/Role: Outreach and Enrollment Lead with partner-liaison officer and community association representatives.

Suggested Timeframe: Recruitment launched Month 1 (2026-11-08); ambassadors hired and onboarded by Month 2 (2026-12-08); orientation and training Month 2–2.5 (2026-12-08 to 2026-12-23).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Ambassador recruitment flyers in community languages and via partner channels
  • Ambassador job descriptions and role expectations
  • Selected ambassador list with language coverage and community affiliations
  • Background-check and reference-check documentation
  • Ambassador orientation and training materials (translated)
  • Signed ambassador agreements and NDA/confidentiality documents

Dependencies:

  • Outreach and Enrollment Lead hired
  • Target language groups identified (4–6 languages by Month 0 = 2026-10-08)
  • Migrant community associations or NGO partners engaged
  • Budget for ambassador stipends and training confirmed

27. Legal lead convenes a partner compliance-and-briefing session with representatives from all ≥4 key intermediary partners (housing associations, social services, NGOs, pharmacies). Agenda: (1) present the finalized data-processing agreements and obtain signatures if not yet signed; (2) brief all partner staff on GDPR obligations, data-protection rules, confidentiality and incident-reporting procedures; (3) distribute outreach scripts, escalation protocols and call-logging templates; (4) confirm partner call-target commitments for the remainder of the season; (5) establish weekly/bi-weekly partner-liaison contact schedule; (6) answer partner questions on consent, data-handling and liability. Document attendance and sign-off from each partner. Provide partners with training materials (slide deck, handout) and digital resources (template call logs, escalation guides).

Responsible Body/Role: Legal lead (0.5–1 FTE) with Outreach and Enrollment Lead, partner-liaison officer and GDPR counsel (advisors).

Suggested Timeframe: Briefing session conducted by Month 2 (2026-12-08); attendance confirmation and sign-off by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Signed data-processing agreements from all partners (or documented timeline for final signature)
  • GDPR and confidentiality briefing slides and handout materials
  • Outreach script and escalation protocol distributed to all partner staff (attendance log)
  • Call-logging template and incident-reporting form provided to partners
  • Partner commitment letter (call targets, data-handling, escalation)
  • Weekly liaison contact schedule published

Dependencies:

  • DPA templates finalized and customized per partner type (Month 1.3 = 2026-11-17)
  • Partners have reviewed DPAs and provided feedback
  • Outreach scripts and escalation protocols finalized (Month 1.8 = 2026-12-02)
  • Legal lead and GDPR counsel available for briefing

28. Heating-systems and procurement coordinator confirms the delivery schedule and logistics for the first batch of cooling kits (30–40% of 2,000, ≈600–800 kits ordered at Month 1.2 = 2026-11-14). Negotiate expedited shipping for February arrival. Arrange intake inspection and inventory verification upon delivery. Set up secure interim storage with climate control (to prevent fan degradation) and an inventory-management system (tracking kit location, condition, hand-off to installers). Prepare a kit-distribution protocol: priority allocation to highest-scoring households (from Home Kit Lead's targeting rubric), geographic batching by neighborhood for installer efficiency, and consent verification before each household's installation is scheduled.

Responsible Body/Role: Procurement specialist (0.5 FTE), Home Kit Lead and logistics coordinator (may be shared with general municipal logistics).

Suggested Timeframe: Delivery logistics finalized by Month 2 (2026-12-08); storage facility prepared by Month 3 (2027-01-08); first kits received ≈Month 4 (2027-02-08).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Kit delivery schedule and shipment confirmations
  • Storage facility access and inventory-management protocol
  • Kit-distribution sequencing and neighborhood/household priority list
  • Installation-scheduling process (consent verification, scheduling letters to residents)
  • Inventory-tracking system and daily intake log

Dependencies:

  • Purchase order for first kit batch placed (Month 1.2 = 2026-11-14)
  • Storage facility identified and contracted (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23)
  • Home Kit Lead hired and targeting rubric finalized (Month 1.8 = 2026-12-02)

29. Establish the heat-response phone line and dispatch-coordination system. Procure or configure telephony infrastructure (dedicated phone line, call queuing, call recording if permitted by Spanish law, call transfer to interpretation services). Set up call-tracking software (shared spreadsheet with partner-liaison officer, or a secure cloud platform) to log all incoming calls, resident details, requests, responses and escalations. Recruit 2–3 FTE phone-line operators (1 permanent + 1–2 surge/part-time) by Month 1.8 (2026-12-02). Conduct training (call scripts, escalation triggers, de-escalation, interpreter coordination, incident reporting) by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23). Conduct a 4–6 hour mock-call drill with 5–8 simulated calls including escalation cases (heat illness, social crisis) by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23) and document results.

Responsible Body/Role: Outreach and Enrollment Lead (phone-line owner) with transport lead (for dispatch coordination), PMO coordinator and occupational health.

Suggested Timeframe: Telephony infrastructure procured and installed by Month 1.8 (2026-12-02); operators hired by Month 1.8 (2026-12-02); training and mock drill completed by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23); system live and operational by Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate.

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Phone-line setup with call-queuing and escalation features (tested)
  • Call-tracking system (spreadsheet template or platform)
  • Trained phone-line operators (employment contracts, training certificates)
  • Call-handling and escalation SOP
  • Mock-call drill report (5–8 simulated calls, ≥3 escalations, success rate ≥80%)
  • Go-live checklist and 24-hour on-call support plan

Dependencies:

  • Budget for phone-line setup and operators confirmed
  • Outreach scripts and escalation protocols finalized
  • Interpretation services contract signed (external provider or municipal arrangement)

30. Recruit, vet and begin training handypersons (target 10 FTE for Months 4–7 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-05-17) responsible for installing cooling kits (exterior shading, fans, thermometers). Vet candidates for occupational health and safety certification (or willingness to obtain it), relevant trade experience, background check and occupational-health clearance. Provide each handyperson with a 1-day safety-and-installation training covering: (1) electrical safety and fan-installation safety; (2) fan-use guidance for residents (directional airflow, outdoor-air intake); (3) shading and wind-resistance assessment; (4) building-code compliance checks; (5) customer communication and consent; (6) incident reporting and feedback. Training conducted by Month 3.5 (2027-01-23). Arrange tools, equipment and safety gear by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Finalize handyperson employment or contract terms by Month 3 (2027-01-08) with start date ≥Month 4 (2027-02-08).

Responsible Body/Role: Home Kit Lead / Installation Coordinator with occupational health and a qualified trades supervisor or external training provider.

Suggested Timeframe: Recruitment launched Month 2 (2026-12-08); hiring completed by Month 2.8 (2027-01-01); training conducted Month 3–3.5 (2027-01-08 to 2027-01-23).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Handyperson job description and qualification criteria
  • Recruitment announcements and applications (target 10 FTE)
  • Vetting documentation (background checks, trade certifications, occupational-health clearance)
  • Handyperson employment or service contracts (10)
  • 1-day safety-and-installation training curriculum and materials
  • Training attendance and assessment results (target ≥80% pass)
  • Handyperson roster, contact details and insurance information

Dependencies:

  • Home Kit Lead hired
  • Budget for handyperson wages/contracts confirmed
  • Kit components and installation specifications finalized
  • Occupational health and safety requirements confirmed

31. PMO coordinator drafts the full-system operational drill protocol for Month 3.2 (2027-01-14). Drill will simulate a Level 2 or Level 3 alert lasting 4–6 hours, activating all systems: cooling centers open to full capacity, transport dispatch handles ≥30 simulated requests (including ≥5 wheelchair-user priority cases targeting 30-min pickup), outreach phone line receives ≥20 calls (mixture of enrollment inquiries, requests for transport, escalation cases), and all partner outreach staff place sample calls (≥300 attempts across all partners). Drill will test: center staffing and operations readiness, accessibility compliance, transport dispatch speed and volunteer/taxi coordination, phone-line call handling and escalation, heat-illness recognition and EMS escalation, and inter-organizational communication. Draft evaluation checklist and success criteria (80% center hours, 60% outreach success, <45 min transport time). Publish protocol to all participants by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23).

Responsible Body/Role: PMO coordinator (project manager) with incident commander, Cooling-center Operations Lead, Transport Lead, Outreach Lead and all governance-body leads.

Suggested Timeframe: Draft protocol completed by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23); drill conducted Month 3.2 (2027-01-14); after-action report completed by Month 3.5 (2027-01-23).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Detailed drill protocol (scenario, timeline, participant roles, success criteria)
  • Drill evaluation checklist and gate-metric data-collection forms
  • Participant briefing and instructions (distributed to all staff and partners)
  • Drill execution log (timeline of events, decisions, issues noted)
  • Drill after-action report (center-hours delivered, outreach contact success rate, transport response times, escalation cases handled correctly)
  • Corrective-action list with owners and completion deadlines

Dependencies:

  • All governance bodies operational and reporting metrics
  • Alert thresholds, operational procedures and escalation protocols finalized
  • Cooling centers, transport, phone line and outreach staff in place or nearly in place

32. Conduct the full-system operational drill on a specified date (Month 3.2 = 2027-01-14) with all governance bodies and operational teams activated. Incident commander declares a simulated Level 2 alert (forecast high ≥35°C and low ≥22°C for 2 consecutive days). Operations Team convenes at 07:00, SITREP at 08:30, partner briefing at 09:30. Cooling centers open their doors at 10:00 with full staffing; transport dispatch stands by with volunteer drivers and taxi operator on standby; phone line opens at 08:00 with operators and (if possible) live interpretation services. Outreach partners place sample calls (target ≥300 attempts across all partners, ≥60% connection success rate). Transport requests are generated (target ≥30 requests, ≥5 wheelchair-user priority cases). After 4–6 hours of continuous operation, incident commander declares stand-down at 16:00. All teams complete incident logs and action-item forms. A debrief is held the same day (17:00–18:30) with all lead roles present.

Responsible Body/Role: Incident commander (exercise controller) with Heat Response Operations Team, all governance-body leads and operational staff (Cooling-center managers, transport dispatchers, phone-line operators, outreach partners).

Suggested Timeframe: Drill conducted Month 3.2 (2027-01-14); debrief completed same day; after-action report drafted within 3 days (by Month 3.3 = 2027-01-17).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Drill execution log with timeline and decision record
  • Center-hours delivered by site (target ≥80% of planned hours)
  • Outreach contact attempts and success rates by partner (target ≥60%)
  • Transport requests received, response times and wheelchair-user accommodation (target <45 min average, <30 min for priority cases)
  • Heat-illness and escalation cases handled (number and outcome)
  • Debrief notes and participant feedback
  • Incident log of issues, gaps and corrective actions

Dependencies:

  • Drill protocol finalized and distributed to all participants
  • All operational systems (phone line, cooling centers, transport dispatch) live and tested
  • Cooling-center staff, transport dispatchers and operators trained and on-call

33. Incident commander and key leads review drill after-action report (completed Month 3.5 = 2027-01-23) and identify all corrective actions needed before the Month 4 (2027-02-08) scale gate. Corrective actions fall into categories: (1) staffing gaps (additional operators, volunteers, center support staff); (2) procedural improvements (revised escalation rules, faster transport routing); (3) technology fixes (phone-line call queuing, dispatch software); (4) training needs (repeat training for staff who did not meet standards). Assign owner and completion deadline (target ≤Month 3.8 = 2027-02-01, within 2 weeks of drill debrief) for each action. Close-out checklist confirms all actions are verified complete by Month 3.9 (2027-02-04). Document closure with evidence (training records, system logs, staffing confirmations).

Responsible Body/Role: PMO coordinator (action-tracking owner) with incident commander and all governance-body leads who own specific corrective actions.

Suggested Timeframe: After-action report completed Month 3.5 (2027-01-23); corrective-action plan finalized Month 3.6 (2027-01-26); actions executed and closed by Month 3.9 (2027-02-04).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Corrective-action list with owners, deadlines and completion evidence
  • Staffing adjustments (additional hires or schedule changes) documented
  • Revised procedures or escalation rules published to all staff
  • Technology fixes or system improvements validated
  • Repeat training or skill assessments completed and documented
  • Closure checklist signed off by each action owner

Dependencies:

  • Drill after-action report completed and shared with all leads
  • Sufficient budget and staffing flexibility to execute corrective actions
  • Steering Committee monitoring of closure status

34. Conduct the Steering Committee's Month 4 (2027-02-08) scale-gate review and funding-release decision. Incident commander presents comprehensive evidence for the four scale-gate criteria: (1) ≥80% of planned cooling-center hours delivered in the drill; (2) ≥60% contact success from ≥300 outreach attempts; (3) mean transport time <45 min over ≥30 requests (including ≥5 wheelchair users); (4) 100% of after-action corrective actions from the drill closed and verified. Additionally present: status of kit procurement and delivery (target ≥40% by Month 4 = 2027-02-08), handyperson training completion (all 10 trained and on-contract), partner compliance audit (GDPR, call-logging, data protection). If all criteria are met, Committee formally approves the release of the full €1.5M tranche-2 funding. If 1 criterion fails but evidence is incomplete (e.g., insufficient natural heat events by Month 4 = 2027-02-08 to validate gates in real conditions), Committee approves conditional release: €750k (50%) immediately, remainder after a re-test in Month 5 (2027-03-08) using real-world heat data. If 2+ criteria fail, Committee does not release tranche-2; corrective actions and re-test planned for Month 5 (2027-03-08) at the earliest. Document formal vote and decision.

Responsible Body/Role: Heat Response Steering Committee (majority vote, quorum 4 of 6 including Chair or Vice-Chair), with incident commander and governance-body leads presenting evidence.

Suggested Timeframe: Month 4 (2027-02-08), scheduled at least 1 week in advance; decision documented same day.

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Scale-gate evidence package (center hours, outreach success rate, transport response times, corrective-action closure, kit procurement status)
  • Steering Committee meeting minutes with formal vote on each criterion
  • Formal funding-release decision letter or memo (full release, conditional release, or no release)
  • Communiqué to all staff and partners confirming gate decision and next steps

Dependencies:

  • Drill completed and after-action report finalized (Month 3.5 = 2027-01-23)
  • All corrective actions closed and verified (Month 3.9 = 2027-02-04)
  • Kit procurement on track (≥40% delivered or in-transit by Month 4 = 2027-02-08)
  • Handyperson recruitment and training completed

35. Following the Month 4 (2027-02-08) scale-gate decision (whether full, conditional or no release), the Steering Committee formally approves and the incident commander confirms the operational readiness of all governance bodies to enter the live operational season (Months 6.8–11.8 = 2027-04-23 to 2027-09-30). Each governance body lead submits a readiness certification covering: (1) staffing (all roles filled, trained, on-call rosters confirmed); (2) systems (phone line, dispatch, cooling centers, partner call-tracking operational and tested); (3) supplies (kits in storage or arriving, handyperson ready to deploy, shelter supplies stocked); (4) protocols (escalation, GDPR, incident reporting, stand-down all documented and drilled); (5) partner commitment (all intermediaries' MOUs signed, staff trained, call targets confirmed). Incident commander and Steering Committee Chair sign off on the overall go-live. A public announcement and pre-season communications campaign (flyers, radio, pharmacy posters, community briefings) launch by Month 6.5 (2027-04-23).

Responsible Body/Role: Incident commander and all governance-body leads, with Steering Committee Chair oversight.

Suggested Timeframe: Readiness certifications submitted by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23); Steering Committee review and go-live approval by Month 5 (2027-03-08).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Readiness certification from each governance body (staffing, systems, supplies, protocols, partner commitment)
  • Consolidated operational-readiness checklist
  • Steering Committee formal approval and go-live authorization
  • Public announcement of program launch (press release, municipal website, social media)
  • Pre-season campaign materials (flyers, radio spots, pharmacy posters, community briefings)

Dependencies:

  • All staffing hired and trained
  • All systems tested and operational
  • Cooling-center accessibility audit and remediation completed
  • Kit procurement and handyperson training on schedule

36. From Month 5 onward (2027-03-08), governance bodies transition from setup and gate-preparation mode to regular operational reporting and rhythm. Monthly Steering Committee meetings (standing: first Monday of each month 14 = 2027-12-08:00, Months 5–12 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-10-08) review: (1) financial forecasts and budget burn; (2) staffing and fatigue status; (3) partner engagement and capacity; (4) procurement delivery status; (5) risk register; (6) preparation for summer season (June–September). Operations Team maintains weekly meetings on non-alert days (Mondays 14:00, Months 5–8 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-06-08) and daily standups with SITREP (08:30) and partner briefing (09:30) during any alert periods. Sub-groups (Cooling Centers, Outreach, Transport, Home Kits) establish their own meeting cadences: Cooling Centers weekly (Tuesdays 14:00 during setup, transitioning to ad-hoc during season); Outreach weekly (Wednesdays 14:00, then daily during alert days); Transport weekly (Thursdays 14:00, then daily during alerts); Home Kits weekly (Mondays 10:00 during installation phase = Months 4–7 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-05-17). Data and evaluation group meets monthly (Fridays 14:00).

Responsible Body/Role: Incident commander (chair of Operations Team), Steering Committee members, and all governance-body leads.

Suggested Timeframe: Governance transition to regular rhythm by Month 5 (2027-03-08); sustained through end of project Month 12 (2027-10-08).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Monthly Steering Committee meeting calendar and standing agendas published
  • Weekly Operations Team and sub-group meeting schedules published
  • Meeting-cadence documentation in the operational playbook
  • Monthly financial and risk-management dashboards prepared by PMO for Steering Committee review

  • Operational systems live and stable

37. From Month 8 onward (2027-06-08), the Evaluation Lead, data analyst and university evaluation partner begin drafting the final Heat Response Playbook, cost model, and evaluation report. Playbook chapters include: (1) strategic decisions and rationale (Alert Trigger Ladder, Refuge Network, Intermediary-Held Lists, Mobility Support, Command Structure, Home Kits, Health Integration, Worker Protection, Communications, Language Access, Evaluation); (2) SOPs and checklists (alert declaration, cooling-center operations, transport dispatch, phone-line handling, escalation, de-escalation, incident reporting, stand-down); (3) procurement and staffing templates (job descriptions, supplier specs, contract terms, partner MOUs); (4) lessons learned and adaptations (what worked, what was hard, what to change for Year 2); (5) unit costs and scaling assumptions (€ per person enrolled, per center-hour, per kit, per transport trip, per staff FTE). University partner analyzes operational and outcome data (EMS, ED, mortality proxies) against the pre-registered protocol. Playbook draft shared with peer EU cities for comment by Month 11 (2027-09-08); final version and evaluation report delivered by Month 12 (2027-10-08).

Responsible Body/Role: Evaluation Lead (0.5–1 FTE) with Playbook Editor (may be Evaluation Lead or separate role), university evaluation partner, and incident commander/governance leads (content contributors).

Suggested Timeframe: Playbook drafting begins Month 8 (2027-06-08); section drafts submitted by Month 10 (2027-08-08); peer-city review Month 11 (2027-09-08); final version Month 12 (2027-10-08).

  • Data and evaluation report (preliminary by Month 11 = 2027-09-08, final Month 12 = 2027-10-08)
  • Year-2 roadmap (expansion priorities, elements to discontinue, estimated budget for Year 2)

  • Health-system outcome data (EMS, ED, mortality) collected and analyzed

Conduct a final Steering Committee meeting (Month 12 = 2027-10-08) to review and formally approve the Heat Response Playbook, scaling cost model, evaluation report and Year-2 roadmap for public release. Committee considers: (1) Are the lessons learned and adaptations clearly documented? (2) Is the cost model transparent and defensible for other EU cities? (3) Are attribution caveats and limitations honestly stated? (4) Is the Year-2 roadmap realistic and funded? Committee votes to approve for publication. Incident commander prepares a final project close-out report (budget reconciliation, staffing outcomes, partner feedback, next-steps). A final debrief meeting is held with all governance-body leads and key partners to capture verbal feedback and recognize contributions. Public launch event (press conference, municipal briefing, dissemination to peer cities and EU networks) scheduled for Month 12 (2027-10-08) or soon after.

Responsible Body/Role: Heat Response Steering Committee (majority vote), with incident commander, Evaluation Lead and playbook editor presenting final deliverables.

Suggested Timeframe: Final Steering Committee meeting Month 12 (2027-10-08); public launch by end of Month 12 (2027-10-08) or early Month 13 (2027-11-08).

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Public-release press release and communications pack
  • Heat Response Playbook published (PDF and possibly online portal)
  • Scaling cost model published with replicability guidance for other EU cities
  • Evaluation report published with peer-reviewed or audited findings

Dependencies:

  • All draft deliverables (Playbook, cost model, evaluation report, roadmap) completed and reviewed by Steering Committee by Month 11 (2027-09-08)
  • Peer-city feedback incorporated (Month 11 = 2027-09-08)
  • University evaluation partner's final report submitted
  • Budget reconciliation and staffing outcomes documented

Decision Escalation Matrix

Month 4 (2027-02-08) Scale-Gate Failure or Unmeasurable Evidence Escalation Level: Heat Response Steering Committee Approval Process: Majority vote (4 of 6 members including Chair or Vice-Chair). Steering Committee reviews gate-measurement evidence (drill data, real-world heat events, corrective-action closure). If gates are failed, the Committee votes on: (1) no release of €1.5M tranche-2 and mandatory corrective re-test by Month 5 (2027-03-08), or (2) conditional 50% release (€750k) if evidence is incomplete due to cool season, with final decision after Month 5 (2027-03-08) re-test. If gates are passed, full €1.5M is approved for immediate release. Rationale: The Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate decision gates control €1.5M funding release (43% of total budget) and determines operational scale for the critical May–September heat season. A failed gate triggers a budget crisis (€200–400k cash gap) and potential service reductions mid-summer. The decision affects public safety, partner continuity, and program credibility. Only the Steering Committee has authority to approve or withhold conditional funding and escalate unmet gates to corrective re-planning. Negative Consequences: Non-release or delayed release of €1.5M by 4–8 weeks would force closure of 25–40% of planned cooling-center hours and transport capacity by August, coinciding with peak summer heat risk. Estimated harm: 500–1,500 fewer high-risk residents reached, 15–25% reduction in outreach contact success, loss of volunteer driver confidence and partner engagement. Reputational damage: audit and funder scrutiny if gates are failed; media coverage if residents are turned away from overcrowded centers during a heat wave.

Budget Overrun or Contingency-Reserve Drawdown Exceeding €20k Escalation Level: Heat Response Steering Committee Approval Process: Incident commander submits a budget-reforecast report documenting: (1) spending by category to date, (2) variance from budget, (3) root cause, (4) corrective action (reduce scope, reallocate budget, draw contingency). Steering Committee reviews and votes to approve the reforecast and contingency drawdown (if >€20k requested). Large drawdowns (>€50k) require documented justification (e.g., supplier price spike, staff absence surge, emergency remediation) and may trigger supplier or scope review. Rationale: The total €3.5M budget is hard-capped with limited contingency (€280k = 8%). Overruns threaten both gates and final deliverables. Overruns may stem from procurement delays requiring expedited shipping, staffing gaps forcing extended taxi retainers, or facility remediation cost growth. Steering Committee authority ensures spending decisions are visible, documented and aligned with strategic priorities (gates > playbook > home kits, in case trade-offs are needed). Negative Consequences: Uncontrolled spending exhausts contingency by Month 6 (2027-04-08), leaving no buffer for summer emergencies (staff illness surge, supplier failure, facility damage). If €280k is drawn and overruns continue, tranche-2 release is at risk. Cumulative overrun of 15% (€525k) creates a funding shortfall of €245k that cannot be covered, forcing either mid-season service cuts or funder request for supplementary funds (likely denied if funder is a municipal council with fixed budgets). Reputational cost: audit finding of budget mismanagement, loss of funder confidence for Year-2 proposal.

GDPR Compliance Breach or Partner Data-Handling Violation Escalation Level: Heat Response Steering Committee Approval Process: Legal and GDPR Lead (with external GDPR legal counsel) investigates any reported or discovered breach. Assessment includes: data scope affected, number of residents, confidentiality risk, partner culpability. Legal team determines if breach must be reported to the Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) within 48 hours (if >100 residents at high risk or health data exposed). Steering Committee is briefed within 24 hours of discovery. If breach is serious (100+ residents, deliberate misuse, regulator notification required), Committee may authorize: (1) contract suspension of breaching partner, (2) resident notification campaign, (3) enhanced oversight, (4) corrective-action plan with funder notification. Decision is documented and, if required, escalated to municipal legal counsel and city council. Rationale: The program relies on intermediary-held contact lists and partner compliance with GDPR and data-protection obligations. A breach (e.g., partner leaks resident contact details or health flags to a third party, or unauthorized contact outside the agreed scope) undermines resident trust, violates the legal basis for the program, and exposes the city to regulatory fines and litigation. GDPR compliance is a hard constraint: failure to resolve a breach promptly risks program suspension or funder withdrawal. Negative Consequences: Serious breach (100+ residents, health data exposed) triggers 48-hour AEPD notification requirement and potential regulatory investigation. Estimated fine under GDPR Article 83: €10k–€50k (minor breach) to €100k–€500k+ (serious breach involving health data). Resident notification and credit-monitoring costs: €5k–€20k. Partner contract termination reduces outreach reach by 10–20% (500–1,000 residents). Loss of public trust and media coverage of 'data leak' damages program credibility and Year-2 funding prospects. Estimated total reputational and financial cost: €100k–€750k.

Critical Incident at a Cooling Center (Serious Injury, Death, Major Safety Failure) Escalation Level: Heat Response Steering Committee (if serious or reputational impact); immediate notification to incident commander and chair within hours Approval Process: Cooling-Center Operations Lead reports incident to incident commander immediately. Incident commander convenes an emergency review (within 24 hours) with operations lead, legal counsel and occupational health to assess: (1) cause (staffing gap, equipment failure, medical emergency, accessibility failure); (2) liability and insurance coverage; (3) immediate corrective action (site closure, additional staffing, equipment repair); (4) public communication and incident disclosure; (5) regulatory reporting (to occupational safety authority if staff injury, to municipal health authority if resident harm). Steering Committee is notified same day if incident involves death, serious injury, or reputational crisis (media attention likely). Committee may authorize: (a) site temporary closure and remediation, (b) external incident investigation, (c) public statement and transparency, (d) enhanced insurance or legal defense. If fatality occurs and program is blamed, funder and city council are notified immediately and Steering Committee meets within 48 hours to decide continuation. Rationale: A serious incident (death, heat-stroke hospitalization, fall, assault) at a cooling center creates immediate liability, regulatory exposure and reputational crisis. The center is municipally managed and staffed; the city is liable for duty of care. Rapid escalation ensures legal protection, incident documentation, corrective action and transparent communication. Transparency and swift action reduce legal and reputational risk; cover-up or delay amplifies damage. Negative Consequences: Serious injury or death at a center followed by delayed or poor response triggers: (1) litigation by resident/family for negligence, seeking €50k–€500k+ damages; (2) media coverage ('municipal heat program fails to protect resident') damaging public trust; (3) occupational safety regulator investigation if staff injured; (4) funder loss of confidence and Year-2 funding denial; (5) city council political pressure to defund or restructure the program; (6) partner and volunteer recruitment collapse due to reputational damage. Estimated cost: €200k–€1M (legal defense, settlement, lost funding, staff replacement).

Volunteer Driver or Outreach Staff Safety Incident (Assault, Abuse, Safeguarding Concern) Escalation Level: Heat Response Steering Committee; immediate escalation to incident commander and occupational health Approval Process: Transport Lead or Outreach Lead reports incident to incident commander and occupational health within 2 hours. Occupational health conducts immediate welfare check and offers counseling/support. HR coordinator and legal counsel assess: (1) whether police/authorities should be notified (assault, threat); (2) incident documentation and log; (3) staff/volunteer leave entitlements and duty-of-care obligations; (4) insurance coverage; (5) safeguarding and volunteer-management protocol review. If incident indicates systemic safeguarding failure (multiple incidents, inadequate training, poor vetting), incident commander escalates to Steering Committee within 24 hours for governance-level decision on: (a) safeguarding protocol audit and retraining, (b) volunteer recruitment pause and re-vetting, (c) additional supervision and insurance requirements, (d) external safeguarding review if serious or repeated incidents. Rationale: Volunteers and staff are municipal program representatives and are exposed to vulnerable residents (elderly, isolated, potentially hostile). Assaults, abuse or safeguarding breaches create duty-of-care obligations, legal liability, and staff safety risks. Swift incident response protects staff welfare, fulfills legal obligations and identifies systemic issues (poor training, insufficient vetting, inadequate supervision) before they recur. Negative Consequences: Unaddressed staff safety incident leads to: (1) volunteer or staff resignation, reducing dispatch and outreach capacity by 5–15%; (2) retained trauma and reduced effectiveness of affected staff; (3) reputation damage affecting future volunteer recruitment; (4) litigation if staff/volunteer claims negligence or inadequate safeguarding; (5) occupational health regulator finding if incident indicates systematic risk. Cumulative impact of 2–3 incidents without remediation could force program pause or external safeguarding takeover. Estimated cost per serious incident: €10k–€50k (legal, counseling, recruitment replacement).

Procurement or Supply-Chain Failure Threatening Month 2 (2026-12-08) Readiness Gate or Home-Kit Deployment Deadline Escalation Level: Heat Response Steering Committee (if delay exceeds 4 weeks or forces budget contingency drawdown >€50k) Approval Process: Procurement specialist and Home Kit Lead (or Cooling-Center Operations Lead) report supply-chain risk to incident commander within 5 working days of discovery. Incident commander convenes emergency review with PMO coordinator, lead role and legal counsel to assess: (1) root cause (supplier bankruptcy, production delay, shipping disruption, quality issue); (2) impact (which gate is at risk, delay duration, cost of expedite/backup supplier); (3) corrective action options (accelerate delivery, use backup supplier, reduce scope); (4) budget impact (does contingency or scope cut avoidable). If delay exceeds 3 weeks or remediation requires >€50k contingency drawdown, incident commander escalates to Steering Committee within 24 hours with: (a) delay timeline and gate-impact assessment, (b) corrective-action options ranked by cost and speed, (c) recommendation (e.g., pay 15% premium for expedite, or defer non-critical items to Month 5 = 2027-03-08). Committee votes on approval and any scope trade-offs (e.g., reduce home-kit count to prioritize cooling centers). Rationale: Cooling kits, transport contracts and center fit-out are on the critical path to the Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate and the May–June summer season. Delays >4 weeks push kit installation or transport readiness into June or July, missing the peak early-summer heat risk and failing gates. Escalation ensures visibility of supply-chain risks, timely use of contingency funds for expedited delivery, and if necessary, scope trade-offs approved by leadership rather than ad-hoc cuts. Negative Consequences: Supply-chain failure causing >6-week delay in kits or transport (e.g., supplier bankruptcy, shipping port disruption) means home interventions cannot be installed before June heat events, reducing estimated mortality reduction by 15–25%. Transport readiness slip forces reliance on taxi-only model (+€150–250k), cutting home-kit budget by €150–250k (500–1,000 fewer kits). Cascading impacts: Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate fails due to incomplete procurement; Month 4 (2027-02-08) scale gate fails due to low home-kit installation numbers; €1.5M tranche-2 is not released on schedule; program enters summer under-resourced. Estimated total cost of 6-week delay: €150–250k contingency drawdown + 15–25% reduced mortality protection + reputational damage (gates failed despite advance planning).

Monitoring Progress

1. Gate-Metric and Operational-KPI Tracking (Month 2 = 2026-12-08 Readiness, Month 4 = 2027-02-08 Scale, Seasonal Performance)

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Gate-Measurement Checklist (Excel/shared spreadsheet)
  • Cooling-Center Hours and Occupancy Log (daily site-by-site tracking)
  • Transport Dispatch Log (request-by-request response-time tracking)
  • Outreach Contact-Attempt and Success-Rate Spreadsheet (by partner, daily)
  • PMO Operations Dashboard (consolidated weekly summary)

Frequency: Daily during alert days (Months 6.8-11.8 = 2027-04-23 to 2027-09-30); weekly on non-alert days during setup (Months 1-5 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-03-08); consolidated monthly for steering committee review.

Responsible Role: PMO Coordinator and Incident Commander, with daily data collection from Cooling-Center Operations Lead, Transport Lead and Outreach Lead.

Adaptation Process: Weekly Operations Team review (Mondays 14:00, non-alert Months 1-5 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-03-08) identifies metric shortfalls (center hours <80%, outreach success <60%, transport time >45 min); incident commander authorizes corrective actions: additional staffing, script revision, route re-optimization, escalation support. Monthly reports to Steering Committee flag trends requiring budget reallocation or scope adjustment. At Month 2 (2026-12-08) and Month 4 (2027-02-08), consolidated gate-evidence package is prepared for formal go/no-go decision.

Adaptation Trigger: Month 2 (2026-12-08) Readiness Gate: if any of the 7 readiness criteria unmet, incident commander convenes 24-hour corrective-action meeting and reports to Steering Committee; if criteria cannot be closed by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), gate is flagged as fail-at-risk. Month 4 (2027-02-08) Scale Gate: if center-hours or outreach-success or transport-time fail the thresholds, no release of tranche-2 €1.5M (triggering €200-400k cash gap); if evidence is insufficient due to cool season, conditional 50% release (€750k) and re-test at Month 5 (2027-03-08). Real-time during season: if transport time rises above 45 min for >1 consecutive alert day, transport lead escalates to incident commander within 2 hours; if persistence >3 days, escalates to Steering Committee as gate-failure risk.

2. Critical Success Factor Tracking: Cooling-Refuge Network Reach and Accessibility (Equity and Access)

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Site-Coverage Map and Equity-Reach Analysis (GIS if available, or spreadsheet with neighborhood postcode data)
  • Cooling-Center Occupancy and Demographics Spreadsheet (age, gender, neighborhood, language, disability accommodation)
  • Accessibility Audit Checklist and Remediation-Tracking Log (per site)
  • Equity Metrics Dashboard (% of target 65+ reached, % from top-deprivation neighborhoods, % in fully accessible sites, % with language support)

Frequency: Monthly during setup (Months 1-5 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-03-08) to confirm site readiness and accessibility; weekly during season (Months 6.8-11.8 = 2027-04-23 to 2027-09-30) to track occupancy by neighborhood and demographic; final equity-coverage summary at Month 12 (2027-10-08).

Responsible Role: Cooling-Center Operations Lead and an Equity Analyst or Data Coordinator (0.5 FTE), reporting to incident commander.

Adaptation Process: Monthly Operations Team review compares actual occupancy and demographics against targets (≥70% of enrolled residents within 800 m; ≥50% of places in fully accessible sites; ≥5% of users identified as non-official-language speaker or wheelchair user). If a site shows low utilization (<20% occupancy on alert days) or if a neighborhood is under-represented (≤20% of expected enrollees), Cooling-Center Operations Lead recommends: (1) extended hours or special programming at underused sites, (2) targeted outreach to under-represented neighborhoods, (3) transport-priority deployment to sites serving highest-need areas. Accessibility shortfalls (e.g., wheelchair users turned away) trigger immediate site remediation or closure; inaccessible sites are closed until remediation is complete (≤4 weeks, ≤€10k).

Adaptation Trigger: Site occupancy <20% over 2 consecutive alert days → Operations Lead meets with site manager within 24 hours to identify barriers (location, hours, comfort, marketing); adjust hours, transport routing, or outreach targeting within 1 week. Site accessibility failure (wheelchair user cannot access toilet, quiet room unavailable, stairs block entry) → reported by center staff or observed in accessibility spot-check; if not immediately remediable, site is closed to new entrants and referrals diverted to accessible sites within 4 hours. Geographic equity gap (highest-deprivation neighborhoods contribute <30% of enrollees by Month 6 = 2027-04-08) → Outreach Lead and partner-liaison officer launch targeted street-team and partner recruitment in those neighborhoods by Month 6.5 (2027-04-23); if coverage gap persists to Month 7 (2027-05-08), incident commander re-allocates outreach resources or requests additional partner commitments.

3. Critical Success Factor Tracking: Outreach Enrollment and Contact Success (60% Gate and Equity Reach)

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Partner Call-Logging Spreadsheet (calls attempted, calls connected, consent obtained, reasons for no-contact, language of contact)
  • Enrollment Registry by Partner and Neighborhood (tracked in intermediary systems; city receives aggregate counts only, GDPR-compliant)
  • Outreach-Success Rate Calculation (success = call connected + information provided or referral accepted; gate = ≥60%)
  • No-Wrong-Door Tracking (phone-line and in-person intake at centers; separate count from partner-based outreach)

Frequency: Daily during alert days to track active outreach; weekly during setup (Months 1-5 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-03-08) to validate scripts and partner readiness; real-time dashboard (rolling 7-day average) during season (Months 6.8-11.8 = 2027-04-23 to 2027-09-30) to identify contact-rate shortfalls before they compound.

Responsible Role: Outreach and Enrollment Lead and phone-line coordinator, with daily data aggregation from all intermediary partners (housing associations, social services, NGOs, pharmacies).

Adaptation Process: Real-time partner feedback loop: if a partner reports call-completion rates <50% on any alert day, Outreach Lead convenes emergency 24-hour review with that partner to diagnose (staff absence, script confusion, technical issue with phone systems, resident unavailability) and implement corrective action (additional staff surge, script simplification, extended calling window). Weekly review (Fridays 14:00, Months 1-5 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-03-08) compares actual script-test results (do residents understand the message and accept referral?) against baseline expectations; if acceptance is <60%, script is revised with partner input and focus-group tested by end of week. During season, if rolling 7-day average contact success falls <60%, Outreach Lead escalates to incident commander within 24 hours with proposed remediation (e.g., additional interpretation support, ambassador pairing with partners, extension of calling hours).

Adaptation Trigger: Individual partner monthly success rate <60% (measured as calls connected / attempts) for 2 consecutive weeks → Outreach Lead and partner representative meet within 48 hours; if partner lacks capacity, assess whether call targets should be reduced (triggering lower total enrollment) or supplemented by a backup partner or city-funded surge staff. If >2 partners fail the 60% threshold simultaneously, incident commander escalates to Steering Committee as a gate-failure risk by Day 7 of the alert week. Non-official-language contact rates <5% of total attempts (city-wide, month-on-month) → Language-access coordinator (Outreach Lead with community ambassadors) increases interpreter deployment or ambassador pairing with partners within 1 week; if gap persists to Month 8 (2027-06-08), escalates to incident commander and Steering Committee as equity-goal failure.

4. Critical Success Factor Tracking: Transport Capacity and Response Time (45-Minute Gate and Wheelchair-User Access)

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Transport Dispatch Log (request timestamp, caller ID, destination choice, volunteer/taxi assignment, pickup time, actual arrival time, user feedback)
  • Volunteer Driver Availability and Utilization Report (daily count of available drivers, requests served, average pickup time by priority level)
  • Taxi-Operator Performance Report (requests assigned to taxi, response times, vehicle type deployed, accessibility match)
  • Transport Stress-Test Results (pre-season May drill and simulated peak-demand scenarios)

Frequency: Real-time logging during alert days; daily summary at end of each alert day; weekly aggregate report on non-alert days during setup (Months 1-5 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-03-08); monthly Steering Committee dashboard during season (Months 6.8-11.8 = 2027-04-23 to 2027-09-30).

Responsible Role: Transport Lead / Dispatch Coordinator (1 FTE) and backup dispatcher (1 FTE), with data aggregation by PMO coordinator.

Adaptation Process: Daily alert-day debrief (18:00, Cooling-Center Operations Lead, Transport Lead, Outreach Lead, incident commander) reviews transport requests, response times, failed requests and reasons (volunteer unavailable, taxi delayed, resident refused transport). If average response time for any alert day is >45 min, Transport Lead convenes same-day remediation meeting with volunteer representative and taxi operator to identify bottleneck (e.g., volunteer geographic clustering, taxi dispatch lag, mismatched destinations). Corrective actions authorized same-day: re-position volunteers, alert taxi operator of high-demand geography, cascade requests to backup volunteers or additional taxi surge. Weekly review (Thursdays 14:00, Months 1-5 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-03-08) compares volunteer recruitment pipeline against targets (target 40, range 30-50; if <20 by Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23, proportionally increase taxi retainer by €10-30k). Wheelchair-user requests are flagged separately; if any wheelchair user waits >45 min or is assigned a non-wheelchair-accessible vehicle, incident commander is notified within 2 hours and Transport Lead submits same-day corrective-action memo.

Adaptation Trigger: Single alert-day average response time >45 min → Transport Lead escalates to incident commander within 4 hours with root-cause summary and corrective action. Sustained average >45 min over 2+ consecutive alert days → incident commander convenes Steering Committee emergency session within 24 hours; gate failure for Month 4 (2027-02-08) is flagged and remediation plan (additional taxi surge, volunteer recruitment acceleration, route optimization, standby expansion) is approved or budget reallocation authorized. Volunteer recruitment <20 by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) → taxi retainer is scaled up by €10-30k (proportional offset) within 48 hours; if volunteer target remains unmet by Month 2 (2026-12-08), Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate is conditional on taxi-retainer adequacy confirmation. Wheelchair-user wait >45 min or non-accessible vehicle assignment → incident commander is notified within 2 hours; if this occurs >1 time per week during season, Transport Lead meets with taxi operator to enforce wheelchair-accessible vehicle availability; if operator cannot comply, backup taxi provider is activated or volunteer recruitment for accessible vehicles accelerates.

5. Major Risk Tracking: Procurement and Supply-Chain Delivery (Cooling Kits and Transport Contracts)

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Procurement Status Dashboard (order-placement dates, supplier lead times, delivery-date forecasts, expedite-cost exposure)
  • Kit-Delivery Tracking Log (units ordered, units received, units in storage, units deployed, inventory aging)
  • Taxi-Retainer Contract Performance Scorecard (standby fee, request volume, response times, vehicle availability, wheelchair-accessible units)

Frequency: Weekly during setup (Months 0-3 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08) to confirm supplier timelines and place orders on schedule; bi-weekly during Months 4-7 (2027-02-08 to 2027-05-17) to track kit delivery, acceptance and handoff to handypersons; monthly thereafter.

Responsible Role: Procurement Specialist (0.5 FTE) and Home Kit Lead, with backup supplier coordination and expedite-authorization by incident commander.

Adaptation Process: Weekly procurement review (Thursdays 10:00, Months 0-3 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08) confirms supplier lead times and confirms first call-off order (30-40% kit volume) is placed by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14); if supplier lead time exceeds 6 weeks, backup suppliers are activated immediately or expedite premium (estimated 10-15% cost increase, €50-100k) is approved by incident commander. Bi-weekly kit-delivery review (Mondays 10:00, Months 4-7 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-05-17) tracks: (1) kits received and passed quality inspection, (2) inventory turnover rate (kits deployed faster than plan indicates under-budgeting or slower indicates lagging installations), (3) handyperson installation pace (target 100% installed by Month 7.3 = 2027-05-17). If 40% of kits are not received by Month 4 (2027-02-08), gap is flagged as Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate-evidence risk; Home Kit Lead requests expedite at supplier or activates backup within 24 hours. Taxi-retainer scorecard (monthly, Mondays 14:00 Transport Lead review) tracks whether operator meets response-time commitment (<20 min), vehicle availability (≥10 vehicles ≥80% of alert days), wheelchair-accessible units (≥3, always available); if operator is underperforming on 2+ metrics 2 consecutive months, contract amendment or termination is escalated to incident commander.

Adaptation Trigger: Supplier delay of >3 weeks detected (e.g., unit does not ship by forecast date) → Procurement Specialist contacts supplier for expedite commit within 24 hours; if manufacturer cannot accelerate, backup supplier is contacted same day for alternative sourcing. Approval for expedite cost ≤€50k is granted by incident commander; cost >€50k requires Steering Committee approval. Kit delivery 2+ weeks late (would miss planned installation before June 1 = Month 6.8 = 2027-05-02 heat events) → Home Kit Lead escalates to incident commander with cost/timeline trade-offs (pay 15% premium for air-freight, or defer installations to July, or reduce kit count from 2,000 to 1,500). Decision is made within 48 hours and escalated to Steering Committee if contingency drawdown >€20k or scope reduction is needed. Taxi-operator performance failure (response time >25 min average, vehicle unavailability >2 alert days per week) detected in monthly scorecard → Transport Lead meets with operator within 48 hours to issue corrective-action notice (cure within 2 weeks or contract amendment/termination considered); if operator cannot cure, incident commander activates backup taxi provider or redirect requests to volunteer-only model if volunteer capacity permits.

6. Major Risk Tracking: GDPR Compliance and Partner Data-Protection (Legal Constraint and Operational Continuity)

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Data-Processing Agreement (DPA) Sign-Off Tracker (status with each of 4+ partners, sign-off deadline Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23)
  • Partner GDPR Compliance Audit Checklist (consent-record spot-check, staff-training attendance, data-handling practices, incident reporting)
  • Breach-Incident Log (any reported or discovered data-handling violation; contact with data-protection authority if required)

Frequency: Monthly during setup (Months 0-2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) to track DPA negotiation and sign-off; quarterly spot-check audit of partner compliance (Month 3 = 2027-01-08, Month 6 = 2027-04-08, Month 9 = 2027-07-08); real-time breach-incident log during entire project.

Responsible Role: Legal and GDPR Lead (0.5-1 FTE, may be municipal legal department or external GDPR counsel), with partner-liaison officer for audit coordination.
