If too tight (high threshold), the program misses hot-night events that drive elderly mortality, potentially leaving 5–10 heat-vulnerable residents unprotected during critical July–August surges. Either scenario—budget collapse or preventable mortality during observed heat event—triggers media scrutiny, funder loss of confidence, and non-release of €1.5M scale funding at Month 4 (2027-02-08). Estimated financial and reputational impact: €200k–400k cash shortfall plus credibility loss for playbook scaling to other EU cities.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 1 (2026-11-08), a complete 15-year AEMET record and validated local university data establish precise city-specific alert thresholds: ≥35°C daytime AND ≥22°C night-time occurs 18–25 days per season historically, and 80%+ of those days correlate with ≥1.3× baseline EMS call load. Threshold-calibrated forecasts reduce false alarms to <15% and ensure real heat events are caught. Baseline temperature-mortality regression (e.g., 2.1 deaths/°C above 32°C threshold) quantifies expected harm without intervention, enabling credible Month 4 (2027-02-08) attribution and scaling cost model ($X per prevented death). Neighborhood heat-mapping reveals that central Castellón reaches 2–3°C hotter than periphery; this directs home-kit and transport resources to highest-risk zones, improving equity and impact. Drill thresholds set using this data are realistic and validate operational readiness. Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate measurement against calibrated, evidence-grounded thresholds is defensible and builds stakeholder and funder confidence in the program's precision, supporting Year-2 continuation and replication to peer EU cities.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If AEMET 15-year record is incomplete or inaccessible, request 5-year minimum baseline (2020–2025) by Month 1 (2026-11-08) and supplement with proxy: published Spanish national summer heat events (AEMET heat warnings, red-alert days) and Castellón newspaper archives (El Periódico de Castellón, La Ronda) documenting observed temperatures and health impacts in 2010–2019; cross-reference with hospital administrative data (admission logs by date, not patient names) to infer EMS call spikes.
  • Contact Universitat Jaume I (Climate and Environmental Sciences group) at Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) to request access to local weather-station records or to conduct a 3–6 month pilot microclimate monitoring (April–September 2027) alongside AEMET data, establishing local calibration for future years.
  • If baseline temperature-mortality relationship cannot be derived from local data (small samples, incomplete coding), use published regression coefficients from peer Spanish cities (Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia) adjusted for Castellón's climate and housing stock, documented in literature (e.g., Spanish National Health Institute reports on heat mortality). Disclose this limitation transparently in the evaluation report and playbook.
  • Conduct a rapid expert-elicitation workshop at Month 1 (2026-11-08) with local public-health physician, EMS medical director and meteorologist: ask them to propose alert thresholds based on professional judgment and prior experience with Castellón heat events. Use their input to validate or adjust quantitative thresholds and document the rationale.
  • If neighborhood-level heat mapping is not available, use proxy: map top-floor flats and poor-insulation social housing (available from municipal building registry) as proxy for heat vulnerability; concentrate home kits and mobile cool-points there, and measure neighborhood coverage equity in the evaluation report.
  • For Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate, use national meteorological forecast thresholds (AEMET red/orange/yellow warnings) as interim alert criteria, documented as provisional; commit to local calibration by Month 4 (2027-02-08) and threshold review by Month 6 (2027-04-08) once real summer 2027 data arrive. This allows gates to proceed on schedule while preserving the option to adjust thresholds for Year 2.

Find Document 3: Castellón de la Plana Municipal Cooling-Center Asset Inventory

ID: f99bad9d-b417-474d-8a99-6239257d50ca

Description: Official list of municipal or accessible public facilities (libraries, community centers, parish halls, sports facilities, schools, government offices) with: location (address, postal code), floor area, occupancy capacity, current opening hours, accessibility features (wheelchair access, toilets, water, parking), utilities (air-conditioning, heating, water supply), and insurance/liability status. Used to identify and audit the 10 proposed cooling-center sites.

Recency Requirement: Current (2024-2025); update if facilities have undergone recent renovation or closure.

Responsible Role Type: Cooling Center Network Manager

Steps to Find:

  • Contact Castellón de la Plana municipal facilities or asset-management department; request comprehensive facility inventory with accessibility audit data.
  • Request municipal facility-use agreements or insurance documentation for liability assessment.
  • Contact library system, municipal sports/recreation department, and social services to cross-check facility capacity and opening-hour availability.
  • Visit or photograph proposed sites to verify accessibility; document any gaps (missing ramps, inadequate toilets, no quiet room).

Access Difficulty: Medium. Municipal facilities data are typically held internally; access requires formal request to facilities management or city procurement office. Some data may be classified (insurance, security). Accessibility audit reports may be incomplete; physical verification required.

Essential Information:

  • Identify and list all municipal and publicly accessible facilities (libraries, community centers, parish halls, sports facilities, schools, government offices) in Castellón de la Plana with complete addresses and postal codes.
  • Document floor area (m²) and current functional occupancy capacity for each site under normal and heat-alert conditions.
  • Map accessibility features for each facility: wheelchair ramps/level entry, accessible toilets (≥1 per 50 occupants), water fountains or supply, parking (general and disabled), quiet/low-stimulus rooms.
  • Record utilities availability: air-conditioning system type and capacity (kW or equivalent); backup power; water supply capacity (liters/hour); heating (not required for summer, note for completeness).
  • Verify current opening hours and flexibility for extended hours (10:00–20:00 standard, 24:00 capability for ≥3 sites at alert Level 3).
  • Confirm liability insurance coverage and facility-use agreement status for each proposed site; identify gaps requiring legal action before Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate.
  • Audit which sites meet accessibility standards (ramps, toilets, water, quiet space) to confirm ≥50% of planned refuge places are in fully accessible facilities, per the refuge-site standard.
  • Identify remediation needs (cost, timeline) for each inaccessible site; confirm remediation cost ≤€10k and timeline ≤4 weeks, else deprioritize or defer the site.
  • Verify capacity of water supply and sanitation under continuous occupancy (10:00–20:00, potentially 200–400 residents per day at Level 2–3 across all sites).
  • Cross-reference each site's location (address, postal code) against the vulnerability heat map to confirm ≥70% of enrolled residents are within 800 m (10-minute walk) of ≥1 refuge.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or outdated facility list: if closed, relocated, or newly renovated sites are not flagged, the city may commit to sites that are unavailable, reducing actual refuge capacity below the planned 400 places and forcing transport-only access for residents who cannot travel.
  • Missing or inaccurate accessibility audit: if ramps, toilets, water or quiet rooms are not documented, the city may open a site that excludes wheelchair users, deaf/hard-of-hearing, or sensory-sensitive residents, violating disability access law and failing the equity gate.
  • Underestimated occupancy capacity: if a site's functional capacity is overstated (e.g., assuming 50 places when furniture/layout allows only 30), the city will overcommit refuge hours and overcrowd sites, increasing heat-illness risk and breaching occupancy fire codes.
  • Insurance and liability gaps: if a facility lacks public-liability insurance or a formal use agreement is not signed by Month 2 (2026-12-08), the city faces litigation exposure if an incident occurs at an unstaffed or inadequately protected site.
  • Utility underestimation: if water supply or sanitation capacity is not verified for continuous 10-hour occupancy, sites may run out of water or face toilet failures during peak alert days, forcing premature closures and resident evacuation.
  • Spatial mismatch to vulnerable populations: if the 10 sites are located in affluent or central districts only, isolated and mobility-limited residents in peripheral neighborhoods will exceed the 800 m walking distance threshold, reducing actual reach by 20–30% and failing the equity intent.
  • Remediation scope creep: if accessibility barriers are discovered after commitment (e.g., structural ramp required), remediation costs and timelines could exceed the €10k and 4-week thresholds, forcing site abandonment mid-setup and destabilizing the network footprint.
  • Misalignment with refuge-hours assumption: if water, sanitation or utilities cannot support extended hours (24:00 at Level 3), the city cannot deliver the promised overnight cooling, reducing protection of hot-night mortality risk among elderly residents.

Worst Case Scenario: The city commits to 10 refuge sites without completing a full accessibility and capacity audit. Two sites (due to be large, central facilities) lack disability ramps and adequate sanitation and require €15k–20k and 6–8 week remediation. The audit is completed only in March (Month 5 = 2027-03-08), past the Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate, leaving no time to fix the sites or find replacements. The city opens the refuges at 70% capacity (280 instead of 400 places) and cannot accommodate wheelchair users at three sites. During the first Level 3 alert in June, water supply fails at one site due to inadequate pressure, forcing evacuation of 80 residents mid-day. Media coverage frames the program as "inaccessible and unsafe." Enrollment collapses by 40%, outreach contact attempts drop to 3,000/month (from 5,000 planned), and the 60% contact-success gate fails. Reputational damage affects the scale decision and Year-2 funding is denied. Estimated reach loss: 900 residents; estimated legal cost: €50k–100k.

Best Case Scenario: A comprehensive, verified asset inventory is completed by Month 1 (2026-11-08), identifying 12 sites (8–12 planned), 450+ places, all with confirmed accessibility and utility capacity. Eight sites meet the fully accessible standard; two require <€8k remediation (ramping, toilet upgrade) on 2-week schedules; two are deferred or dropped. All sites are mapped against the vulnerability heat map, confirming ≥75% of enrolled residents within 800 m. Insurance, facility-use agreements and liability coverage are confirmed and signed by Month 2 (2026-12-08). Water-supply testing at each site confirms capacity for 10–24 hour continuous operation. Staffing and accessibility briefings occur without gaps. The first Level 3 alert in June opens all refuges at full capacity, water and sanitation function flawlessly, wheelchair and sensory-access accommodations are validated, and residents report feeling safe. Enrollment and contact rates hit 80% of target by Month 4 (2027-02-08). The scale gate is met. Documented accessibility and contingency infrastructure become a reusable model for other EU cities, strengthening the scaling playbook.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If a comprehensive municipal inventory cannot be obtained by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), engage a facility-assessment consultant (estimated cost €8k–12k, timeline 2–3 weeks) to conduct rapid site surveys and accessibility audits of the top 15 candidate facilities, prioritizing those already contracted or in frequent public use.
  • If a single municipal facilities department cannot provide complete data, create a cross-departmental working group (libraries, sports/recreation, social services, public works) at Month 0 (2026-10-08) to pool facility ownership and operational information; designate one lead coordinator to compile a unified inventory by Month 1 (2026-11-08).
  • If insurance or liability documentation is incomplete or outdated, require each site to obtain a renewal certificate of public-liability insurance (covering the heat-response activity) and a formal facility-use agreement signed by the facility owner/manager and the city legal department by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); estimated cost €500–1,500 per site.
  • If water-supply or sanitation capacity cannot be verified through existing utility records, conduct on-site water-pressure and flow tests (5–10 minutes per site) and a sanitation load assessment (occupancy × toilet ratio) in Month 1 (2026-11-08); estimated cost €1,500–2,500 for all sites; engage a municipal water/sanitation engineer.
  • If accessibility audit findings exceed the €10k or 4-week remediation threshold for a site, immediately (by Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23) identify a backup facility (10–15 candidate replacements identified at Month 0 = 2026-10-08) and shift the refuge allocation; estimate 1–2 backup sites will be needed.
  • If the spatial distribution of sites does not meet the 800 m walking-distance target for ≥70% of enrolled residents, augment the network with informal cool points (pharmacies, parish halls, shopping centers, sheltered housing) that are already air-conditioned and trusted by residents, requiring no new infrastructure investment but adding staffing coordination cost (estimated €50k–80k).
  • If full 24-hour capability at three sites cannot be confirmed by Month 2 (2026-12-08), scale back to 10:00–22:00 hours at Level 2–3 and offer 24-hour transport-and-phone triage instead; this extends the transport model but keeps the refuge footprint viable.

Find Document 4: Castellón de la Plana Baseline Heat-Related Mortality & Excess-Death Estimates

ID: 0bf77087-1fd6-46b3-ac5c-2546b74f0704

Description: Three-year historical data on deaths attributed to heat (ICD-10 code T67 or documentation of 'heat-related' in death certificate) or excess mortality during summer months (May-September) compared to expected seasonal baseline (e.g., via statistical/demographic methods). Used to establish baseline harm and to assess program attribution post-hoc. May be obtained from regional health authority, national health statistics office, or municipal vital statistics.

Recency Requirement: Most recent 3-5 years of data (2020-2025); supplement with 2010-2019 trend if available to establish longer-term patterns.

Responsible Role Type: Data and Evaluation Coordinator / Health Epidemiologist

Steps to Find:

  • Contact regional health authority (SSVS) or Valencian public-health institute (Agencia de Salut Pública) for mortality data by cause of death, including heat-related codes (T67.0-T67.9).
  • Request municipal vital statistics (registro civil) for death certificates with heat or heat-related condition notation.
  • Search Spanish national health statistics portal (Instituto de Salud Carlos III) for Castellón excess-mortality or heat-attributable-death estimates.
  • Contact university epidemiology department or research institute in Valencia region; they may have conducted prior heat-mortality studies with Castellón data.
  • Request from national statistical office (INE) if mortality data by cause and municipality are published.

Access Difficulty: Hard. Mortality data are sensitive and privacy-protected. Individual death certificates are restricted-access. Aggregated mortality counts (by heat-code ICD-10 or monthly excess-death estimates) are more accessible via health authorities. University researchers may have already analyzed this data; a research partnership may accelerate access.

Essential Information:

  • Confirm 3–5 years of historical heat-related mortality data (2020–2025) by ICD-10 heat codes (T67.0–T67.9) or death-certificate notation; provide annual counts, seasonal distribution (May–September focus), and geographic breakdowns by district or neighborhood within Castellón de la Plana.
  • Establish baseline excess mortality during summer months using temperature-adjusted statistical methods (e.g., expected deaths minus observed deaths, or regression of deaths on temperature lagged 0–3 days); quantify 95% confidence intervals around baseline estimates to anchor uncertainty for Year-1 attribution analysis.
  • Document data quality and coding consistency across years and providers (municipal vital records, regional health authority, EMS): identify gaps, coding rule changes, or incomplete records that may inflate or deflate baseline estimates by >10%.
  • Provide demographic and geographic breakdowns of baseline by age bands (65–74, 75–84, 85+), living situation (alone vs. household), housing type (top-floor vs. ground, social vs. private), and neighborhood deprivation index or postal code to confirm vulnerability mapping used in the program design.
  • List data custodians, access agreements, and confidentiality constraints; confirm whether aggregate counts (deaths by heat code) are openly available or require a data-processing agreement; specify retention period and deletion protocols post-evaluation.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or under-coded baseline (e.g., heat-related deaths coded as 'cardiovascular' rather than T67) will systematically underestimate true baseline, making any Year-1 program impact appear artificially large and undermining credibility of the scaling cost model when presented to peer EU cities.
  • Inconsistent coding across years (e.g., 2020 excluded heat codes but 2021–2025 included them) introduces trend noise that cannot be distinguished from program effect, causing Month 4 (2027-02-08) attribution gates to fail or produce uninterpretable results.
  • Missing or delayed access to data by Month 1 (2026-11-08) will delay coding-agreement meetings with EMS and health partners, pushing the MOU sign-off past the Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate and preventing drill-based validation of daily aggregate reporting protocols.
  • Baseline estimates with wide confidence intervals (e.g., ±30–50% around point estimate) or small cell counts in demographic subgroups will make it impossible to detect plausible program effects (15–25% reduction in heat deaths, estimate) with statistical power, weakening evaluation credibility and funder confidence in Year-2 funding decisions.
  • Lack of geographic granularity (e.g., only city-wide totals, not by neighborhood) prevents the program from validating whether targeted intervention in high-risk districts achieved equity gains or merely reproduced prior patterns.

Worst Case Scenario: The program operates for 12 months, implements cooling centers, transport, outreach and home kits, and measures outcomes at Month 12 (2027-10-08). However, the baseline data are either unavailable, incomplete (coding gaps, missing years), or inconsistently defined. At evaluation, the team cannot distinguish program-driven mortality reduction from year-to-year noise or seasonal variation, and any claimed reduction (e.g., 20% fewer heat deaths) is challenged as unverifiable. The playbook is published with a caveat that attribution was not possible, undermining its credibility for other EU cities. Peer-city adoption is delayed or abandoned, and Year-2 funding (€2.3M, estimate) is withheld pending a stronger evaluation design, leaving the program unable to scale. Reputational damage: municipal government loses confidence in evidence-based health interventions.

Best Case Scenario: Baseline data are obtained by Month 1 (2026-11-08), coded consistently across years, with demographic and geographic breakdowns and 95% confidence intervals. The team validates the baseline via a partner audit at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), achieves full coding agreement with EMS and hospitals by Month 2 (2026-12-08), and uses this to pre-specify the attribution analysis protocol. Daily aggregate reporting from health partners is validated during drills. At Month 12 (2027-10-08), evaluation shows plausible 12–18% reduction in heat-related EMS calls and 10–15% reduction in excess deaths with narrow confidence intervals. The playbook and scaling cost model are published with high credibility, attracting peer-city interest and securing Year-2 funding commitment from funder or new source. Program expands to city-wide by Month 15 (2028-01-08).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If municipal vital-statistics records are unavailable or restricted-access, request aggregated excess-mortality estimates (observed minus expected deaths by month and age band) from the regional health authority (SSVS) or Valencian public-health institute (Agencia de Salut Pública), which may already have published this analysis for policy purposes.
  • If historical EMS data by heat-code are not routinely extracted, commission a rapid retrospective review of EMS call records for Months 5–9 (2027-03-08 to 2027-07-08) of 2023–2025 using a simple triage form (call chief complaint, location, outcome, temperature that day); use the sample to estimate annual heat-call volume and seasonal pattern, accepting wider confidence intervals.
  • If individual-level data access is blocked by privacy regulation, partner with a university epidemiology department or regional research institute (e.g., University of Valencia) that holds a data-use agreement with the health authority; they can compute baseline statistics under their institutional oversight and provide aggregate results to the city under a data-processing agreement.
  • If baseline data collection will take >6 weeks and delay the Month 1 (2026-11-08) legal-review milestone, adopt a provisional baseline from published national or regional heat-mortality statistics (e.g., Spanish National Statistics Institute mortality tables) as a placeholder for drill planning and procurement; commit to replacing it with local data by Month 3 (2027-01-08).
  • If demographic and neighborhood-level breakdowns of baseline cannot be linked to individual death records due to privacy constraints, use census and housing data to construct a vulnerability-weighted proxy baseline (e.g., age-stratified mortality rates applied to census age distribution in each neighborhood), which can be validated against aggregate totals and refined after Year 1.

Find Document 5: Spanish & Valencian GDPR & Health-Data Protection Guidance

ID: 88109013-c68c-4514-9aae-15c88b189001

Description: Official regulatory guidance from Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) and regional health authorities on: lawful basis for processing health data for public-health emergencies (Article 6 GDPR), consent requirements and withdrawal procedures (Article 7), data-processing agreements (Article 28), and special-category data rules (Article 9). Clarifies whether heat-alert contact is a 'public task' (Article 6(1)(e)) or requires explicit consent, and how intermediary-held health data (housing associations, social services) is governed.

Recency Requirement: Current GDPR guidance (2021 or later); AEPD published criteria or decisions preferred.

Responsible Role Type: GDPR Compliance Officer / Legal Counsel

Steps to Find:

  • Visit Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) website (aepd.es) and search for guidance on health data, public-health emergencies, and intermediary data sharing; download published documents and criteria.
  • Request AEPD published decisions or opinions on heat-alert contact lawful basis (may be available as case studies or FAQ).
  • Contact AEPD directly via email or phone for guidance on whether the intermediary-held-list model complies with Spanish law (they may issue formal written guidance).
  • Search Valencian regional law (Generalitat Valenciana) for any regional data-protection guidance or health-privacy guidance (beyond national GDPR).
  • Review Catalan Data Protection Authority (APDCAT) or other Spanish regional authority guidance for heat or emergency health contexts; may be transferable precedent.
  • Consult with municipal legal department or GDPR counsel for case law or AEPD decisions on public-health and emergency-context data processing.

Access Difficulty: Easy to Medium. AEPD website has public guidance in Spanish; English translation may be needed. AEPD accepts guidance requests but response time varies (2-8 weeks). Regional authorities may have fewer published resources. Legal counsel familiar with Spanish GDPR practice is helpful.

Essential Information:

  • Clarify whether heat-alert contact to intermediary-held residents (housing associations, social services, NGOs, pharmacies) qualifies as a 'public task' under GDPR Article 6(1)(e) or requires explicit consent under Article 7, and under which Spanish/Valencian legal authority.
  • Define the lawful basis and data-processing chain for aggregate heat-related EMS and ED counts shared daily from hospitals and EMS to the city incident commander (Article 6 GDPR and Spanish health-privacy law equivalents).
  • Specify retention periods, deletion procedures and conditions for re-consent if heat-alert operations continue into Year 2 beyond the initial 12-month pilot.
  • Confirm whether data-processing agreements (Article 28 GDPR) with intermediary partners are mandatory or whether a simpler MOU suffices if no personal data is transferred to the city.
  • Identify AEPD published decisions, guidance documents or case studies on heat emergencies, public-health alerts or intermediary-held health data to support the legal interpretation.
  • State the procedure and timeline for notifying AEPD (or regional equivalent) if a data breach occurs during outreach (e.g., partner staff misconduct, accidental disclosure).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Inaccurate or outdated GDPR guidance could lead to a legal challenge from data subjects or AEPD, delaying partner sign-off by 2–4 weeks and forcing redesign of the outreach model mid-implementation (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08 readiness gate risk).
  • If the lawful basis is unclear, housing associations, social services or NGOs may withdraw from partnerships, reducing outreach reach by 10–25% and failing the Month 4 (2027-02-08) 60% contact-success gate.
  • Guidance that incorrectly interprets Spanish data-protection law (beyond GDPR) could expose the city to additional liability under regional regulations, incurring unexpected legal fees (€15,000–30,000) and reputational damage.
  • Missing guidance on breach notification timelines could cause the city to miss AEPD reporting deadlines (48 hours), triggering regulatory penalties and media scrutiny.
  • Absence of precedent or case studies on heat emergencies could force reliance on generic GDPR guidance, leaving ambiguities about risk allocation between city and intermediary partners unresolved, leading to disputes during the season.

Worst Case Scenario: The city proceeds with the intermediary-held-list model without legal clearance, believing the 'public task' basis is solid. In June–July, a partner (e.g., housing association) faces AEPD scrutiny or a resident complaint about data handling. AEPD issues a provisional halt to data sharing pending investigation (typical 2–8 weeks). Outreach contact attempts drop from 5,000/month to 500–1,000/month, failing the 60% contact-success gate. The €1.5M scale funding is withheld at Month 4 (2027-02-08). The city must halt or drastically reduce operations by August during peak summer heat risk, leaving 1,500–2,000 enrolled residents without check-in support. Estimated harm: 5–15 preventable excess deaths in the unprotected population; legal remediation and potential fines €50,000–100,000; program credibility destroyed for Year 2 and EU scaling.

Best Case Scenario: AEPD or regional authority issues clear, published guidance by Month 1 (2026-11-08) confirming the intermediary-held-list model complies with Spanish law under the 'public task' basis, with specific language on retention and deletion. Template data-processing agreements are provided or confirmed as unnecessary. Partners (housing associations, social services, NGOs) sign MOUs by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) with confidence. Outreach proceeds uninterrupted through the season, achieving ≥60% contact success and meeting the Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate. The €1.5M scale funding is released on schedule. The playbook documents this legal pathway as a reusable precedent for other EU cities, reducing their legal-review timeline and cost by 50% and accelerating pan-European adoption of the heat-response model.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Obtain a formal written GDPR legal opinion from a specialist Spanish data-protection counsel by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) if AEPD guidance is unavailable or delayed. Budget €15,000–30,000 and use the opinion as the basis for partner MOUs; this is slower than published guidance but provides contractual liability protection.
  • Shift to a consent-based registry model (opt-in enrollment through GPs, pharmacies and cooling centers) if the public-task interpretation is rejected. This reduces legal risk but lowers reach to isolated, offline residents by an estimated 15–25%; combine with building-level canvassing via local sentinels to recover reach (adds €100,000–150,000 in outreach staffing and 4–6 weeks of timeline).
  • Request a formal AEPD guidance opinion via the agency's guidance-request process (typically 4–8 weeks); parallel this with legal counsel drafting interim MOUs so that no delay occurs if AEPD response is slow.
  • Engage a regional university law school or public-health research center as a partner to co-author a position paper on heat-emergency data sharing and submit it to AEPD as a reference; this builds precedent and may accelerate clarity (timeline 6–10 weeks, cost €5,000–10,000 co-funding).
  • Pilot the intermediary-held-list model with one trusted partner (e.g., the largest housing association or social service) in Month 1–2 (2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08) under informal data-sharing practices, gather 2–4 weeks of operational data on partner capacity and resident response, then formally obtain legal clearance and scale to all partners by Month 3 (2027-01-08). This de-risks the model with evidence but delays full-scale outreach by 3–4 weeks.

Find Document 6: EU & Spanish Public Procurement Rules & Thresholds (2024-2025)

ID: 27dfc82c-e0be-46ce-a7c8-90f12cae8251

Description: Current EU public-procurement directives (2014/24/EU, 2014/25/EU) and Spanish national transposition (LCSP - Ley de Contratos del Sector Público) specifying procurement thresholds (below-threshold vs. tender-required amounts), simplified procedures for emergency or low-value purchases, framework-agreement rules, and audit requirements. Used to determine legal procurement route for cooling kits, transport, and handyperson services within the €3.5M budget.

Recency Requirement: Current (2024-2025); Spanish LCSP as amended 2023-2024; EU Directive 2014/24/EU.

Responsible Role Type: Municipal Procurement Officer / Contract Law Specialist

Steps to Find:

  • Download Spanish public-procurement law (LCSP, Ley 9/2017) from official government source (boe.es).
  • Search Spanish Public Sector Contracts Board (Junta de Contratación del Sector Público) website for current thresholds, guidance, and case studies.
  • Download EU Directive 2014/24/EU (Procurement Directive) and its preamble from EUR-Lex.
  • Contact Spanish municipal association (FEMP) or local municipal procurement office for practical guidance on below-threshold purchasing and framework-agreement procedures in Spain.
  • Search for OECD or EU publications on emergency procurement procedures (may be relevant if heat response is framed as emergency/public-health urgency).

Access Difficulty: Easy. Spanish law is public and available via boe.es; EU directives are on EUR-Lex. Municipal associations provide practical templates and training. Complexity is moderate; a municipal procurement officer or external legal counsel familiar with Spanish rules is helpful.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the current EU and Spanish public-procurement regulatory framework (Directives 2014/24/EU, 2014/25/EU and LCSP transposition) applicable to the city of Castellón de la Plana in 2024–2025.
  • Quantify the euro thresholds that trigger mandatory competitive tender vs. simplified/below-threshold procurement for each purchase category (cooling kits, transport retainer, handyperson services, refuge fit-out, security contracts).
  • Determine which procurement pathways (framework call-offs, below-threshold direct award, simplified emergency procedures, competitive tender) are available to meet the Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate without violating audit requirements.
  • Document the audit-readiness requirements for each pathway: file documentation, competitive justification, price benchmarking, single-source authorization, and record retention.
  • Clarify whether heat-response can be framed as an emergency or public-health urgency under Spanish law to justify expedited or non-competitive procedures.
  • Specify template contract language required under LCSP for framework agreements and standby retainers (e.g., minimum capacity guarantees, call-off procedures, price escalation caps).
  • Identify any Spanish municipal-association (FEMP) or regional government guidance on procurement templates or pre-vetted supplier lists for kits, transport, or security services.
  • Define the liability and audit exposure if the city uses below-threshold purchasing repeatedly to avoid transparency or competitive bidding, and what documentation mitigates this risk.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If thresholds are misunderstood or applied inconsistently, orders may be challenged as non-compliant, forcing re-tendering mid-season and delaying delivery by 4–8 weeks past the Month 2 (2026-12-08) gate.
  • Lack of audit-ready documentation (e.g., missing competitive justification for sole-source awards, price benchmarking, or call-off records) exposes the city to regulatory audit findings, reputational damage and potential contract invalidation.
  • Ambiguity on whether heat-response qualifies for emergency-procurement exemptions could lead to legal challenge by excluded bidders, tying up resources in dispute resolution.
  • If handyperson, kit or transport contracts lack proper LCSP-compliant escalation-cap clauses, summer demand spikes could trigger cost increases of €50k–150k, forcing mid-season service cuts.
  • Repeated use of below-threshold purchasing without transparent competitive process invites scrutiny from auditors, EU funder reviews and political opponents, undermining the program's credibility.
  • Template contract language that fails to align with LCSP requirements (e.g., standby-retainer guarantees, call-off procedures, payment terms) could result in supplier disputes, non-performance claims or cost disputes during alert days.

Worst Case Scenario: The city misapplies procurement thresholds or uses expedited procedures without proper legal basis, triggering an audit finding or legal challenge by an excluded bidder. Contracts are invalidated mid-season; retenders delay kit delivery and transport contracting past March, preventing home interventions and forcing the transport model to taxi-only at +€150k–250k cost. Schedule slip of 4–8 weeks forces closure of Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate. €1.5M scale funding is withheld. Program credibility erodes; playbook reuse by other EU cities is compromised. Estimated financial and reputational cost: €50k–100k legal remediation + €150k–250k operational overrun + loss of scaling opportunity.

Best Case Scenario: Clear, auditable procurement pathways are documented by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01), thresholds and justifications are pre-vetted by legal counsel, and a hybrid strategy (frameworks for speed, competitive tenders for tranche 2) meets the Month 2 (2026-12-08) gate without audit exposure. All kit and transport orders are placed by Month 2 (2026-12-08), delivery milestones are met by April, and home interventions and transport are operational by May. Procurement is transparent and replicable; other EU cities adopt the same templates and procedures, reducing their procurement time and risk. Public trust in municipal governance is strengthened. Program meets all gates and scales successfully.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Engage a specialized Spanish public-procurement law firm by Month 0 (2026-10-08) (cost ≈€15k–30k) to provide written legal opinion on thresholds, eligible procedures, audit requirements and template contracts. Use the opinion to justify procurement decisions in writing and build audit-ready files.
  • Contact the Spanish municipal association (FEMP) and request template procurement files, supplier pre-qualification lists, and guidance on heat-response emergencies. FEMP may have published case studies or model tenders for similar services.
  • Consult the regional government (Generalitat Valenciana) procurement office to clarify whether regional or national frameworks for emergency public health exist, and whether they offer pre-qualified supplier lists or expedited procedures.
  • Identify whether Castellón de la Plana has an existing municipal procurement framework (e.g., for energy, transport, or facilities management) that can be leveraged via call-off orders rather than new tenders.
  • If competitive tendering cannot be completed by Month 2 (2026-12-08), split procurement into two phases: place 30–40% of kits and transport via below-threshold or framework by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14), then conduct a full competitive tender for the remainder starting Month 2 (2026-12-08), with delivery expected by Month 5 (2027-03-08). Document the split as a staged delivery strategy, not as avoidance of competition.
  • Request a waiver or confirmation letter from the local EU funder (likely a national or regional ministry) clarifying whether the heat-response program qualifies for public-health emergency treatment under procurement rules, and in writing.

Find Document 7: Castellón de la Plana NGO & Social Services Directory (Housing Associations, Social Care, Homeless Services, Migrant Organizations)

ID: b501f078-895b-4278-b459-d0b4227342d4

Description: Comprehensive list of local non-governmental and community organizations, including: housing associations/cooperatives (vivienda social), social services (servicios sociales), homeless or rough-sleeping services, migrant integration organizations, faith-based groups, and language/cultural associations. Includes contact names, phone, email, service scope, and current client base. Used to identify and engage partners for intermediary-held outreach, street contact, language access, and community trust-building.

Recency Requirement: Current (2024-2025); update annually; some turnover in staff/leadership expected.

Responsible Role Type: Partner Liaison Officer / Community Engagement Lead

Steps to Find:

  • Contact Castellón municipal social services department for official registry of partner organizations and referral networks.
  • Request municipal integration or migration office directory of migrant associations and support organizations.
  • Search online directories: Plataforma del Voluntariado de España (Spanish volunteer directory), Guía del Tercer Sector (Spanish NGO directory), and regional Valencian NGO networks.
  • Contact Castellón archdiocese or religious affairs office for list of faith-based organizations (mosques, churches, synagogues) active in social care.
  • Inquire with municipal housing authority about housing associations and their outreach/welfare roles.
  • Request homeless-service NGO directory from Castellón social services or regional authorities.

Access Difficulty: Easy to Medium. Municipal social services maintain partner registries (usually shared readily). Online directories and faith organizations are publicly listed. Contact details may be incomplete; direct phone verification needed.

Essential Information:

  • Identify and list all active housing associations, social cooperatives (vivienda social) and social-housing managers operating in Castellón de la Plana with current contact names, phone numbers, email addresses, service areas and estimated client bases (target: 5-10 organizations).
  • Obtain complete registry of municipal and regional social services offices (servicios sociales) with department heads, phone, email and service scope (elderly care, disability support, family services); confirm which offices manage outreach capacity for heat-alert campaigns.
  • Compile comprehensive directory of homeless-services NGOs, rough-sleeping outreach teams and emergency shelter operators active in Castellón, including overnight shelter capacity, day-center locations, current client counts and outreach staff rosters.
  • Locate and verify 4-6 migrant-integration organizations, language associations and cultural centers serving non-Spanish speaking communities (Arabic, Romanian, Portuguese speakers confirmed; others TBD at Month 0 = 2026-10-08), including staff, current client populations and existing community-trust relationships.
  • Obtain contact details and social-mission descriptions for all active faith-based organizations (Christian churches, mosques, synagogues, other faiths) engaged in social outreach or welfare services in Castellón.
  • Identify public libraries, community centers, parish halls and other existing assets (owners, facility managers, opening hours, accessibility status, water and toilet provision, security arrangements) suitable for conversion to cooling refuges.
  • Document any existing data-sharing or welfare-referral partnerships between organizations (e.g., housing association → social services → NGO → pharmacy chains) to understand formal consent and data-handling agreements already in place.
  • Confirm which organizations hold lawful bases (contractual duty, existing consent frameworks or public-task authority) for contacting their own clients or residents, and which would need new consent or data-processing agreements under GDPR.
  • Quantify total potential reach: sum of enrolled clients, residents and service users across all identified partner organizations to validate whether 3,000 enrolled high-risk residents by Month 7 (2027-05-08) is achievable.
  • Identify any known gaps in geographic coverage (neighborhoods or populations underserved by existing organizations) to inform recruitment of additional partners or direct municipal outreach.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or outdated partner directory means some high-risk residents will not be identified or contacted, reducing outreach reach below the 60% contact-success gate (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) and equity coverage by neighborhood.
  • Inaccurate contact details (wrong phone, departed staff) lead to failed enrollment calls, wasting outreach capacity and delaying partner engagement, compressing the hiring and training timeline before Month 2 (2026-12-08).
  • Missing or incorrect data on partner organization lawful bases and consent frameworks forces redundant GDPR vetting and delays MOU signature, potentially pushing data-processing agreements past the Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) deadline.
  • Underestimating partner capacity (e.g., not knowing a housing association manages 8,000 residents) leads to unrealistic outreach targets and partner fatigue, causing mid-season partner dropout and loss of 10-20% of planned contacts.
  • Failure to map existing data-sharing agreements and trust relationships causes duplicate consent requests or partner confusion about consent scope, eroding community trust and NGO cooperation.
  • Unverified accessibility or facility information for proposed cooling-refuge sites (e.g., library lacking wheelchair access, parish hall lacking water) forces late-stage site remediation or substitution, jeopardizing the Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate.
  • Missing information on migrant-community organizations and language capabilities means language-access targets (≥5% of outreach in non-official languages, Month 4 = 2027-02-08) are unachievable, failing equity metrics.
  • Lack of clarity on faith-leader involvement and trust relationships slows recruitment of trusted messengers, reducing uptake of communications and enrollment among faith-affiliated residents.

Worst Case Scenario: If the directory is incomplete, inaccurate or outdated, the outreach model collapses. Partner organizations cannot be contacted reliably, delaying engagement by 2-4 weeks and compressing MOU negotiation into a 2-week window before Month 2 (2026-12-08). Critical partners (social services, housing associations) may withdraw if GDPR concerns are not pre-cleared, reducing reach by 15-25% and invalidating the 3,000-enrollment target. Geographic gaps mean entire neighborhoods of vulnerable residents (e.g., migrant enclaves, homeless populations) are missed. A failed refresh of the directory mid-season (staff turnover in partner organizations) could orphan the outreach operation by July, collapsing the 60% contact-success gate and forcing the program to rely solely on self-enrollment at refuges, reducing demonstrated harm reduction and jeopardizing the Month 4 (2027-02-08) scale release of €1.5M.

Best Case Scenario: A current, verified directory with 50+ confirmed partner contacts enables rapid, parallel partner engagement from Month 0 (2026-10-08). GDPR compliance is pre-cleared via legal review of existing consent frameworks, accelerating MOU signature by Month 1 (2026-11-08). Outreach targets and partner capacity are realistic, lowering mid-season fatigue and dropout. Mapping of existing data-sharing agreements avoids consent redundancy and builds on established trust. Cooling-refuge sites are pre-verified for accessibility and facility readiness, eliminating remediation delays. Migrant organizations are identified and briefed early, enabling 8-12 community ambassadors to be recruited, vetted and trained by Month 2 (2026-12-08), supporting language-access targets. Faith-leader networks accelerate trusted-messenger recruitment. By Month 4 (2027-02-08), 3,000+ high-risk residents are enrolled and 60%+ are contacted, gates are met, and the program scales with credibility across EU peer cities.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If municipal registry is outdated or incomplete, conduct rapid community canvas by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23): partner liaison officer and 2-3 community volunteers visit neighborhoods, query libraries, pharmacies, post offices, markets and faith centers by phone and in-person to build a current contact list. Budget: €3k-5k; timeline: 2-3 weeks.
  • If formal social-services registry is unavailable, request the municipal integration officer or health department to provide names and phone numbers of known social organizations and programs; cross-check against online directories (Plataforma del Voluntariado de España, regional NGO databases, Linkedin searches for organization staff).
  • If housing-association data is fragmented across municipal housing authority and regional cooperatives, issue a formal information request (solicitud de acceso) by Month 0 (2026-10-08) to municipal housing authority and regional government housing office, with 10-day statutory response time.
  • If faith-organization contacts are weak, contact the Castellón archdiocese, the regional Islamic Federation (FEERI), and municipal religious affairs office for list of registered congregations and their social-outreach leaders; follow with phone verification of active programs.
  • If migrant-community organizations are sparse in the directory, engage the municipal integration office (oficina de inmigración) or regional integration authority to request names and contacts of established migrant associations; cross-check census data on non-Spanish speakers by neighborhood to identify likely locations for targeting outreach.
  • If partner data-governance frameworks are unclear, conduct a rapid 30-minute legal screening call with GDPR counsel (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23) to identify which partners likely have lawful bases (public-task welfare duties, existing client consent) and which require new consent; use findings to prioritize GDPR vetting.
  • If partner outreach capacity is reported as uncertain or minimal, propose a small pilot engagement with 2-3 partners (e.g., one housing association, one NGO, one pharmacy chain) in Month 1 (2026-11-08) to test call volumes and success rates before scaling to all partners; adjust targets and recruitment based on pilot results.
  • If accessibility or facility readiness data for proposed refuge sites is missing, conduct a rapid site survey by municipal facilities/accessibility officer and partner liaison officer in Month 1 (2026-11-08): checklist inspection (ramps, toilets, water, AED, parking) of each proposed site, documented with photos and remediation cost estimates; drop or defer sites requiring >€10k remediation or >4 weeks work (per threshold).
  • If cooling-refuge sites prove inadequate after survey, activate contingency site list (e.g., larger malls with seasonal tenants, municipal sports halls with off-season availability, temporary modular cooling units if budget allows); re-plan network footprint by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23).
  • If the directory cannot be completed by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), proceed with identified partners (50-70% of initial target) by Month 1 (2026-11-08) and backfill additional partners by Month 2 (2026-12-08); accept a 5-10% reduction in enrolled-resident target and geo-coverage to avoid delaying GDPR vetting and partner engagement.

Find Document 8: Cooling Kit Suppliers & Availability (Exterior Shading, Reflective Blinds, Fans, Thermometers)

ID: 5e244756-36a0-4a28-a693-3aeede639bd9

Description: Supplier market survey for home-kit components: manufacturers or distributors of exterior shading/blinds, window fans, digital thermometers, and hygrometers available in Spain or Europe; unit costs, minimum order quantities, lead times (weeks to delivery), expedite options, and product specifications (quality, durability, safety standards for fans). Used to finalize kit procurement specifications and budget, and to validate whether €800k is sufficient for 2,000 homes.

Recency Requirement: Current pricing & availability (2024-2025); valid for 2-3 months lead time.

Responsible Role Type: Home Interventions and Handyperson Coordinator

Steps to Find:

  • Conduct online search for EU/Spanish suppliers of: exterior aluminum blinds/shading (e.g., Bandalux, Gradus, Hunter Douglas, or local Spanish brands), reflective window treatments, directional window fans (6-8 inch, safe for elderly use), and digital thermometer/hygrometer kits.
  • Request quotes from ≥3 suppliers per component (shading, blinds, fans, thermometers) for bulk orders (600-2,000 units); specify quality standards (safety, durability), lead time, and per-unit cost.
  • Check if municipal procurement framework agreements already exist for energy-efficiency or home-improvement kits; may allow faster ordering.
  • Request lead-time and expedite-cost information for Q1-Q2 2027 (Feb-May 2027) delivery to align with project schedule.
  • Inquire about bulk discounts, payment terms, and product warranties.

Access Difficulty: Medium. Supplier information is available online or via direct contact; competition is moderate. Pricing varies by supplier, quality, and order size; multiple quotes are essential for cost validation.

Essential Information:

  • Identify supplier options for exterior aluminum shading/blinds (e.g., Bandalux, Gradus, Hunter Douglas, local Spanish brands) with unit costs, minimum order quantities and lead times (weeks to delivery) for bulk orders (600–2,000 units).
  • Confirm availability and lead times for 6–8 inch directional window fans safe for elderly use, with safety certifications (CE, UL or equivalent) and durability specifications.
  • List digital thermometer/hygrometer kits suitable for distributed placement; specify accuracy, display readability for vision-impaired users and battery life.
  • Obtain quotes from ≥3 suppliers per component (shading, blinds, fans, thermometers); compare per-unit cost, bulk discounts, payment terms and product warranties.
  • Verify whether municipal procurement framework agreements already exist for energy-efficiency or home-improvement kits that could accelerate ordering.
  • Confirm expedite-cost premium (% markup) and feasibility of Q1–Q2 2027 delivery (February–May 2027) to align with project home-installation schedule.
  • Validate whether €300 per-home cost assumption (€250 hardware + €50 installation labour) is achievable under current market conditions or requires adjustment.
  • Identify backup suppliers (2–3 per category) to mitigate single-source delay risk, with lead times and alternative product specifications.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Supplier quotes not obtained by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01) delay first call-off order to after Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), pushing 40–50% kit delivery past Month 4 (2027-02-08) and home installations beyond May–June peak-risk season; estimated delay 4–8 weeks and lost mortality protection.
  • Inaccurate cost data (e.g., suppliers quoting higher per-unit prices than budget assumed) reveals a shortfall in the €800k home-kit allocation mid-procurement, forcing cuts to kit quantity (500–1,000 fewer homes) or quality, or triggering budget reallocation that defunds transport or outreach.
  • Supplier lead times longer than 4–6 weeks (e.g., 8–10 weeks from Asian supply-chain issues) make February delivery impossible without expensive expedite premiums (10–15%, €50k–100k estimate), exhausting contingency reserve.
  • Fan products lacking proper safety certifications or durability for Mediterranean climate (e.g., corrosion in salt air) lead to resident safety incidents, liability claims or equipment failures mid-season requiring replacement.
  • No identified backup suppliers means a single-source production delay or supplier bankruptcy forces abandonment of that component or sourcing at emergency premium costs.
  • Missing framework agreement research causes re-procurement from scratch using slower competitive tendering, delaying orders by 3–4 weeks and missing the Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate.

Worst Case Scenario: Supplier availability survey is delayed or returns inadequate data (no confirmed quotes, lead times >8 weeks, per-unit costs 20–30% higher than budgeted). The project cannot place first call-off orders by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14) and misses the Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate procurement deadline. Home kits do not arrive until May–June at earliest, leaving no time for installation before summer peak-heat season (Months 6.8–11.8 = 2027-05-08 to 2027-10-08). Project is forced to cut kit scope from 2,000 homes to <1,000 or abandon home interventions entirely, reducing estimated mortality protection by 15–25% and failing to meet equity targets for top-floor and social-housing priority units. Budget shortfall of €100k–200k forces cuts to transport retainer or outreach staffing, jeopardizing the Month 4 (2027-02-08) gates and credibility of the pilot.

Best Case Scenario: Supplier survey identifies 3–4 competitive suppliers per component by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01) with per-unit costs within or below budget (€250 hardware), lead times 4–6 weeks, and established frameworks or bulk-discount terms. First call-off order for 600–800 kits (30–40% of 2,000) placed by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14) with expedite delivery to February; 40–50% stock in place by Month 4 (2027-02-08) allows installation pipeline to reach 80% completion by Month 7.3 (2027-05-17), covering 1,600 homes before and during peak summer heat. Backup suppliers identified and pre-qualified reduce single-source risk. Full-scale home-intervention coverage meets equity targets for top-floor and social-housing priority units. Cost savings from early competitive bidding preserve €50k–100k of contingency for other risks.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If lead times >6 weeks: negotiate expedite fees (10–15% premium, €50k–100k estimate) with top 2–3 suppliers for February delivery to maintain timeline; absorb cost within the €800k home-kit budget or draw from contingency.
  • If per-unit costs 15–20% above budget: reduce target kit quantity from 2,000 to 1,500–1,700 homes, prioritizing top-floor and social-housing units; scale lower without proportionally reducing installation quality.
  • If preferred suppliers unavailable or backlogged: activate 2–3 pre-identified backup suppliers by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01) and conduct parallel procurement (split order across suppliers) to diversify risk and ensure volume.
  • If municipal frameworks do not exist: conduct a fast competitive tender in two lots (shading/blinds in one lot, fans/thermometers in another) by Month 1 (2026-11-08), with 2-week turnaround to place orders by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23).
  • If installation costs higher than €50/unit: negotiate fixed-price handyperson contracts by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) or train municipal or volunteer installers (2–3 week ramp) to reduce labour cost.
  • If no home kits available by April: defer non-priority (lower-scoring rubric) installations to Year 2 or shift to a seasonal lending scheme (May install, September collection) to stretch existing stock across multiple summers and reduce upfront procurement burden.

Strengths

  • Established practice: heat action plans, refuges and welfare checks are proven, giving low novelty risk.
  • Existing municipal assets (libraries, community centers, parish halls) allow about 10 refuge sites (~400 places) without construction.
  • Intermediary-held lists keep personal data with trusted partners, lowering GDPR exposure and reaching offline residents.
  • Mayoral-level command with a public-health deputy speeds cross-department approvals and procurement.
  • Disciplined design: a tiered alert ladder (Level 1 advisory) limits alert fatigue, explicit gates and a €280k contingency (8%).
  • Strong NGO networks and a nearby university (Valencia) support outreach, language access and evaluation.

Weaknesses

  • KILLER APPLICATION MISSING: no single compelling flagship use-case yet exists that makes residents, partners and other cities adopt the model. The plan is a bundle of seven workstreams, so the value proposition is diffuse and hard to communicate or scale.
  • Month 2 (2026-12-08) and Month 4 (2027-02-08) gates fall in the cool season, so evidence rests on drills, which funders may see as weaker.
  • Hard critical path: procurement, hiring (43 peak FTE) and vetting of ≥20 volunteers all compress into Months 0-2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08).
  • Baseline data (80-120 EMS calls, 15-25 excess deaths, provisional estimates) is unverified, and small-area counts are noisy.
  • Contingency (€280k) cannot cover both the taxi-only fallback and a delayed release (exposure €350-650k, estimate).
  • No identified funding for Year 2 (≈€2.3M/year, estimate).
  • Opt-in/intermediary reach: 3,000 enrolled residents is ≈9% of 65+ (estimate), leaving most at-risk people unreached.

Opportunities

  • Develop a killer application: a 'Hot Night Guarantee' for enrolled high-risk residents. Any Level 2-3 alert triggers a trusted-person call within a set time, a ride to a refuge within 45 minutes, and a fitted cool home. One simple promise could drive enrollment, trust and funder interest. Obstacles: it depends on volunteer and taxi capacity, partner call capacity, GDPR-limited reach, a cool-season launch, and a promise that must be kept at surge.
  • Use the 2,000 home kits (rubric-scored) as a visible, tangible benefit that supports enrollment.
  • Learn from Barcelona's refuge network and Paris's registry protocols, and from Ahmedabad's tiered alerts and evaluation.
  • Publish a reusable playbook and cost model (€/center-hour, €/trip, €/enrollee) to attract EU funding for scaling.
  • Use trusted messengers (pharmacists, GPs, caretakers, faith leaders) and ambassadors to build trust and referrals.
  • Local data from the first season can calibrate alert thresholds for Year 2.

Threats

  • Cool June-July weather could leave the gates untestable, delaying the €1.5M and causing a €200-400k cash gap (estimate).
  • Supply-chain slippage of 4-8 weeks could push kit installation past the first heat events.
  • Volunteer shortfall could push pickup times above 45 minutes or force taxi-only operation (+€150-250k).
  • GDPR challenge or partner withdrawal could cut outreach reach by 10-25%.
  • Reputational damage from an incident at a refuge, an outreach assault or a failed response under media attention.
  • Staff fatigue and surge in multi-day heat waves could cut service 10-25%.
  • Misinformation (alcohol, fan misuse) and weak trust among migrants.
  • Political turnover or competing crises could weaken incident command.

Recommendations

  • Month 0-1 (2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08): Incident commander and communications lead define the 'Hot Night Guarantee' (call, ride, cool home) as the flagship offer. Test its wording with focus groups by Month 1 (2026-11-08).
  • Month 1 (2026-11-08): Procurement lead issues specs by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01), places the first 30-40% kit call-off at Month 1.2 (2026-11-14) and signs the taxi retainer (cap €80k), with 2-3 backup suppliers per category.
  • Month 0.5-1.5: Legal counsel and partner liaison officer obtain the GDPR opinion (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) and sign partner DPAs (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23).
  • Month 0-3 (2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08): HR coordinator and volunteer lead recruit in fortnightly cohorts, with ≥20 vetted by Month 2 (2026-12-08). If fewer than 20 are in the pipeline at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), scale the retainer.
  • Month 2.5-4: Operations lead finalizes the drill protocol (Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23), runs the full-system drill (Month 3.2 = 2027-01-14) and closes after-action items by Month 3.9 (2027-02-04). The funder is briefed on the 50% partial-release rule.
  • Month 2-7 (2026-12-08 to 2027-05-08): Health deputy and university partner agree EMS/ED coding and a pre-specified evaluation protocol. They also identify a Year-2 funding source by Month 9 (2027-07-08).

Strategic Objectives

  • Pass the Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate: ≥8 of 10 refuge sites signed, ≥50% of places accessible, retainer signed, ≥20 volunteers vetted, and 100% of tranche-1 orders placed.
  • Pass the Month 4 (2027-02-08) scale gate: ≥80% of planned refuge hours delivered in the drill, ≥60% contact success from ≥300 attempts, mean pickup <45 min over ≥30 requests, and all after-action items closed.
  • Enroll 3,000 high-risk residents by Month 7 (2027-05-08), with ≥5% of outreach calls in non-official languages.
  • Install kits in 2,000 homes (rubric score ≥60) by Month 7.3 (2027-05-17), with 10-20% of installs inspected.
  • By Month 12 (2027-10-08), deliver the playbook, cost model, evaluation report and a Year-2 roadmap with an identified funding source.

Assumptions

  • Castellón de la Plana (~170k residents) is the pilot site; population estimates (65+ ≈34,000) are unverified.
  • Baseline of 80-120 EMS calls and 15-25 excess deaths per summer is provisional.
  • Alert thresholds (≥33°C/20°C advisory; ≥35°C/22°C alert) are proposed and will be reviewed after the first season.
  • The funder accepts drill evidence for the Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate and the 50% partial-release rule.
  • No new legislation is needed, and the mayor signs the delegation of authority by Month 1 (2026-11-08).
  • The budget is 100% grant-financed, with no revenue.

Missing Information

  • Verified local EMS, ED and mortality history, and heat coding practice.
  • Recruitment evidence for volunteer drivers and taxi retainer quotes.
  • Partner call-center capacity and lawful basis confirmed by counsel (AEPD view).
  • Resident research on what offer would drive enrollment (killer-app validation).
  • Accessibility audit results for candidate sites.
  • Funder's written position on drill-based gates.
  • Year-2 funding source.
  • Local migrant language mix, to be confirmed Month 0 (2026-10-08).

Questions

  • Which single promise to residents would make an isolated 75-year-old enroll, and can the city keep it on its worst day?
  • Is the 45-minute pickup target realistic for wheelchair users with 40 volunteers and a capped €80k retainer?
  • What happens if the funder rejects drill evidence at Month 4 (2027-02-08), and can the €160k tranche-1 contingency cover the gap?
  • Does the intermediary-list model reach the most isolated residents, or does it mainly reach people already known to services?
  • Who funds Year 2, and which components would be cut if funding is only partial?

Roles Needed & Example People

Roles

1. Heat Response Incident Commander

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Incident Commander must maintain continuous authority and institutional knowledge across a 12-month program with critical decision points at Months 2 and 4 (2026-12-08, 2027-02-08). This role drives daily governance, procurement approvals, and cross-department coordination throughout setup and operational phases. Political accountability and delegation-of-authority requirements demand a stable, authorized municipal officer, not a contractor or temporary arrangement.

Explanation: Serves as the single point of authority for all alert declarations, operational decisions and cross-department coordination. Resides in or is delegated from the mayor's office, with a public-health deputy. Declares alerts, authorizes spending per tier, chairs daily SITREPs, and is accountable to the city for all response actions. Essential for speed, clarity and political legitimacy during real or simulated heat events.

Consequences: Without clear, single-authority incident command, alert declarations will be delayed or contested across departments. Cross-department orders may conflict. Procurement approvals will stall. Political accountability will blur, inviting media scrutiny if a response fails. The city will fail to meet the Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate (incident command authority signed and operational).

People Count: 1 primary incident commander (mayor's office or delegated) + 1 deputy (public health) = 2 total. The deputy must be capable of full authority if the primary is unavailable.

Typical Activities: Declares heat alerts based on forecast thresholds within 1 hour of trigger; chairs daily SITREPs at 08:30 during alerts; authorizes spending per alert tier and resolves disputes between departments (e.g., cooling-center hours vs. budget); signs incident-command delegation letters and updates authorities if unavailable; reviews daily aggregate EMS/ED counts and escalates if volume exceeds thresholds; signs off on after-action reports and gate assessments; maintains continuity briefings with successor if political transitions occur.

Background Story: María José García Ribera, 58, from Valencia, is a seasoned municipal administrator with 22 years in city government, including 8 years managing civil-protection responses to flooding and industrial incidents. She holds a degree in public administration and an executive qualification in emergency management. For the past 3 years, she has advised the mayor's office on resilience and sustainability. Her familiarity with heat-response protocols is limited but her authority to coordinate cross-department action is established; the mayor has explicitly delegated heat-alert declaration to her with written authority. She is known for decisive, evidence-based decision-making under time pressure.

Equipment Needs: Computer with dual monitors and secure municipal network access; secure phone line and encrypted mobile device; incident-command software or shared access to alert tracking spreadsheet; audio-video conferencing system for daily SITREPs (08:30 briefings across departments); municipal authorization letter and delegation documentation (signed, filed); weather alert feed direct from national meteorological service (AEMET); real-time EMS/ED aggregate data dashboard (view-only secure access); alert-declaration templates and checklist documents.

Facility Needs: Private office at mayor's office or civil protection HQ with 24-hour access during Months 6–11 (2027-04-08 to 2027-09-08); desk, phone and network connectivity; backup command-post facility (civil protection or health department) with same connectivity in case primary office is unavailable; secure meeting room for daily SITREPs (10–12 person capacity, AV equipment); access to municipal procurement and budget-authority systems.

2. Cooling Center Network Manager

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Cooling Center Network Manager must contract sites, conduct accessibility audits, oversee staffing, and ensure 80% planned-hours delivery at the Month 4 gate (2027-02-08). This is continuous core accountability from Month 0 (2026-10-08) through Month 12 (2027-10-08), with front-loaded site-contracting work (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) and sustained operational oversight during the season (Months 6–11 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-09-08). Staffing and safety protocols at 10 sites require institutional knowledge and real-time decision-making that only a full-time dedicated manager can deliver.

Explanation: Owns the end-to-end delivery of the 10-site cooling refuge network: facility contracting, accessibility audits, staffing oversight, scheduling of opening hours by alert level, safety protocols (first-aid, AED, escalation), and utilization reporting. Ensures 80% of planned center-hours are delivered and ≥50% of places are fully accessible. Reports daily occupancy and any incidents to incident command during alerts.

Consequences: Without a single center manager, site contracting and accessibility will slip past the Month 2 (2026-12-08) gate. Staffing will be uncoordinated; openings will miss scheduled hours. The 80% planned-hours gate (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) will fail. Residents will arrive at closed or over-capacity sites, harming credibility and equity.

People Count: 1 center network manager (full-time, Months 0-12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08). Plus 18 FTE part-time center staff (14 core + 4 reserve) across 10 sites, hired in cohorts during Months 3-5 (2027-01-08 to 2027-03-08).

Typical Activities: Identifies and audits 10 cooling-center sites (libraries, community centers, parish halls) for accessibility (wheelchair ramps, water points, accessible toilets, quiet rooms); contracts facility-use MOUs specifying hours and staffing responsibility; hires and onboards 18 part-time center staff in cohorts; publishes center accessibility information (routes, toilets, parking) in plain language; ensures ≥1 first-aid-certified staffer and AED per site; schedules opening hours by alert level (10:00–20:00 at Level 2, 24-hour at Level 3); reports daily occupancy, staffing and incidents to command.

Background Story: Ricardo Martínez López, 45, from Castellón, holds a degree in architecture and has managed municipal facilities for 15 years, including libraries and community centers. He has overseen accessibility audits for disability compliance and has experience contracting maintenance and security services. His knowledge of heat-response infrastructure is new; he attended a 2-day climate-resilience training in Barcelona in 2024. He is detail-oriented, process-driven and skilled at managing relationships with external facility managers and contractors. He speaks Spanish and Valencian fluently.

Equipment Needs: Site-inspection checklist forms (printable, wheel-measure for distances, camera); accessibility audit tool (wheelchair-simulation, bathroom-door-width gauge, step height measure); first-aid certification tracking spreadsheet; AED procurement specifications and maintenance contracts; staffing rota software or shared spreadsheet; cooling-center occupancy/incident-reporting forms; communication devices (mobile phone, landline at office); cooling-center signage templates (printed, large-format for accessibility).

Facility Needs: Office space (0.5-desk footprint) at municipal facilities department or city hall; internet access and phone line; secure storage for site-audit documentation and facility contracts; access to all 10 cooling-center sites for inspections (transport/vehicle or reimbursement); meeting space at each site for handover briefings with facility managers (10 visits, ~2 hours each); access to municipal procurement and facilities-management systems.

3. Transport Dispatch and Mobility Coordinator

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Transport Dispatch and Mobility Coordinator must recruit, vet and manage 30–50 volunteer drivers (4–8 week vetting process), negotiate and manage a taxi standby-retainer contract, and operate dispatch during peak alert-day demand. This role spans continuous procurement and safeguarding accountability (Months 0–4 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-02-08) and sustained operational leadership (Months 5–12 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-10-08). The 45-minute transport-time gate (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) depends on this coordinator's ability to execute complex multi-vendor coordination and volunteer-management infrastructure that cannot be built or maintained part-time.

Explanation: Recruits, vets and schedules volunteer drivers (target 40); manages the taxi standby-retainer contract; operates the transport dispatch center during alert days; coordinates with cooling centers on occupancy; tracks request-to-pickup time and escalates delays. Ensures mean pickup time <45 minutes and 100% of transport requests are attempted. Responsible for safeguarding vetting (background checks, insurance, training) and volunteer driver retention.

Consequences: Without a dedicated coordinator, volunteer recruitment will stall and vetting will not be completed by Month 2 (2026-12-08). Taxi retainers will be unsigned or unmanaged. Dispatch will lack capacity during peak alert days, causing wait times to exceed 45 minutes and the transport-time gate to fail. Safeguarding breaches are more likely if vetting is weak or decentralized.

People Count: 1 mobility coordinator (full-time, Months 0-12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08) + 2 dispatch operators (alert-day hours, May-September, ~40% FTE seasonal) + 1 backup coordinator (standby, ~20% FTE). Total 1.6 FTE equivalent. Plus volunteer driver recruitment support from Month 0 (2026-10-08) and taxi/paratransit vendor management.

Typical Activities: Recruits and vets 30–50 volunteer drivers via NGO networks and community outreach; conducts background checks, insurance verification and safeguarding training (4–8 weeks per cohort); manages a taxi standby-retainer contract with 2–3 suppliers; coordinates with dispatch operators to log transport requests, assign drivers and track time-to-pickup; escalates delays >45 minutes and reallocates drivers dynamically; conducts transport stress tests and drills; maintains volunteer driver rota and substitute coverage; reports mean pickup time and request-fulfillment rates daily during alerts.

Background Story: Ahmed Hassan El-Sayed, 52, originally from Egypt, settled in Valencia 18 years ago and holds Spanish citizenship. He has 20 years of experience in transportation and logistics, including fleet management for a taxi cooperative. He is fluent in Spanish, Valencian, Arabic and English. He has no formal training in heat response but has worked with vulnerable populations through volunteer ambulance-driver roles. He is known for reliability, problem-solving and an ability to build trust with drivers and community partners. He understands insurance requirements and background-check processes.

Equipment Needs: Transport dispatch software (spreadsheet or low-code platform) with real-time visibility to volunteer-driver location, transport requests, and arrival times; secure phone and mobile radio system for dispatchers; volunteer-driver insurance and vetting database (secure spreadsheet or minimal HR system); driver scheduling/rota software; stress-test scenario protocols and timing tools; transport-contract templates and vendor-management files; safeguarding incident-reporting forms.

Facility Needs: Dedicated dispatch office or workstation (3 FTE: 2 operators + 1 backup/coordinator) with dual monitors per operator; 24-hour phone line and mobile coverage; secure climate-controlled facility for volunteer-driver records (vetting, insurance); meeting space for volunteer-driver training (20–30 person capacity, 4-hour sessions, fortnightly cohorts Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08); fleet-staging area or parking for volunteer vehicles pre-positioned on alert days; access to municipal vehicle insurance and background-check processes.

4. Outreach and Street Contact Lead

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Outreach and Street Contact Lead must design outreach protocols, partner with 4–6 intermediary organizations, conduct escalation training for 25–35 staff, and manage the 60% contact-success gate (Month 4 = 2027-02-08). This role requires continuous engagement with partners, design iteration based on early feedback, and real-time monitoring during alert days. The scope spans governance (MOUs, training), operations (contact tracking, escalation), and equity (reach monitoring), all of which demand a full-time institution-facing role, not episodic consulting.

Explanation: Designs and deploys door-knock and street-contact protocols for high-risk residents. Works with housing associations, social services, NGOs and pharmacies to conduct phone and in-person outreach; manages a 'no wrong door' enrollment pathway via the heat line and in-person at cooling centers. Owns heat-illness escalation training for outreach staff, safety protocols for street-contact teams, and monitoring of the 60% contact-success gate. Reports daily outreach metrics to command during alerts.

Consequences: Without dedicated outreach leadership, intermediary partners (housing associations, NGOs, social services) will operate inconsistently or not at all. Contact success will fall below 60%, failing the Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate. Unhoused residents will be missed entirely if street-contact protocols are not designed. Escalation training will not occur, increasing risk of delayed EMS calls during heat illness.

People Count: 1 outreach lead (full-time, Months 0-12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08) + 6 FTE outreach staff (door-knock teams, phone check-in staff, street-contact coordinators) hired in Months 3-5 (2027-01-08 to 2027-03-08). Plus partner-coordination roles split with the partner-liaison officer.
