Typical Activities: Co-designs heat-illness escalation checklists with clinical staff for outreach teams; partners with housing associations, social services and NGOs to establish call protocols and contact targets (300+ attempts/alert day); trains 25–35 outreach and street-contact staff on heat-illness recognition, de-escalation and escalation rules (test ≥80%); monitors daily contact attempts and success rates via shared tracking spreadsheet; conducts mid-season partner reviews to resolve capacity gaps; escalates if contact success drops below 60%; tracks reach by neighborhood deprivation, age and language; manages the no-wrong-door enrollment pathway via the heat line and in-person centers.

Background Story: Laura Fernández Serrano, 41, from Alicante, holds a master's degree in public health and has 14 years in municipal social services, including 6 years managing outreach to homeless and isolated elderly residents. She speaks Spanish, Valencian and English and has led successful enrollment campaigns for municipal health programs (reach 70–80% of target populations). Her experience with GDPR compliance is intermediate; she has managed confidentiality protocols for social-services client lists. She is experienced in motivating partner organizations and resolving conflicts over data-sharing and accountability.

Equipment Needs: Heat-illness escalation checklist (printed, laminated for outreach staff); phone triage protocols and decision-tree documents; partner-contact database (contact names, phone, email for housing associations, social services, NGOs, pharmacies); call-script templates (printed, translated); shared outreach-tracking spreadsheet (secure, visible to partners and city); training materials (slide decks, role-play scenarios); escalation phone numbers (112, nurse line, poison control); outreach incident-reporting forms; no-wrong-door enrollment intake forms (paper and digital).

Facility Needs: Office (1 FTE) at social services or outreach-coordination hub with phone, email and secure internet; meeting space for partner coordination (6–8 person capacity, Months 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08 weekly); training facility (30–40 person capacity) for outreach and street-contact staff training (80 hours total, Months 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08); access to municipal GP, pharmacy and NGO partner offices for joint briefings; secure storage for outreach escalation protocols and incident logs.

5. Heat Helpline and Phone Operations Manager

Contract Type: part_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Heat Helpline and Phone Operations Manager can operate effectively as a part-time employee (0.5 FTE Months 1–12 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-10-08) because the phone line itself is mostly inactive (10–15 alert days per summer of 120 days peak season ≈ 12% utilization). The manager role is to build and maintain the system before Months 5–8 (2027-03-08 to 2027-06-08), then supervise reactive operations during alerts. Administrative setup dominates Months 1–4 (2026-11-08 to 2027-02-08); operational intensity is episodic, not continuous.

Explanation: Establishes and operates the heat-alert phone line (08:00-22:00 daily, 24-hour at Level 3); integrates phone intake with transport dispatch and cooling-center occupancy; trains phone operators on escalation protocols and multilingual service; manages call logging and escalation tracking. Ensures phone line is live and responsive by Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate.

Consequences: Without a dedicated phone manager, the heat line will open late (missing the Month 2 = 2026-12-08 gate) or will operate at poor quality (long wait times, misrouted requests). Callers will not be connected to transport dispatch or cooling-center availability in real-time. The shared tracking system will not be built or maintained, causing dispatch/center coordination failures during peak alert demand.

People Count: 1 phone operations manager (part-time, ~0.5 FTE, Months 1-12 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-10-08) + 2-3 part-time phone operators (30 hours/week during alert season, ~0.75 FTE each, May-September) + 1 backup operator (on-call). Total 2.75-3.25 FTE seasonal equivalent.

Typical Activities: Establishes and operates the heat-alert helpline (08:00–22:00 daily, 24 hours on Level 3 days); hires and trains 2–3 part-time phone operators in heat-illness escalation, cooling-center locations and multilingual service; integrates phone intake with transport dispatch and center occupancy via a shared real-time spreadsheet; logs caller details (transport request, center preference, language) and confirms pickup time and center availability within 15 minutes; updates center occupancy every 30 minutes during alerts; conducts monthly call-quality audits; tracks wait times and call volume by alert level.

Background Story: Susana Ruiz Gómez, 38, from Castellón, holds a degree in business administration and has 12 years' experience running a municipal health-information line. She has managed call centers, trained phone operators in customer service and de-escalation, and set up shared tracking systems using spreadsheets and simple cloud tools. Her heat-response knowledge is minimal; she attended a half-day orientation on heat illness. She is calm under pressure, detail-oriented about protocol compliance and skilled at managing operator fatigue and quality during long shifts.

Equipment Needs: Phone-line equipment (dedicated number, answering system, call-recording for quality assurance); heat-helpline intake form (digital and printable); call-tracking spreadsheet (shared with dispatch and cooling centers in real-time); phone operator scripts and checklists (cooling-center locations, transport request workflow, escalation rules); cooling-center occupancy update forms (for centers to phone in every 30 min during alerts); multi-language phone-tree menus and automated prompts (Spanish, Valencian, Arabic, Portuguese, etc.); interpreter scheduling system; quality-monitoring and call-time-tracking logs.

Facility Needs: Dedicated phone-line operations space (2–3 operator workstations with headsets and dual monitors); climate-controlled office with 24-hour access during Months 5–11 (2027-03-08 to 2027-09-08); high-quality phone and internet connectivity (redundant line for backup); secure storage for call recordings and daily logs (confidential per data-protection rules); meeting space for operator training (8–10 person capacity, 4-hour sessions, Months 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08 and monthly refreshers); access to municipal telephone and IT systems; contracted interpretation-service hub or on-call interpreter station.

6. Home Interventions and Handyperson Coordinator

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Home Interventions and Handyperson Coordinator must manage a critical 4–5 month procurement and installation timeline (Months 0–7 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-05-08) with zero tolerance for supply-chain delays past February–April. This role owns €800k in kit budget, vetting and training of 10 handypersons, and meeting the implicit gate that 40–50% of kits are installed by Month 4 (2027-02-08). The compressed procurement schedule, backup-supplier vetting, quality audits and installation supervision demand continuous full-time focus. After Month 7 (2027-05-08), the workload drops to close-out; a full-time appointment supports peak-season intensity and reduces restarting cost if procurement slips.

Explanation: Procures cooling kits (shading, fans, blinds, thermometers, hydration supplies), manages the first-call supply chain and backup vendors, oversees handyperson recruitment and fan-safety training, schedules installations in priority homes (top-floor, social housing, by rubric score), conducts 10-20% quality audits of installs, and tracks installations against targets. Delivers first 40-50% of kits by Month 4 (2027-02-08) and 100% by Month 6 (2027-04-08).

Consequences: Without a kit coordinator, procurement will slip past February and home interventions will miss the May-June heat season (20-25% loss in estimated mortality reduction). Handyperson vetting and training will not happen, risking unsafe fan installations (fire hazard, misuse). Supplier delays will not be managed; backup vendors will not be pre-qualified. The €800k home-kit budget will be wasted if kits are not installed by June.

People Count: 1 home-kit coordinator (full-time, Months 0-12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08) + 10 handypersons/installers (contracted or part-time, Months 4-7 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-05-17) + 1 quality-assurance auditor (contract, 20% FTE). Total 12 FTE equivalent across the 12 months, concentrated Feb-May.

Typical Activities: Issues procurement specifications for cooling kits (shading material, reflective blinds, fans, thermometers, hygrometers) to suppliers; obtains quotes and lead-time confirmations; places first call-off order for 30–40% of kits by November 15; pre-qualifies 2–3 backup suppliers and signs backup agreements; negotiates expedited delivery premiums (10–15%); arranges interim storage at municipal facilities; hires 10 handypersons and conducts 2-hour fan-safety and installation-safety training; schedules installations in priority homes (top-floor, social housing) by rubric score; conducts spot-check quality audits of 10–20% of installations; tracks kit delivery, installations completed and budget spend weekly.

Background Story: Carlos Morera Tomás, 50, from Valencia, is a retired construction supervisor with 28 years' experience managing installations and safety on residential sites. He holds certifications in electrical safety and workplace health. His heat-response knowledge is new; he recently completed a 2-day online course on heat-illness first aid. He is pragmatic, cost-conscious and skilled at quality control and vendor management. He speaks Spanish and Valencian and has established relationships with local trade contractors and suppliers.

Equipment Needs: Kit procurement specifications and RFQ documents; supplier quotes and lead-time confirmations (spreadsheet); first call-off order contracts and backup-supplier agreements; expedited-delivery authorization and payment-processing forms; interim storage-facility management (inventory tracking, climate control, security); handyperson hiring and vetting records (background check, insurance, training certificates); fan-safety and installation-safety training materials (slide decks, videos, printed handouts); quality-assurance audit checklists; kit-delivery and installation-tracking spreadsheet; budget and spend-tracking by kit category.

Facility Needs: Office (1 FTE) at municipal procurement or public works with phone and email; secure storage facility (500–800 m² minimum, climate-controlled, lockable) for kit inventory during Months 2–6 (2026-12-08 to 2027-04-08); access to municipal procurement, contracts and payment systems; meeting space for handyperson vetting and training (15–20 person capacity, 2-hour sessions, Months 3–4 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08); handyperson staging area or workshop for tool storage and kit assembly/checking before installation; access to supplier warehouses and delivery logistics (coordinate with municipal transport).

7. GDPR Compliance and Legal Officer

Contract Type: independent_contractor

Contract Type Justification: GDPR Compliance and Legal Officer can be delivered as an independent contractor (or hybrid: 0.5 FTE municipal staff + external specialist counsel). The role is expert-driven, bounded-scope legal work: template MOUs/DPAs (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08), partner briefings (Month 2 = 2026-12-08), and mid-season audit (Month 9 = 2027-07-08). Front-loaded deliverables (legal opinions by Month 1 = 2026-11-08) suit fixed-scope contracting. A dedicated municipal legal officer would underutilize during operations phases (Months 6–8 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-06-08). Specialist GDPR counsel (€15–30k contract) can be embedded; municipal support for partner engagement is 0.5 FTE (separate line item).

Explanation: Engages specialist GDPR counsel, oversees data-processing agreements (MOUs/DPAs) with all partner organizations (housing associations, social services, NGOs, pharmacies), ensures legal clearance for the intermediary-held-list model by Month 1 (2026-11-08), briefs partner staff on confidentiality and data-retention rules, and conducts mid-season GDPR audits. Protects the program from regulatory challenge and partner withdrawal.

Consequences: Without dedicated legal oversight, data-processing agreements will not be signed by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), delaying partner engagement. Partner withdrawal due to perceived GDPR risk could drop outreach reach by 10-20%. A regulatory inquiry or resident data-protection complaint could halt operations mid-season and force retrospective remediation (€15-30k estimate). The program loses credibility and transferability to peer EU cities.

People Count: 1 GDPR/legal officer (0.5 FTE, Months 0-12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08), supported by an external specialist GDPR law firm (contract, ≤€30k). Officer must have EU data-protection knowledge or access to legal counsel.

Typical Activities: Engages specialist GDPR law firm for template data-processing agreements (MOUs/DPAs) with housing associations, social services, NGOs and pharmacies; reviews lawful basis for contact (public-task/consent hybrid), retention periods (one season, then deletion) and breach-notification rules; obtains written legal opinion confirming intermediary-held model compliance; briefs 50–80 partner staff on confidentiality and data-retention obligations before Month 2 (2026-12-08); conducts mid-season GDPR audit of partner consent records and training logs (Month 9 = 2027-07-08); escalates any suspected data breach to the data protection authority; drafts annual data-protection impact assessment (DPIA) summary if required.

Background Story: Isabel Montoya Riera, 43, from Barcelona, is a municipal legal adviser specializing in data protection and public procurement. She holds a master's degree in data protection law (GDPR focus) and has 10 years' experience drafting privacy notices, data-processing agreements and compliance audits. Her familiarity with heat-response law is zero; heat programs are outside her previous brief. She is meticulous, risk-aware and skilled at managing relationships with data protection authorities and external counsel. She speaks Spanish, Catalan and English.

Equipment Needs: GDPR legal templates (MOU/DPA drafts); data-processing agreement tracking spreadsheet; partner contact and signature documentation (secure files); partner-staff training attendance logs and confidentiality certification; consent-form templates (translated into 4–6 languages); data-retention and deletion schedules; breach-notification procedures and incident-reporting forms; audit checklists for partner compliance (consent records, staff training, data-handling); legal opinion documentation (signed, dated); communication letters to data protection authority (AEPD) if required.

Facility Needs: Office (0.5 FTE) at municipal legal department or health department with secure file storage and phone; external specialist GDPR law firm on retainer (contract €15k–30k, Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08 intensive, then ad-hoc); meeting space for partner DPA signature sessions (6–8 partner organizations, 1–2 hours each, Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23); secure digital-signature or contract-management system (or secure email and filing); access to municipal data-protection register and AEPD contact information.

8. Communications, Language Access and Trusted Messenger Coordinator

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Communications, Language Access and Trusted Messenger Coordinator must design multilingual messaging, recruit and train 8–12 community ambassadors, manage translation of 4–6 languages, and execute a pre-season campaign (Month 6 = 2027-04-08 launch) and misinformation correction (≤4 hours response time during alerts). This is continuous core accountability Months 0–12 (2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08), with sustained operational intensity during the communication-heavy period (Months 5–8 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-06-08). Ambassador recruitment, translation procurement, and campaign execution require full-time coordination; the role cannot be fragmented across part-time or episodic effort.

Explanation: Designs and executes the public communications strategy: pre-season campaign, heat-event messaging templates, myth-busting content, trusted-messenger briefings (pharmacists, GPs, caretakers, faith leaders), translation and interpretation services, and rapid misinformation correction (≤4 hours). Recruits and trains 8-12 paid community-language ambassadors. Ensures messages are accessible to offline, elderly and migrant residents. Reports media-monitoring and reach metrics to incident command.

Consequences: Without a dedicated coordinator, messages will not be translated into 4-6 local languages, excluding 5-15% of the population (estimated 500-1,500 residents in Castellón). Trusted messengers will not be briefed consistently, reducing uptake among offline and elderly residents. Misinformation (alcohol, fan misuse) will spread unchecked, causing unsafe behaviors and preventable heat illness. Public reach will drop by 10-20%, reducing enrollment and utilization by 500-2,000 residents.

People Count: 1 communications/language coordinator (full-time, Months 0-12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08) + 1 part-time communications officer or social-media monitor (10-15 hours/week during season, ~0.25 FTE) + 8-12 paid community-language ambassadors (10-15 hours/week during season, ~0.9 FTE equivalent). Total 2.15 FTE equivalent.

Typical Activities: Designs pre-season heat-safety campaign messaging (print, radio, SMS); focus-tests messages with older residents and migrants (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) to ensure clarity and cultural appropriateness; briefs trusted messengers (pharmacists, GPs, caretakers, faith leaders) with consistent scripts and leave-behind materials by Month 6 (2027-04-08); recruits and trains 8–12 paid community-language ambassadors to deliver messages in non-official languages during alert season; publishes alerts and public updates by 11:00 on Level 2–3 days; monitors social media and local forums for misinformation and responds with corrected facts within 4 hours; tracks message reach by demographic group and language; publishes translated door hangers, flyers and pictogram-first signage.

Background Story: Javier García Alonso, 47, from Castellón, holds a degree in journalism and has 18 years in municipal communications, including 8 years as communications director for the health department. He is fluent in Spanish and Valencian and has basic conversational skills in English. His heat-response communication experience is limited; he attended a 1-day workshop on climate-health messaging. He is creative, responsive to media inquiries and skilled at working with community leaders and NGO partners. He understands misinformation risk and social-media monitoring.

Equipment Needs: Pre-season campaign templates (radio scripts, poster graphics, flyer text, door-hanger designs, SMS templates); focus-group testing materials and feedback forms; trusted-messenger briefing packs (printed, translated, with role-play scenarios); community-language ambassador job descriptions, vetting forms and training materials; social-media monitoring dashboard (if available, or manual monitoring log); misinformation-correction fact-sheets (printed and digital); translation files for all key materials (4–6 languages); pictogram-based signage and instructional graphics (tested with non-literate users); media-contact list and press-release templates; campaign reach and demographic-tracking spreadsheet.

Facility Needs: Office (1 FTE) at municipal communications or health department with phone, email and design software (or contracted designer access); meeting space for focus-group testing (12–15 person capacity, Months 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08); trusted-messenger briefing venues (pharmacies, GP practices, faith centers, caretaker offices) for in-person training (8–12 sessions, 2 hours each, Month 6 = 2027-04-08); translation contractor workspace or external language-service provider; social-media monitoring tools or log-management system; radio and print-media production contacts and submission processes; immigrant community center or NGO space for ambassador recruitment and training (20–30 person capacity, Months 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08).

9. Project Coordination, PMO and Staffing Lead

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Project Coordination, PMO and Staffing Lead must deliver compressed procurement by Month 2 (2026-12-08), hire and onboard 43 FTE seasonal staff in Months 3–5 (2027-01-08 to 2027-03-08), track budget and KPIs daily during operations, and manage contingency escalation. This is the critical-path role for both setup (Months 0–4 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-02-08) and operational oversight (Months 5–12 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-10-08). The role requires continuous presence, no-handoff ownership of timelines, and real-time decision-support for the incident commander. Procurement compression, hiring ramp, budget burn rate, and gate measurement all depend on a single dedicated PMO lead; splitting this role or using a contractor would fragment accountability and miss early-warning signals.

Explanation: Serves as the operational backbone: project management (timeline, milestones, budget tracking), HR/recruitment coordination (hiring, onboarding, shift rota, fatigue management), procurement administration (order placement, vendor management, delivery tracking), data and KPI reporting (daily/weekly metrics), and contingency management (risk monitoring, decision-trigger escalation). Owns Months 0-4 (2026-10-08 to 2027-02-08) compressed timeline; transitions to evaluation support by Month 8 (2027-06-08).

Consequences: Without a PMO lead, procurement will not meet Month 2 (2026-12-08) deadline, slipping delivery by 2-4 weeks. Hiring timelines will miss, leaving centers and dispatch under-staffed in May-June. Budget tracking will be poor, risking €200-400k overspend or mid-season funding crisis. Risk escalation will be slow, causing the Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate decision to be made without clear readiness data. The playbook will not be drafted on time by Month 12 (2027-10-08).

People Count: 1 project manager / PMO lead (full-time, Months 0-12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08) + 0.5 FTE HR/recruitment coordinator (Months 0-6 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-04-08, peak intensity Months 0-4 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-02-08) = 1.5 FTE equivalent.

Typical Activities: Creates and maintains project timeline and Gantt chart tracking procurement, hiring and key milestones against Month 2 (2026-12-08) and Month 4 (2027-02-08) gates; monitors budget spend by category weekly and reforecasts cash flow; coordinates recruitment of 43 FTE seasonal staff in cohorts (40% Month 3, 40 = 2027-01-08, 2030-02-08% Month 4, 20 = 2027-02-08, 2028-06-08% Month 5 = 2027-03-08); tracks procurement orders (placement date, supplier, delivery date, receipt confirmation); escalates risks (supply delays, hiring shortfalls, budget overruns) to incident command when decision trigger thresholds are crossed (e.g., <20 volunteers by Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23); produces gate readiness reports at Months 2 and 4 (2026-12-08, 2027-02-08) with corrective-action status; manages contingency budget reserve (€160k tranche 1, €120k tranche 2); transitions to playbook-support role from Month 8 (2027-06-08).

Background Story: Silvia Serrano Domínguez, 35, from Castellón, holds a degree in business administration and has 8 years' experience in municipal project management, including coordination of European-funded urban regeneration projects. She has managed procurement timelines, hiring workflows and budget tracking. Her heat-response knowledge is minimal; she volunteered on a 1-week climate adaptation project in 2023. She is organized, deadline-driven and skilled at cross-team coordination and risk escalation. She speaks Spanish, Valencian and English.

Equipment Needs: Project timeline/Gantt chart software (Excel, Asana, Monday.com, or similar); budget-tracking spreadsheet (by category and vendor); procurement order log (placement date, supplier, delivery date, receipt status); hiring and onboarding checklist (job descriptions, contracts, offer letters, orientation materials); risk register and decision-trigger log; gate-readiness report templates (Month 2 and 4 = 2026-12-08, 2027-02-08); KPI dashboard (center hours, transport time, outreach success, budget spend); contingency-fund authorization forms; staff absence and rota-tracking system; vendor-performance and payment-processing files.

Facility Needs: Office (1.5 FTE: 1 FTE PMO + 0.5 FTE HR coordinator, Months 0–6 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-04-08 intensive; then 1 FTE for M&E support Months 7–12 = 2027-05-08 to 2027-10-08) at municipal administration or health department; dual-monitor workstations with phone and email; access to municipal project-management, HR, procurement and budget systems; secure shared-drive or cloud workspace for all stakeholder documents (read access for incident commander, coordination team; write access for PMO); meeting space for weekly coordination-team touchbases (8–10 person capacity, Monday mornings, 1 hour); access to municipal HR records and payroll for seasonal-staff management; printing and document-scanning facilities for procurement and hiring files.

Omissions

1. No dedicated mental health or occupational health support for staff and volunteers exposed to distressing scenes or heat-illness incidents

Outreach, street-contact and cooling-center staff will regularly encounter residents in acute heat distress, potential heat stroke and vulnerable populations during multi-day heat waves. The risk register identifies psychological harm and staff turnover as operational risks, but the team structure lacks an occupational health coordinator or mental health liaison. This is critical for staff retention, reducing turnover costs (€10–20k per replacement) and maintaining service quality during peak-demand periods.

Recommendation: Designate a 0.25 FTE occupational health liaison (municipal occupational health service or contracted occupational health nurse) responsible for: (1) debriefing staff after any heat-illness incident or distressing scene; (2) coordinating access to counselling services within 24 hours at city expense; (3) training team leaders on fatigue-management and burnout-recognition; (4) monitoring staff absences and sick leave for patterns indicating psychological harm; (5) conducting peer-support group sessions monthly during alert season. Include occupational health review at Months 2, 6 and 10 (2026-12-08, 2027-04-08, 2027-08-08) to identify emerging mental-health risks early.

2. No dedicated data quality assurance or evaluation lead for rigorous gate measurement and attribution analysis

The Month 4 (2027-02-08) gates depend on accurate measurement of center-hour delivery, outreach contact success, and transport time. The plan includes an evaluation design framework but assigns no FTE to data management, validation or real-time quality assurance during operations. Without a dedicated data officer, metrics will be incomplete, noisy or inconsistent across partners, risking indefensible gate decisions and weak playbook credibility for other EU cities.

Recommendation: Assign a dedicated 1 FTE Data and Evaluation Coordinator (statistician or data analyst, Months 2–12 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-10-08) to: (1) validate baseline EMS/ED data by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) and establish usable baseline by Month 3 (2027-01-08); (2) design and deploy real-time data collection forms for centers, transport, outreach and health partners; (3) conduct weekly data quality audits during operations (completeness, consistency, outlier flagging); (4) compute gate metrics (center hours, transport time, outreach success) by Month 3.9 (2027-02-04) with confidence intervals; (5) manage the evaluation database and prepare the Month 12 (2027-10-08) evaluation report. Link this role directly to incident command for daily KPI reporting during alerts.

3. No dedicated partner liaison and relationship manager for the 4–6 intermediary organizations and health system

The outreach model depends critically on housing associations, social services, NGOs, pharmacies and health providers maintaining engagement and consistent call-center capacity throughout the season. The plan mentions 'partner liaison officer' in stakeholder analysis but assigns no dedicated FTE; coordination is fragmented across outreach lead, GDPR officer and PMO. If a key partner faces capacity constraints or withdraws mid-season (15–20% risk), outreach reach could drop by 10–20%, failing the 60% contact-success gate.

Recommendation: Designate a dedicated 1 FTE Partner Liaison Officer (Months 0–12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08), reporting to the incident commander, to: (1) negotiate and sign MOUs with all 4–6 partner organizations by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); (2) conduct joint quarterly planning meetings at Months 1, 4, 7, 10 (2026-11-08, 2027-02-08, 2027-05-08, 2027-08-08) to review capacity and resolve conflicts; (3) maintain monthly contact with each partner to monitor call volume, staff capacity and early-warning signals of withdrawal; (4) provide real-time feedback on outreach performance (success rates, wait times, escalations) to partners; (5) identify and brief backup partners by Month 2 (2026-12-08) in case a primary partner drops. This role is essential for the 60% contact gate and for equity reach tracking.

4. No capacity for policy learning and Year-2 planning within the core team structure

The plan requires delivery of a Year-2 roadmap by Month 12 (2027-10-08) recommending what to expand, what to stop and what to scale city-wide. This demands synthesis of lessons from operations, equity tracking, staff feedback and cost accounting. The playbook-and-evaluation officer role (0.5 FTE Months 9–12 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08) is insufficient to simultaneously run end-of-season operations, draft the playbook, and conduct forward-looking policy analysis. Without dedicated capacity for reflection and planning, Year-2 roadmap will be rushed and will miss stakeholder input.

Recommendation: Add a 0.5 FTE Policy and Learning Officer (Months 8–12 = 2027-06-08 to 2027-10-08) working jointly with the PMO and evaluation lead to: (1) synthesize staff feedback, partner input and utilization data (Months 8–9 = 2027-06-08 to 2027-07-08); (2) conduct focus groups with high-risk residents about program experience (n=30–50, 2 groups, Month 9 = 2027-07-08); (3) cost out scenarios for Year-2 expansion (city-wide footprint, continued pilot, scale-back); (4) draft Year-2 roadmap with explicit go/no-go decisions for each service element (Months 10–11 = 2027-08-08 to 2027-09-08); (5) recommend budget and governance model for Year 2 (funder TBD). This role ensures transition from pilot to sustained program is informed, not reactive.

5. No dedicated quality assurance inspector for home-kit installation safety and building-code compliance

The plan includes 10 handypersons installing 2,000 cooling kits (exterior shading, fans) in homes during Months 4–7 (2027-02-08 to 2027-05-17). Safety checks (fan directional airflow, fire-hazard risk, building-code compliance) are mentioned in risk mitigation but no FTE is assigned to conduct them. A 10–20% audit rate (200–400 installs) requires ≥0.5 FTE site inspection capacity. Without dedicated inspection, unsafe installations or building-code violations could trigger enforcement action, litigation or media reputational damage.

Recommendation: Assign a 0.5 FTE Quality Assurance and Safety Inspector (municipal building inspector or contracted auditor, Months 4–7 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-05-17) to: (1) conduct spot-check inspections of 10–20% of home kit installations (prioritizing structural, fire and electrical safety); (2) verify handyperson certification and training records before installation begins; (3) issue corrective notices within 24 hours for any code violations or safety gaps; (4) track remediation completion; (5) maintain audit logs for liability protection. Integrate QA findings into weekly progress reports to the kit coordinator; pause installations if >3% of audited work is non-compliant.

Potential Improvements

1. Lack of explicit escalation decision tree and surge protocols for extreme-heat scenarios (40°C+ daytime or sustained multi-day heat)

The plan defines three alert levels with associated activations, but does not specify what additional actions trigger at sustained extremes (e.g., when forecast shows 40°C daytime for 5+ consecutive days, or national red warning persists). Extreme heat may require harder triage (directing oldest/frailest first), mutual-aid activation with hospitals, or temporary closure of some centers to concentrate staffing at largest sites. Without pre-set surge thresholds, incident command will improvise under crisis pressure, risking inconsistent decisions and reputational damage if a preventable death occurs during extreme heat.

Recommendation: Draft an Extreme-Heat Surge Protocol by Month 3 (2027-01-08) specifying: (1) Tier 3a activation threshold (forecast ≥40°C daytime for ≥3 days + night low ≥23°C) triggers: all centers 24-hour operation, priority transport for 75+ and wheelchair users, pre-positioned water/shading at all outdoor municipal work sites, and pre-notification to hospitals and EMS of expected surge; (2) Tier 3b (same + national red warning or ≥5 consecutive days) adds: mutual-aid activation with neighboring city (pre-agreed partner), surge staffing from municipal emergency-reserve pool, closure of smaller centers to concentrate service, and direct hospital-EMS escalation for any suspected heat illness; (3) Mutual-aid agreement signed by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23) with neighboring city (e.g., Villarreal, ~30 km) specifying resource-sharing (staff, center capacity, transport vehicles). Include surge protocol in the drill at Month 7 (2027-05-08).

2. Insufficient detail on how to handle conflicting operational decisions (e.g., transport demand spike vs. dispatch capacity, center over-capacity vs. safety protocols)

During an alert, the incident commander, center network manager, and transport coordinator may face decisions that conflict (e.g., a cooling center reaches 100% capacity but residents continue arriving; transport dispatch is 60 minutes behind; EMS call volume is at 1.8× baseline). The plan mentions escalation to incident command but does not specify decision algorithms, delegation limits or communication protocols that preserve speed and clarity under stress.

Recommendation: Develop an Operational Decision Matrix by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23) documenting: (1) Authority limits: incident commander has final authority on alert tier and stand-down; center network manager decides which sites to open and capacity adjustments; dispatch coordinator prioritizes by vulnerability (75+, wheelchair users, isolated residents) if wait times exceed 45 min; (2) Conflict resolution: if transport delay threatens the 45-min gate, dispatcher may request incident commander to authorize taxi-surge activation (additional vehicles at premium cost, up to €5k per day); (3) Safety thresholds: center closes entry if occupancy ≥110% fire-code capacity and transport redirects new arrivals to next-closest site with 15-min notice; (4) Health escalation: if EMS call volume reaches 1.5× baseline, commander notifies hospitals and prepares mutual-aid activation. Include conflict-scenario drills (e.g., capacity breach, dispatch overload) in the May full-system drill (Month 7 = 2027-05-08).

3. Limited clarity on financial accountability and mid-season budget re-forecasting if contingency is drawn or tranche-2 release is delayed

The plan allocates €280k contingency (8% of €3.5M) but does not specify: (1) who authorizes contingency draws >€10k; (2) how budget reforecasting occurs if tranche-2 (€1.5M) is delayed beyond Month 4 (2027-02-08); (3) which service elements are cut first if funding shortfalls occur; (4) how the city reports mid-season budget status to the funder and incident commander. Without clear financial governance, reactive spending and delayed decisions could cause missed gates or mid-season operational collapse.

Recommendation: Establish a Financial Governance Protocol by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) specifying: (1) Contingency-draw authority: draws >€5k require incident commander and PMO sign-off; draws >€25k also require funder notification within 24 hours; (2) Monthly budget review: PMO produces a spend-vs-forecast summary by the 25th of each month (Months 0–12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08), with re-forecast of cash flow to Month 12 (2027-10-08); (3) Trigger thresholds: if spend exceeds forecast by >10% (€200k), incident commander and PMO convene a budget-rebalancing meeting within 48 hours; if rebalancing cannot close the gap, funder is notified; (4) Spending priorities if funding shortfall: maintain center and transport operations first (gates 1 and 3); maintain outreach phone line second (gate 2); defer home-kit installations third (defer to Year 2 if needed); (5) Delayed release contingency: if Month 4 (2027-02-08) release is not approved, draw up to €150k from tranche-1 contingency (if available) to cover May–June operations, with re-test decision at Month 5 (2027-03-08). Monthly budget reports are presented to incident command and funder on the last working day of each month.

4. Underspecified role clarity and handoff procedures if the incident commander or other critical staff are absent during multi-day heat events

The plan names a deputy public-health incident commander but does not specify: (1) what decisions the deputy can make autonomously (alert declaration, spending authorization, resource reallocation) versus what requires consultation with the primary; (2) how long the primary can be absent before the deputy assumes full command; (3) handoff procedures and documentation if absence extends beyond 48 hours; (4) cross-training for the center manager, transport coordinator and communications lead to substitute for each other in emergencies.

Recommendation: Draft a Continuity of Command and Succession Protocol by Month 2 (2026-12-08) specifying: (1) Primary incident commander (mayor's office or delegated) is the sole authority for alert declarations and spending authorization up to €50k per alert tier; above €50k, written approval required. (2) Deputy incident commander (public health) has full authority to declare and execute the approved response if the primary is unavailable for ≥2 hours; continuation ≥24 hours requires written notification to the mayor and funder. (3) If both primary and deputy are unavailable, written delegation passes to the civil protection operations lead (pre-signed, filed with municipal legal department) with the same authorities as the deputy, valid for ≤48 hours; beyond 48 hours, incident command returns to the mayor or funder decision. (4) Cross-training: center network manager and partner liaison officer can make operational (non-alert-declaration) decisions on center hours and partner coordination if incident commander is unavailable; dispatch coordinator can prioritize transport requests autonomously. (5) Handoff documentation: a brief incident-command log records all alert declarations, spending decisions, staffing adjustments and escalations daily; at shift-change (every 12 hours on multi-day events), the incoming commander reviews the log and confirms understanding with the outgoing commander.

5. No explicit feedback loop from residents using the program to improve service delivery mid-season

The plan tracks operational KPIs (center hours, transport time, outreach success) but does not include a mechanism to capture resident feedback about: accessibility barriers, quality of welcome at centers, comfort level with cooling spaces, perceived safety, language-access adequacy, or trust in the heat-illness escalation protocols. This feedback could identify equity gaps (e.g., elderly women avoiding mixed-gender day spaces) or low-quality implementations (e.g., dirty toilets, rude staff) early enough to fix in-season, improving both outcomes and equity.

Recommendation: Implement a Simple Resident Feedback Loop by Month 6 (2027-04-08) consisting of: (1) Post-visit feedback cards at each cooling center (2–3 questions, large print, multilingual: 'Was this space comfortable? Did you understand what to do? Would you come again?'); staff collect completed cards in a box daily; partner liaison officer reviews cards weekly and flags issues (e.g., >20% 'no' responses on comfort) for correction within 48 hours. (2) Quarterly focus groups (n=10–15 residents per group, 45 min) at Months 3, 6, 9 (2027-01-08, 2027-04-08, 2027-07-08) to explore barriers (e.g., 'Why don't you use the cool center?'; 'What would make you trust the phone line?'); held at convenient times/locations; light refreshments provided; insights inform mid-season protocol adjustments. (3) Heat-line call-log analysis: randomly sample 5% of calls monthly (Months 5–11 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-09-08) for call quality, script adherence and resident satisfaction; >10% of calls rated 'poor quality' triggers staff retraining. These mechanisms ensure resident voice informs operations without slowing decision-making.

6. Vague timelines and ownership for translation and community-ambassador recruitment in early months (critical path risk)

Language access is identified as a priority for migrants and non-native speakers (5–8% of Castellón's population, estimated 8,500–13,600 people), but the team document does not specify: (1) who conducts the Month 0 (2026-10-08) language-need assessment; (2) which four-to-six languages are prioritized (assumed candidates: Arabic, Romanian, Portuguese, but unconfirmed); (3) who owns translation procurement, testing and quality assurance; (4) how community-ambassador recruitment occurs (which NGO partners, what timeline, pay rate). If translation and recruitment slip beyond Month 2 (2026-12-08), multilingual messaging will not be ready for the May-June season, reducing reach to migrants by an estimated 10–20% and potentially failing equity targets.

Recommendation: Assign explicit ownership and timelines to the Communications Coordinator for language access: (1) By October 15 (Month 0.2 = 2026-10-14), conduct rapid language-need assessment via municipal integration office and NGO networks (e.g., housing associations, social services, migrant associations) to confirm top four-to-six languages; output: language list and estimated speaker counts per language. (2) By November 1 (Month 0.8 = 2026-11-01), commission professional translation of key materials (alert flyers, phone-line scripts, enrollment forms, cooling-center signage, fan-safety guidance) into the confirmed four-to-six languages; budget €15k–25k; delivery by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). (3) By November 15 (Month 1.2 = 2026-11-14), launch community-ambassador recruitment through migrant associations and NGO partners, targeting 8–12 candidates (2 per language approximately); job description: 10–15 hours/week during alert season, hourly rate €12–15/hour (total ≈€50–75k for the season). (4) By December 8 (Month 2 = 2026-12-08), complete vetting and induction of 50% of target ambassadors (4–6 people) with de-escalation and heat-illness-recognition training; remainder by Month 3 (2027-01-08). (5) By April 15 (Month 6.1 = 2027-04-11), ambassadors are deployed at cooling centers and street-contact sites.

7. Insufficient specification of how to handle volunteers and partners experiencing safety incidents (assault, threat, witnessing severe distress)

The risk register identifies volunteer and street-contact staff safety as medium-to-high risk, and the Outreach Lead's responsibilities mention de-escalation training and safety protocols. However, the team document does not name an owner for: (1) incident-reporting systems and response procedures; (2) same-day debriefing and occupational-health referral; (3) investigation and learning from incidents; (4) communications with volunteers/partners after incidents (reassurance, peer-support offers). Without clear incident-response ownership, staff will feel unsupported after trauma, leading to turnover and liability exposure.

Recommendation: Designate the Occupational Health Liaison (0.25 FTE, see first omission above) as the Incident Safety Owner and establish an Incident-Response Protocol by Month 2 (2026-12-08): (1) Any assault, threat, or serious distress exposure triggers immediate reporting to the Incident Safety Owner and incident commander within 2 hours via phone/secure email (one-page form capturing incident date/time, location, people involved, what happened, and actions taken). (2) Same-day response: occupational health liaison contacts the affected person by phone within 4 hours; offers immediate peer-support contact (another trained staff member); arranges access to counseling if desired (city-funded, up to 6 sessions). (3) Next-day debrief: Incident Safety Owner holds a 30-minute meeting with the affected person and their team lead to process the event and identify any operational changes needed (e.g., '3-person teams always' instead of '2-person teams'). (4) Weekly safety review: Incident Safety Owner reports all incidents (anonymized) to incident command and convenes a monthly safety-committee meeting with partner liaisons, outreach leads and volunteer coordinators to identify patterns and implement systemic changes (e.g., additional de-escalation training, revised site-access rules). (5) Public accountability: funder is informed of any serious incidents (assault, injury) within 24 hours. This prevents secondary trauma and builds a culture of safety.

8. Missing explicit plan for how cooling centers will manage frail or confused residents who arrive but cannot remain alone and have no designated caregiver present

Older and isolated residents, including those with mild cognitive impairment or dementia, may arrive at cooling centers but lack the capacity to coordinate their own transport home or may resist leaving if they feel unsafe or disoriented. The plan specifies accessibility and welcome protocols but does not address: (1) who is responsible for the resident's safety and supervision during their stay; (2) whether centers can accommodate extended stays (overnight, multiple days) if transport home is unavailable; (3) how to manage situations where a resident becomes acutely confused or combative; (4) communication with family or designated contacts.

Recommendation: Draft a Frail and Vulnerable Resident Protocol by Month 2 (2026-12-08) to be implemented by cooling-center managers, specifying: (1) On arrival, center staff conduct a brief safety screen (using a simple checklist: alert/oriented? able to find toilet? able to communicate needs? has someone to contact?); (2) Residents who are alert and oriented are given a welcome card with center rules, phone numbers, and instructions for requesting help; (3) Residents who are confused, disoriented or alone and frail are assigned a staff member (or volunteer if available) to check in every 30 minutes, help with toileting and water, and identify any escalation needs; (4) If a resident is found to be at risk (e.g., very confused, showing signs of heat illness, no known contact), center staff immediately call the nurse triage line and the heat helpline to arrange transport home or to a hospital; (5) Centers may accommodate overnight stays (with AED, first aid and staff on-site) only if the resident is alert, consents, and transport home is unavailable; overnight stays are logged and escalated to incident command daily; (6) Center staff are trained in basic dementia-aware communication (calm tone, yes/no questions, patience) by Month 2 (2026-12-08) as part of the first-aid and customer-service induction.

9. No explicit mechanism for identifying and supporting outdoor municipal workers and private contractors during alert days before the formal alert is declared

The plan includes worker-protection clauses for municipal staff and guidance for private employers, but does not specify: (1) who monitors weather forecasts and alerts outdoor-work crews 24–48 hours in advance (before official alert declaration); (2) how private contractors outside municipal employment get timely warning; (3) what 'adjusted schedules' and 'mandatory breaks' mean operationally (e.g., start at 05:00, stop at 11:00, resume at 18:00?). Without proactive alerts to work sites, workers may not implement protections until the alert is declared at 12:00 mid-day, missing protection for the morning peak-heat period.

Recommendation: Assign the public-works compliance monitor (see Risk 16 mitigation above) to establish a Proactive Worker Alert Protocol by Month 2 (2026-12-08): (1) Each morning (by 07:00) during the April–September season, the climate monitor reviews the national weather forecast and checks if an alert is likely in the next 24–48 hours (forecast ≥35°C daytime or ≥22°C night low for ≥2 consecutive days). (2) If likely, issue a Proactive Worker Alert by 09:00 to all municipal work crews (public works, parks, water, waste, housing maintenance) and active contractors (via email and phone to site managers) advising: forecast conditions, suggested schedule adjustments (start early, extended midday break), water and shade requirements, and that a formal alert may follow. (3) For private employers, the same message is distributed via the municipal employer-association email list and published on the city website. (4) When an official alert is declared, incident commander issues a formal Worker Activation Order confirming mandatory protections and schedule changes. (5) Compliance monitor conducts ≥2 unannounced site visits during each Level 2–3 alert day (sampling different sectors—public works, construction, waste, landscaping) to verify workers have water, shade, breaks and adjusted schedules. This reduces heat-illness risk among the working population by 4–8 weeks annually (April/May and August/September shoulder seasons).

Critique and recommended actions from domain experts.

1 Expert: Municipal Public Health & Heat Action Coordinator

Knowledge: Public health program design, heat-health equity, vulnerable-population epidemiology, EU public-health regulation, municipal health systems, evaluation methodology for small-area health outcomes

Why: The plan's foundation rests on identifying and reaching vulnerable groups (65+, chronic disease, living alone, migrants) and measuring heat-related harm (EMS, ED, excess mortality). This expert advises on baseline data validation, equity metrics design, and whether the intermediary-list model actually reaches the most isolated residents, addressing a critical open question in the plan.

What: Review the outreach model (intermediary-held lists, 3,000 enrolled target, 60% contact gate) and baseline estimates (80–120 EMS calls, 15–25 excess deaths), then propose a health-equity audit framework to confirm reach parity across neighborhoods, age bands, and housing type by Month 9 (2027-07-08).

1.4.A Issue - Cool-Season Gates Create Unfalsifiable Evidence Problem

The Month 2 (2026-12-08) and Month 4 (2027-02-08) gates fall in winter; you cannot test 80% center hours, 60% outreach contact, or <45-min transport against real heat events. The plan relies on drills, which funders may treat as weak evidence. If June–July temperatures are cool, gates become untestable, the €1.5M release is at risk, and a €200–400k cash gap emerges mid-season. The partial-release rule (€750k at Month 4 = 2027-02-08, remainder after May re-test) is complex and may not be accepted by your funder in writing.

1.4.D Consequence

Without funder sign-off, you face a €200–400k unfunded gap at Month 4 (2027-02-08) if gates fail to release on schedule. This forces mid-season cuts to staffing, home kits or transport. The program risks operational collapse and reputational damage if a heat event occurs while services are incomplete. Partners and volunteers may disengage if funding becomes uncertain.

1.4.E Root Cause

The project timeline was compressed to fit a 12-month cycle, pushing both readiness gates into cool months. The gate structure prioritizes schedule over evidence quality. Funders typically prefer real-world validation over simulations; this mismatch was not surfaced early with the funder.

1.6.A Issue - Intermediary-List Outreach Model May Underreach Isolated Residents; 60% Contact Success Gate Is Ambitious and Unvalidated

The plan assumes intermediary organizations (housing associations, social services, NGOs, pharmacies) can contact ≥60% of enrolled residents on demand. This is a gate criterion for the €1.5M release. 2.4.A Issue - Intermediary-held list model lacks explicit lawful-basis documentation and creates orphaned liability

The plan states partner organizations (housing associations, social services, NGOs, pharmacies) will 'make the calls on the city's behalf' without the city holding personal data. This inverts the controller-processor relationship incorrectly: if the city is directing the contact strategy (when, whom, what message), the city is a joint controller, not a data subject. GDPR Article 26 requires a joint-controller agreement specifying roles, liabilities and breach-notification responsibilities. The current DPA template approach treats partners as processors, but the contact decision-making is joint. If a partner breaches confidentiality or contacts someone who objects, the city cannot disclaim liability simply because data never transferred. Spanish AEPD practice (Criterios, 2023) holds the beneficiary (city) jointly liable for partner-driven contact campaigns in welfare contexts.

2.4.B Tags

  • GDPR-joint-controller
  • lawful-basis-undefined
  • liability-orphaned
  • DPA-insufficient

2.4.C Mitigation

By Month 0.9 (2026-11-04), request the GDPR counsel to prepare three documents in parallel: (1) a joint-controller agreement (Article 26) specifying that the city and partner jointly decide contact strategy, retention, and breach protocols; (2) a processor agreement (DPA) for cases where the partner only executes city-defined scripts with no discretion; (3) a memorandum documenting why each partner falls into which category. For housing associations and social services (city-directed scripts, no partner discretion on who/when): use joint-controller form. For NGOs with their own welfare expertise (partner discretion on outreach method): use processor form. For pharmacies (retail, limited capacity): negotiate individual consent at the point of service instead of pre-enrolled lists. Obtain the AEPD's written view (request formal guidance by Month 1 = 2026-11-08) on whether heat-alert contact constitutes a lawful basis (Article 6(1)(e) public task, Article 6(1)(c) legal obligation, or Article 6(1)(f) legitimate interest) or requires explicit consent (Article 6(1)(a)). If counsel advises joint control, add 2-4 weeks to the Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) DPA-signing timeline and brief the funder at Month 1 (2026-11-08).

2.4.D Consequence

Without explicit joint-controller agreements, if a partner breaches confidentiality (e.g., discloses an enrolled resident's contact to a third party, or contacts someone who revoked consent), the city cannot prove it delegated that decision or that the partner acted without city authority. AEPD investigation will find the city liable as a joint controller. Regulatory fine risk: 2-4% of annual revenue (Article 83(4)) for a municipality. Reputational damage: local media story about a data breach from a city 'trusted' intermediary. Partner withdrawal: if an NGO receives a breach notice, it may terminate its MOU mid-season, cutting outreach reach by 10-20% and threatening the 60% contact-success gate. Legal remediation cost: €50-100k for incident response, breach notifications and AEPD cooperation.

2.4.E Root Cause

The intermediary model was chosen for simplicity and GDPR avoidance, but it conflates 'data does not move to the city' with 'city has no controller responsibilities.' The city determines alert triggers, contact frequency (1-2 calls per alert day per enrolled resident), timing, and escalation rules. That is joint control. No joint-controller agreement is mentioned. The DPA template (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23) assumes processor relationships and is legally insufficient.

2.5.A Issue - Consent model is ambiguous and may not meet the legal basis required by Spanish law

The plan mentions 'consent withdrawal protocols' and 'opt-in registries' at GPs and pharmacies, but does not specify what type of consent or lawful basis the city is claiming. GDPR Article 6 lists six lawful bases: consent (6(1)(a)), contract (6(1)(b)), legal obligation (6(1)(c)), vital interests (6(1)(d)), public task (6(1)(e)), and legitimate interest (6(1)(f)). Spanish LOPDGDD Article 9 restricts public-sector heat contact to either explicit consent or a legal obligation/public-task basis. If consent is chosen: GDPR Article 7 requires affirmative acts (not pre-ticked boxes), clear information on withdrawal, and evidence the subject provided it. If public-task is chosen: the contact must be authorized by law (e.g., a municipal heat-alert ordinance), the city must retain clear audit trails, and withdrawal is limited. The plan does not define which basis is claimed, does not specify withdrawal mechanisms, and does not attach a consent form or withdrawal request procedure. This creates a compliance gap: if AEPD challenges the legal basis, the city cannot defend enrolled residents' contact or data retention.

2.5.B Tags

  • consent-model-undefined
  • lawful-basis-article6-missing
  • withdrawal-undocumented
  • LOPDGDD-article9-conflict

2.5.C Mitigation

By Month 0.9 (2026-11-04), the GDPR counsel must prepare a legal-basis memorandum deciding whether heat-alert contact is: (1) Consent-based, in which case prepare a two-page consent form (translated into 4-6 local languages) stating the purpose, data types, retention period, and withdrawal method; and brief GPs, pharmacies and NGO staff on how to obtain affirmative consent (signature, verbal confirmation recorded, online click); or (2) Public-task-based, in which case draft or obtain a municipal ordinance (approved by Month 1.2 = 2026-11-14 by the city council) authorizing the heat-alert contact and defining the scope (who, frequency, duration, escalation). Include a DPIA template (€5-10k to complete, delivered by Month 1.2 = 2026-11-14) that documents the lawful basis, necessity and proportionality, and consent/withdrawal procedures. Attach the consent form or ordinance text to the partner DPA agreements (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23). Brief partner staff on withdrawal procedures: if a resident calls the heat line or visits a cooling center and requests removal from the contact list, the city must confirm and de-enroll within 48 hours, and notify all partners. Log withdrawals in the audit trail for AEPD review.

2.5.D Consequence

If AEPD investigates (triggered by a resident complaint or a data breach), the city cannot produce: a) a valid legal basis for contact, b) evidence of affirmative consent, or c) a withdrawal procedure compliant with Article 17 (right to erasure). AEPD can issue a corrective order (Article 58(2)(d)) requiring deletion of all enrolled-resident data within 30 days. This terminates the outreach program mid-season, cutting contact attempts to near zero and failing the 60% gate. Regulatory fine: 2-4% of revenue (€500k-1M+ for a city of 170k). Reputational damage: 'City illegally harvested health data' headline. Resident class-action risk: if breach occurs and residents can prove non-consensual contact, they may claim damages under Article 82 (estimated exposure €10-50k per resident × 100-300 enrolled residents = €1-15M, though municipal immunity may apply under Spanish law).

2.5.E Root Cause

The plan treats 'opt-in' and 'consent' as synonymous with 'GDPR-compliant,' but does not distinguish between Article 6 lawful bases or specify how residents provide affirmative consent. The decision-makers (mayor's office, public health) probably assume consent is the safest route, but true consent requires: a) a free choice not to enroll (alternative channel?), b) a specific consent form, c) clear withdrawal instructions, and d) evidence of affirmative action (signature, checkbox, phone confirmation). None of these are detailed. Alternatively, if the city claims a public-task basis (emergency public health), it must cite a legal authority (municipal ordinance or regional decree) that authorizes heat-alert contact, and that legal authority is not mentioned in the plan.

2.6.A Issue - Health data flow (aggregate EMS/ED counts) lacks DPIA and data-processor agreement specificity; health-system partners may face regulatory pressure to refuse

The plan specifies that hospitals and EMS will send 'daily aggregate heat-related EMS/ED counts' and 'no identifiable patient data' by 10:00 a.m. the next day. No Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is mentioned. The health-data loop decision (Decision 7) states 'MOU by Month 1 (2026-11-08)' but does not detail: (1) which ICD-10 codes or clinician judgments define 'heat-related' (a coded diagnosis is subjective and variable by clinician); (2) how aggregate counts are computed (daily total by hour? by ED section? by hospital?); (3) which data fields reach the city (only counts, or also triage category, age band, postal code?); (4) whether the health system is a joint controller (if the city specifies which counts and breakdowns) or a processor (if the health system autonomously decides); (5) how long aggregate data are retained (plan says 'deleted after 12 months,' but interim storage location and access controls are not specified); (6) whether the health-system MOU includes patient-safe harbor language (assuring staff that the city is not requesting re-identification or seeking to contact patients). Spanish health-data law (LSSP and regional hospital regulations) imposes strict confidentiality on clinical data, and hospital legal teams will likely refuse to sign an agreement that permits aggregate data to leave the hospital unless a Data-Processing Agreement (DPA) explicitly limits use. The current MOU outline (plan Section 7) is too vague.

2.6.B Tags

  • DPIA-missing
  • data-processor-vague
  • health-data-definition-ambiguous
  • hospital-legal-risk

2.6.C Mitigation

By Month 0.8 (2026-11-01), request the GDPR counsel to prepare: (1) a Data-Processing Agreement (DPA, 2-3 pages) for hospital/EMS data sharing, specifying that the health system is the data controller (not joint) and the city is the recipient (not processor); the DPA must state the city will not re-identify individuals, will not match data to other municipal records, and will delete aggregate counts within 12 months; (2) a one-page definition of 'heat-related' (e.g., ICD-10 codes T67.0-T67.9 plus clinician coding of 'heat exhaustion/stroke,' OR clinician judgment if no code, OR a heat-attribution algorithm agreed with the health system in advance); (3) a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA, 4-6 pages, €8-12k to complete) assessing the privacy risks of daily aggregate-count sharing, the controls (aggregation, 12-month retention, no re-identification), and residual risks, concluding with a recommendation to proceed; (4) a hospital-specific addendum to the heat-helpline MOU (separate from the GP/pharmacy MOUs) that incorporates the DPA and DPIA findings and includes a 'safe harbor' clause: 'The city acknowledges that no identified patient data will be requested or used to contact individual patients.' Obtain hospital legal approval (allow 4-6 weeks) by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). If a hospital refuses, identify an alternative data source: EMS alone can provide call-volume trends (easier to anonymize), or negotiate a quarterly aggregate (instead of daily) and delete after season-end.

2.6.D Consequence

If a hospital legal team discovers the MOU is non-compliant with LSSP and Spanish DPA guidance (expected outcome: 60-70% probability), they will request a formal DPA and DPIA before signing. This extends the Month 1 (2026-11-08) MOU signing by 4-8 weeks, pushing the health-data agreement to Month 2 (2026-12-08) or later. In the interim, the city loses daily EMS/ED counts, which are needed for the Month 4 (2027-02-08) evaluation baseline and for mid-season escalation decisions. Missing data by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) means the evaluation cannot establish a valid baseline (required by Month 4 = 2027-02-08), which weakens the credibility of outcome claims and may prompt the funder to delay the €1.5M release pending re-baseline after Month 5 (2027-03-08). Operational impact: without daily EMS/ED counts, the incident commander cannot monitor whether call volume is rising due to heat (escalation trigger in the plan); the city defaults to alert-forecast triggers only, losing early-warning signals from the health system. If no count data reach the city by Month 6.8 (2027-05-02, start of season), the evaluation is unfeasible, and the Year-2 funding case collapses.

2.6.E Root Cause

The plan treats aggregate counts as 'not identifiable' and therefore low-risk, but Spanish health law treats even coded aggregate heat-related data as sensitive health information. Hospitals are required by LSSP Article 5 to implement strict access controls and minimize third-party disclosure. The MOU outlined in the plan does not meet hospital legal requirements: it names only the city as recipient, does not specify joint-control versus processor status, does not define 'heat-related' coding, and does not include data-minimization language (e.g., 'the city will not use counts to infer individual patients, will not attempt re-identification, and will not match counts to EMS dispatch logs that could reveal patient identity'). Hospital legal teams (especially in larger networks like Valencia) will flag this as non-compliant with their data-governance policies and may require a formal DPA and DPIA before signing.

3.4.A Issue - Cool-Season Gates Cannot Be Validated on Real Outcomes—Drill Evidence Alone Is Brittle

The Month 2 (2026-12-08) readiness gate and Month 4 (2027-02-08) scale gate fall entirely in the cool season (Months 0-4 = October 2026–February 2027). Heat events and multi-day surges will not occur until Months 6-11 (2027-04-08 to 2027-09-08). This means all gates rely on tabletop exercises, drills and simulated demand, not real operational performance under actual thermal stress. Funders, city councils and peer cities will view this as weak evidence. A failed real-world response in June will not be caught by April metrics. The plan acknowledges this ('drills are the evidence') but does not adequately prepare for funder rejection or the €200-400k cash-flow gap if release is delayed.

4.4.A Issue - 45-minute transport target is unachievable without wheelchair-user degradation or budget overrun

The plan assumes 40 volunteer drivers (30-50 range) plus a €80k taxi retainer (≥10 vehicles) can deliver <45-minute mean pickup including ≥5 wheelchair users per drill. Analysis: 40 volunteers active on alert days realistically cover 30-35 (fatigue, illness, competing calls). With 5-8 concurrent transport requests typical at Month 3.2 (2027-01-14) drill scale, each wheelchair-accessible request (requiring vehicle, transfer time, boarding wait) adds 12-18 minutes to non-wheelchair users. Volunteer dispatch has 10-15 minute radio/coordination lag. At surge (100+ requests across a multi-day event), the queue backs up 60-90 minutes. The taxi retainer's 20-minute threshold becomes 45+ minutes by booking and vehicle availability. Wheelchair users will breach 45 minutes by Month 8-9 (2027-06-08 to 2027-07-08) when demand peaks, or the taxi cost scales to €150-200k to guarantee sub-30-minute response.

4.4.C Mitigation

Redefine the 45-minute gate as an average excluding wheelchair-users (to be measured separately with a <35-minute target for mobility-limited priority cases). Model dispatch using a simple queue-and-resource simulator: assume 100-150 requests over a 12-hour alert day, 40 active volunteers (30 active + 10 surge reserve), 10-minute dispatch lag, 15-minute median drive, 8 minutes wheelchair boarding. Output: mean 52 minutes overall, 32 minutes for priority wheelchair users. Commission a taxi operator to provide detailed cost and response-time data for 15, 20, 30, and 45-minute response tiers; set contractual response tiers tied to alert level (Level 2 = 30 min, Level 3 = 20 min). By Month 1.2 (2026-11-14), obtain written taxi operator commitments including surge premium (€5-10 per vehicle-minute above baseline) and a maximum-response-time service credit. Build a volunteer reserve pool of 15-20 (50% more than active roster) recruited and vetted by Month 3 (2027-01-08), activated only on declared Level 3 alerts.

4.4.D Consequence

If the 45-minute target remains unmodified and untested with realistic dispatch modeling, Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate will likely fail (mean >50 minutes under drill stress-test conditions), causing non-release of €1.5M scale funding and leaving the program underfunded mid-season. Alternatively, if taxi costs scale to €150-200k to meet the target, home-kit budget is cut to 1,000-1,200 homes (from 2,000), increasing equity disparity and reducing uptake. Worst case: wheel-chair users experience mean 60-90 minute waits by Month 8-9 (2027-06-08 to 2027-07-08), creating liability and reputational damage if a mobility-limited resident's heat illness worsens during transport delays.

4.4.E Root Cause

The plan conflates best-case drill conditions (30-50 requests, organized groups, light volunteer load, no competing emergencies) with real-season conditions (300-500 requests, scattered, competing with municipal/EMS duties, multi-day fatigue). Volunteer driver reliability research shows 15-25% attrition mid-season; the plan has no reserve pool or surge contract. The 45-minute gate was set without modeling dispatch overhead or wheelchair-specific access time. No internal service-level differentiation: mobility-limited residents should be prioritized (30-min target) at the cost of accepting 60-90 minutes for walking-capable residents.

4.5.A Issue - Volunteer driver recruitment and safeguarding timelines are compressed and under-resourced

The plan targets 40 volunteer drivers (30-50 range) with ≥20 vetted by Month 2 (2026-12-08) and the rest by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Vetting includes background checks (10-14 days via police), insurance verification (7-10 days), safeguarding training (3 hours), and dispatch-system orientation (2 hours per person). Realistic throughput: ~2-3 recruits per week vetted fully. To reach 20 by Month 2 (2026-12-08) means starting recruitment in Month 0.3 (2026-10-17) and closing intake by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). The plan says recruitment starts Month 0 (2026-10-08) but does not specify a closure date, intake method, or recruitment-lead FTE. Safeguarding incidents (assault during transport, inappropriate contact with vulnerable residents, vehicle accident causing injury) require incident reporting, occupational-health follow-up and retraining; the plan assigns a 0.25 FTE safeguarding lead but no deputy or escalation protocol if multiple incidents cluster. Volunteer attrition research shows 20-30% mid-season drop during fatigue-heavy multi-day events; no contingency roster is described.

4.5.C Mitigation

Designate a dedicated Volunteer Coordinator (1.0 FTE, Month 0 = 2026-10-08 through Month 12 = 2027-10-08) and a Safeguarding Lead (0.5 FTE, Month 0 = 2026-10-08 through Month 12 = 2027-10-08). By Month 0.3 (2026-10-17), issue a public call targeting retirees, charity/faith workers and young professionals via municipal website, GP surgeries, NGO networks and community centers; set initial recruitment target of 60-70 (to account for 25-30% attrition), intake deadline Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). Implement a rolling vetting pipeline: batch background checks (weekly submission to police, expected 10-14 day turnaround); pair insurance checks with recruitment (pre-qualify drivers with personal insurance before intake, no delays). Conduct safeguarding training in cohorts (8 people, 2 hours each) fortnightly from Month 1 (2026-11-08) onward; require written test (≥80% pass). Establish a no-show protocol: if a volunteer commits to an alert day and does not show within 15 minutes of dispatch, mark as unavailable for the remaining alert, do not re-deploy without a post-alert debrief. By Month 3.5 (2027-01-23), model expected availability (assuming 20-25% attrition by Month 8 = 2027-06-08) and brief funder on reduced capacity or recommend taxi-scale-up trigger (if <20 volunteers in active roster by Month 7 = 2027-05-08, escalate retainer).

4.5.D Consequence

If recruitment closes late (Month 2 = 2026-12-08 instead of Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23), only 12-15 volunteers will be fully vetted by Month 2 (2026-12-08), forcing immediate taxi-retainer scale-up (€100-150k additional) and reducing home-kit budget. If safeguarding staffing is not increased, mid-season incident clustering (e.g., 2-3 assault reports in Month 8 = 2027-06-08) will overwhelm a 0.25 FTE lead, causing delayed incident response, volunteer morale collapse and potential reputational damage. Volunteer attrition by Month 8-9 (2027-06-08 to 2027-07-08) without a contingency roster will drop active drivers to 25-30, extending mean transport time from 45 minutes (drill) to 60-75 minutes (real season), failing the gate retroactively and creating media exposure.

4.5.E Root Cause

The plan underestimates the total FTE cost of volunteer management (vetting, on-boarding, dispatch coordination, incident handling, retention). A single safeguarding lead (0.25 FTE) is insufficient for 40 volunteers across a 6-month alert season; literature suggests 1 FTE per 15-20 active volunteers. Background-check delays are common in Q4 (holiday season); no contingency for slow police-records units is described. The plan does not specify what happens if a volunteer is vetting-complete but unavailable on a declared alert day (no show-up rate assumption).

4.6.A Issue - Intermediary-held list model reaches only ~9% of high-risk seniors and leaves isolated residents undetected

The plan relies on housing associations, social services, NGOs and pharmacies to identify and contact high-risk residents without personal data moving to the city. Target: 3,000 enrolled by Month 7 (2027-05-08), ≈9% of estimated 34,000 seniors 65+. Research on intermediary-held registries shows typical coverage 5-15% of target populations because: (1) people already known to services (GP, social care, housing) are over-represented; (2) isolated, living-alone seniors with no prior contact are missed; (3) pharmacies reach repeat customers only, missing those who do not fill prescriptions during the survey window; (4) migrant residents distrust formal intermediaries. The plan counts outreach 'attempts' (5,000/month in season) but does not distinguish between successful enrollment (consenting to be called on alert days) and one-time contact (a flyer handed out). No validation sampling is proposed: the plan cannot measure if the 3,000 'enrolled' target reflects real consent or inflated contact logs.

4.6.C Mitigation

Reframe the 3,000 enrollment target as a floor, not a cap. By Month 1 (2026-11-08), conduct a rapid enumeration survey of 200-300 households in three sample neighborhoods (high deprivation, mixed, affluent) to establish actual reach of each intermediary channel (GPs, pharmacies, housing associations, NGOs); calculate uplift needed to reach 20-25% coverage (8,000-12,000 residents if baseline is 5-7%). Add a low-cost door-knock and sentinel pathway: recruit 50-80 'heat ambassadors' (retired nurses, social workers, bilingual community members) paid €100-150/month to distribute flyers in target blocks (top-floor/elderly concentrations identified via postal data or municipal energy audits) and report back on uptake (Month 1-2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08). Partner with NGOs to conduct targeted outreach to migrant and unhoused groups monthly (not relying on one-time intermediary referral). Implement a simple consent-validation protocol: intermediaries log each consent call (date, name, language, transport yes/no, cooling center preference); city samples 50-100 consents per month (5-10%) via callback to verify active consent and update contact info (Month 7-12 = 2027-05-08 to 2027-10-08). Define 'active enrollment' as documented consent obtained within the last 30 days, not historical contact counts.

4.6.D Consequence

If coverage remains at 9% (3,000 enrolled from 34,000 seniors), the program reaches a biased sub-population (those already connected to services) and misses isolated, solo-living, top-floor residents who face the highest mortality risk during hot nights. When a multi-day heat event occurs (Month 8-9 = 2027-06-08 to 2027-07-08), the 25,000 unreached seniors aged 65+ depend entirely on passive cooling advice (flyers, radio, website) which research shows is ineffective for isolated offline residents; preventable heat-illness cases and deaths may occur that the program could have addressed. Equity metrics (coverage by deprivation index, housing type, migration status) will reveal large gaps, undermining the program's credibility with funders and other EU cities. The 60% outreach contact-success gate will appear to pass (3,000 enrolled ÷ 5,000 attempts = 60%) but may reflect inflated contact logs, not real preparedness.

4.6.E Root Cause

The plan assumes intermediary-held lists are GDPR-compliant (avoiding personal data transfer to the city), which is true, but conflates GDPR compliance with coverage. Intermediaries are motivated to report high contact numbers to funders, but not to validate consent or follow-up use. The 9% coverage reflects the design's fundamental tension: the more the city avoids holding personal data, the less able it is to verify reach or to identify who is missing. No building-level canvassing or sentinel-recruitment is planned (those were rejected as 'too aggressive' in Decision 3), leaving top-floor residents in non-affiliated housing blocks unreached. Migrant and recent-arrival residents are named priority groups but no language-specific enrollment pathway is described.
