However, these intermediaries predominantly reach people already connected to services. The most isolated—particularly older residents living alone, recent migrants with language barriers, and people with historical trauma regarding authorities—are systematically absent from these lists. Canvassing by building and street sentinels are mentioned but not resourced as primary routes, leaving a coverage gap of 15,000–20,000 high-risk people unreached by alert calls. Without a 'no-wrong-door' enrollment strategy that meets people where they are (markets, religious settings, soup kitchens), the program will concentrate resources on the easiest-to-reach 10% and miss those with highest mortality risk.

7.4.B Tags

  • outreach-coverage-gap
  • isolation-exclusion
  • trust-deficit-migrant-elderly
  • enrollment-bottleneck
  • equity-blind-design

7.4.C Mitigation

By Month 1 (2026-11-08), commission rapid resident research (10–15 focus groups, 100–150 interviews) with older isolated residents, recent migrants, and people experiencing homelessness to identify what trust-building offer would drive enrollment (e.g., a trusted community messenger making the first call, a visible cooling kit as proof of benefit, a named human contact guarantee). Use findings to design a dual-track enrollment: intermediary-held lists for the reachable 10%, plus a community-ambassador-led outreach-to-isolation strategy for the remaining 90%. Allocate ≥€80k and 2 FTE from the communications budget to deploy 12–15 paid 'heat guides' in markets, places of worship, migrant/Roma associations, and soup kitchens from Month 3 (2027-01-08). Redefine the 60% outreach-success gate to measure contact attempts within 200 m of the target population's geographic clusters, not just the enrolled registry.

7.4.D Consequence

Without mitigation, 80% of the highest-risk isolated residents will remain outside the program, defeating the equity mandate. A heat event in July will reveal that enrolled residents are predominantly already-connected, employed older adults in formal housing—not the most vulnerable. The program's legitimacy with migrants, Roma, and homeless communities will collapse; subsequent Year-2 outreach will face active mistrust. Media coverage will frame the program as 'helping the connected and abandoning the isolated.' Reputational damage will undermine municipal capacity to run future public-health programs in marginalized communities.

7.4.E Root Cause

The intermediary-list model was selected for GDPR simplicity and speed, not for reach. The plan conflates legal safety with equitable coverage. No resident research was done to validate what would drive enrollment among the most distrustful cohorts (e.g., undocumented migrants, older people who have never called a government helpline). The plan also conflates 'opt-in' with 'accessible': an opt-in registry run by housing associations will miss people who are not tenants (subletting, informal arrangements).

7.5.A Issue - Language-access architecture is under-resourced and will fail to reach non-Spanish speakers at point of urgent need; interpretation is a compliance checkbox, not a trust-building lever

The plan allocates ≈€67k and 8–12 ambassadors (10–15 h/week) to serve 4–6 non-official languages across a city where migrant populations are concentrated in specific neighborhoods. The helpline will have telephone interpretation, but the outreach model depends on partner staff (housing caretakers, social workers, pharmacists) who are predominantly Spanish-monolingual. Door-knock teams will arrive with flyers in multiple languages but no bilingual staff. Cooling-center welcome desks will rely on pictograms and short phrases, which fail to convey safety-critical advice (fan use in extreme heat, medication interactions, heat-illness escalation). Recent migrants—identified as a priority group—will receive alert messages but not consent-based enrollment conversations in their preferred language, reducing uptake by an estimated 30–50%. Language access has been framed as a translation task, not as a trust-building infrastructure that requires bilingual staff presence in the field.

7.5.B Tags

  • language-access-failure
  • compliance-checkbox
  • migrant-exclusion
  • trust-infrastructure-missing
  • point-of-contact-gap

7.5.C Mitigation

By Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), conduct a rapid language-mapping survey of Castellón de la Plana's migrant and elderly neighborhoods (20–30 short interviews in each of the 5–7 highest-concentration areas, plus municipal social services data) to identify the actual top 4–5 languages and geographic clusters. Allocate ≥€120k (€50k additional language budget) to hire 2–3 full-time bilingual outreach coordinators (one per major language cluster) from Month 2 (2026-12-08) onward, with authority to make enrollment calls and lead first-contact door-knock teams. Train these staff as 'heat health navigators' with brief clinical training (2-hour heat-illness recognition module), not just interpreters. Relocate ≥30% of the ambassador budget to support these coordinators. By Month 6 (2027-04-08), require all cooling-center sites to have at least one bilingual staff member on duty during alert hours, not just access to a phone line.

7.5.D Consequence

Without mitigation, non-Spanish speakers will fail to understand heat alerts, will not enroll, and will not seek cooling even when alerted. A multi-lingual heat event with media coverage will show that migrant residents were unreached, creating political pressure for a response that comes too late. Healthcare systems will see heat-related ED visits concentrated in non-Spanish-speaking cohorts, signaling a failed targeted intervention. Loss of trust among migrant communities will ripple into future public-health programs. The City will be seen as having allocated €67k to language work but not delivering accessible services to the named priority group.

7.5.E Root Cause

Budget and hiring constraints pushed language access to the margins. The plan treats translation as a cost item (leaflets, interpretation line) rather than as core field capacity. No labor model exists for bilingual outreach staff, and the ambassador model is part-time and concentrated in a narrow budget. The plan also lacks mapping of migrant neighborhoods and demographic data on which languages are spoken where; decisions are being made on assumed language mix ('candidates: Arabic, Romanian, Portuguese, to be confirmed') rather than verified local data.

7.6.A Issue - Trust infrastructure is entirely missing; there is no strategy to activate faith leaders, peer networks, and community organizations as credible messengers before the first heat event, making the program dependent on official channels that marginalized residents avoid

The plan mentions 'trusted messengers'—pharmacists, GPs, caretakers, faith leaders—but allocates no budget, no hiring, and no institutional relationship-building before Month 6 (2027-04-08), when the pre-season campaign launches. There is no evidence that faith leaders, Roma association heads, migrant mutual-aid networks, or peer-support groups have been contacted, briefed, or contracted to co-design heat-safety messaging. The 8–12 language ambassadors are part-time and paid, not embedded in community structures. When the first alert arrives in June, the city will attempt to reach isolated residents via official phone lines and cooling centers—the exact channels these residents distrust. No counterspeech infrastructure exists to counter misinformation (alcohol, misused fans) that will inevitably circulate in informal networks. The plan frames communication as a campaign (messages broadcasted to a mass audience) rather than as a dialogue-and-relationship ecosystem that makes people believe a safety message enough to act on it.

7.6.B Tags

  • trust-infrastructure-absent
  • community-partnership-shallow
  • misinformation-undefended
  • faith-leader-engagement-tokenistic
  • peer-network-bypassed

7.6.C Mitigation

By Month 0 (2026-10-08), immediately allocate ≥€150k and one dedicated 'Community Trust Lead' (0.75 FTE, reporting to the incident commander) to map and engage faith leaders, migrant associations, Roma community representatives, homeless-service NGOs, older-resident peer groups, and women's networks in Castellón de la Plana. By Month 1 (2026-11-08), hold 5–7 structured co-design workshops with representatives of each community, asking: 'What would make you believe a heat-health message?' and 'Who in your community would you trust to deliver it?' Use findings to design community-specific heat-safety messaging (not centralized campaign templates) and to identify and contract 8–12 peer ambassadors per community (not language interpreters, but trusted community members). By Month 2 (2026-12-08), finalize and brief all contracted messengers on heat-illness recognition, escalation rules, and misinformation rebuttals (specific scripts for alcohol myths, fan misuse, etc.). Allocate a rapid-response budget (€30k) to activate messenger networks within 4 hours of a misinformation alert (e.g., WhatsApp groups, phone trees, local radio spots) to correct false advice. Establish a weekly 'messenger feedback loop' where community members report back on what they're hearing in informal networks, feeding into daily operational briefings.

7.6.D Consequence

Without mitigation, the program will spend €170k on communications that do not reach or persuade the most isolated residents. When the first heat event occurs, isolated older residents and migrants will not answer official calls; they will rely on family advice, street gossip, and informal networks—many of which will promote unsafe practices (opening windows, alcohol, lying in the sun). Heat-illness cases will spike in populations the program claimed to serve. Media investigation will reveal that the city paid for multilingual flyers that sat in community centers but never reached residents. Community leaders will report (privately, then publicly) that the city never asked them to help. Trust in municipal public health will drop for a generation; subsequent interventions will be met with skepticism and refusal to participate.

7.6.E Root Cause

The plan is a municipal operations document, not a community-trust document. Trusted-messenger engagement is a secondary decision (Decision 9), allocated ≈€50–70k, and scheduled to happen after procurement and operational setup are complete. The underlying logic is that official channels (phone lines, centers, flyers) can deliver messages, and trusted messengers are a nice-to-have amplifier. But for migrants, Roma, homeless people, and isolated older residents, official channels have low credibility; the messenger IS the message. The plan also has no community-co-design process; it was written by a municipal team with external input, not co-designed with the priority communities themselves.

8 Expert: Heat-Health Evaluation & Data Science Lead

Knowledge: Heat-attribution epidemiology, small-area health data analysis, temperature-adjusted mortality modeling, EMS/ED coding standards, time-series analysis with seasonal adjustment, heat-threshold calibration, comparison-group design, data-quality and validation workflows

Why: The plan's evaluation strategy is sketched lightly: 'pilot vs matched districts and prior years, temperature-adjusted, aggregate counts only.' However, four critical gaps exist: (1) baseline EMS/ED/mortality data is provisional (80-120 EMS, 15-25 deaths) and unvalidated; (2) coding practice for 'heat-related' varies by hospital and EMS service (explicit ICD-10 codes vs clinician judgment vs proxy indicators); (3) small-area counts in a 170k city are noisy, so the evaluation may be unable to detect real effects within one season; (4) the Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate includes no mortality outcome, only operational KPIs, so credibility of 'harm reduction' claims rests on EMS/ED data quality. This expert validates baselines, agrees coding standards with health partners, and specifies a realistic evaluation design that accounts for small-area limitations.

What: By Month 0 (2026-10-08), request detailed EMS and hospital baseline data (heat-coded calls, ED visits, timestamps) for ≥2 prior summers, and clarify coding practice (which ICD-10 codes count as 'heat-related'?). By Month 1 (2026-11-08), audit the data quality: completeness (% of records with heat coding), consistency (same codes across services), and temporal pattern (do peaks match known heat events?). By Month 2 (2026-12-08), finalize definitions and agree a temperature-adjusted baseline (e.g., average heat-related calls per 1°C above 32°C). By Month 4 (2027-02-08), pre-specify the evaluation protocol (comparison group selection, adjustment variables, statistical methods, subgroup analyses) and register it with a university partner; specify realistic power to detect a 10-15% reduction. By Month 12 (2027-10-08), deliver evaluation report with explicit confidence ranges and attribution limits (e.g., 'attributable to the program' vs 'coincident with').

Skills: Epidemiologic analysis and attribution methods, time-series temperature adjustment, small-area analysis and privacy protection, EMS/ED data validation and coding, comparison-group design, statistical power calculation, heat-health thresholds and calibration, data visualization for non-technical audiences

Search: heat health epidemiology evaluation, EMS ED coding standards heat illness, small-area health data analysis, temperature attribution mortality, heat threshold calibration

8.1 Primary Actions

  • Obtain written funder sign-off on the drill-as-evidence protocol and the partial-release rule (€750k at Month 4 = 2027-02-08 if insufficient real evidence, remainder after May re-test) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23). If the funder will not accept this, immediately escalate and renegotiate the funding structure (full disbursement with clawback, or identify contingency funding) before proceeding to any other work.
  • Replan procurement timeline: issue specs by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), pre-qualify backup suppliers with emergency-activation agreements by Month 1 (2026-11-08), place first-tranche kit orders by Month 1 (2026-11-08) (not Month 1.2 = 2026-11-14), and arrange interim storage by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). Commit the €200k expedite premium immediately; do not hold it contingent. Confirm all first-tranche deliveries locked in for February 2027 by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23).
  • Expand outreach target from 3,000 enrolled to 5,000–6,000 total contact attempts, aiming for ≥2,500 enrolled + 1,500–2,500 one-time reached. Add a targeted door-knock phase for top-floor and social-housing blocks in Months 5–6 (2027-03-08 to 2027-04-08) with 3 temporary staff to reach isolated residents missed by intermediaries. Redefine the 60% contact-success gate to measure contact rate by neighborhood deprivation index and housing type, not just enrollment rate.
  • Place cooling-center facility contracts and execute accessibility audits by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). Confirm ≥50% of places are fully accessible (wheelchair ramps, accessible toilets, quiet rooms) by Month 2 (2026-12-08). Any site that cannot meet accessibility by Month 2 (2026-12-08) should be deferred to July or replaced; do not defer until later.
  • Engage a GDPR specialist law firm and obtain written legal opinion confirming that the intermediary-held-list model complies with Spanish law and GDPR by Month 1 (2026-11-08). Finalize and execute data-processing agreements with all partner organizations (housing associations, social services, NGOs, pharmacies) by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). Brief 50–80 partner staff on confidentiality and consent protocols by Month 2 (2026-12-08). Do not rely on informal verbal agreement.

8.2 Secondary Actions

  • Commission verified baseline data on heat-related EMS calls, ED visits and mortality coding from the municipal hospital, EMS service and primary-care network by Month 1 (2026-11-08). Compare to the plan's provisional estimates (80–120 EMS calls, 15–25 excess deaths); flag any material gaps and adjust the evaluation design and gates if baseline is much smaller or larger than estimated.
  • Establish a monthly risk-review checkpoint at the project steering committee: Month 1 (2026-11-08), Month 2 (2026-12-08), Month 3 (2027-01-08), and Month 4 (2027-02-08, 2026-12-08, 2027-01-08, 2027-02-08). At each checkpoint, review: (1) funder confirmation status, (2) procurement order status and delivery confirmation, (3) volunteer recruitment pipeline and vetting progress, (4) partner DPA and consent tracking, (5) facility accessibility audit results. If any item is >2 weeks behind, escalate to the incident commander and activate contingency plans (e.g., scale taxi retainer if volunteers lag).
  • Conduct a focus group test of the 'Hot Night Guarantee' messaging (call within X hours, ride within 45 minutes, cool home) with 15–20 high-risk residents (age 70+, living alone, low digital literacy) by Month 1 (2026-11-08). Measure: Would this offer make you enroll? What changes would make it more credible? Use results to refine enrollment messaging and ensure the promise is realistic given transport and staffing capacity.
  • Pre-specify the drill protocol (final by Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23) with explicit realism criteria: simulate multi-day heat event (48–72 hours), include 3–5 volunteer failures/absences, test center occupancy surge to 80% capacity, simulate 2–3 escalations to EMS, and measure staff fatigue/error rates after 48 hours. Document drill evidence standards in writing and share with the funder by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23) so no surprises emerge at the Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate.
  • Recruit volunteer drivers in fortnightly cohorts starting Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), with vetting and training 4–8 weeks. Require background checks, insurance verification, and 2-hour safeguarding training per person. Target ≥20 vetted by Month 2 (2026-12-08); if <15 are in the pipeline by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), immediately scale the taxi retainer proportionally (estimate +€20–40k per 10-volunteer shortfall). Do not wait until Month 4 (2027-02-08) to discover insufficient volunteer capacity.
  • Establish a nurse-advice triage line (0.5 FTE) by Month 2 (2026-12-08) for outreach staff to call with suspected heat-illness cases. Develop a checklist of escalation criteria (confusion, loss of consciousness, skin temperature, core-temperature indicators) and train all 25–35 outreach staff on the protocol by Month 2 (2026-12-08). Test the line with 3–5 mock calls during the month-2 readiness gate drill to ensure it integrates with EMS dispatch.

If no source is identified by Month 10 (2027-08-08), recommend to the funder and municipality which components would be cut to fit a reduced Year-2 budget (likely: home kits and handyperson service, retaining refuges and transport). Include this tradeoff in the Year-2 roadmap.

8.3 Follow Up Consultation

At the next consultation (recommended Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23), bring: (1) written funder response to the drill-as-evidence and partial-release rule; (2) preliminary supplier quotes and lead-time confirmations for kits and transport; (3) baseline EMS/ED/mortality data from hospital and EMS; (4) confirmed facility-use commitments from ≥8 of 10 proposed cooling-center sites; (5) volunteer-recruitment progress (numbers in pipeline, vetting timeline per candidate); (6) GDPR counsel engagement letter and preliminary legal advice on the intermediary-list model; (7) results of the 'Hot Night Guarantee' focus group. These six items are the leading indicators of whether the Month 2 (2026-12-08) and Month 4 (2027-02-08) gates are achievable. If any is stalled or shows negative indicators, escalate immediately to incident command.

8.4.A Issue - Cool-Season Gates Create Unmeasurable Evidence Problem

The Month 2 (2026-12-08) and Month 4 (2027-02-08) gates fall entirely in the cool season (November–February in Spain). Real heat events will not occur until June at earliest. The plan proposes drill-based evidence instead, but drills cannot replicate multi-day fatigue, heat-stress decision-making, or volunteer/staff burnout under real conditions. Funders and regulators may reject drill evidence as insufficient. If the €1.5M tranche-2 release is delayed pending real heat data, a €200–400k cash gap emerges that exceeds the €160k available tranche-1 contingency. This is a structural flaw, not a minor risk.

8.4.B Tags

  • gate-evidence-gap
  • cash-flow-risk
  • funder-assumption-undocumented
  • seasonal-timing-mismatch

8.4.C Mitigation

Immediately (by Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23) obtain written funder sign-off on the partial-release rule and drill-as-evidence protocol before any other work begins. If the funder will not accept drills, propose three alternatives: (a) redefine gates to require only operational readiness (contracts signed, staff hired, no performance thresholds) and defer performance gates to post-season; (b) negotiate a full €3.5M front-loaded disbursement with a clawback clause if gates are missed; (c) identify contingency funding (EU climate or health grants) to cover the €200–400k gap if tranche-2 is delayed. Document the chosen path in a signed amendment to the funding agreement by Month 1 (2026-11-08).

8.4.D Consequence

Without funder written agreement before Month 2 (2026-12-08), the program faces a 40–60% risk of tranche-2 withholding at Month 4 (2027-02-08). This forces mid-season cuts to transport retainer (raising pickup times above 45 min), cooling-center hours, or outreach staff. Service will degrade during the first real heat event, causing harm to enrolled residents and generating reputational damage ('pilot failed when it mattered'). The playbook becomes unusable for other cities because the pilot could not demonstrate operational success.

8.4.E Root Cause

The plan was designed to meet a two-month delivery deadline (Month 0 = 2026-10-08 to Month 2 = 2026-12-08 to 2026-12-08) in a cold climate. The gates were set to happen early to release tranche-2 before the funding year ends, but early means cool-season. No one documented the funder's appetite for drill-based evidence, so the gap was not surfaced until now. The root cause is compressed timeline + seasonal mismatch + undocumented assumption about evidence standards.

8.5.A Issue - Procurement Critical Path Compressed into 8 Weeks; Supply-Chain Buffer Missing

The plan requires all tranche-1 procurement orders placed by Month 2 (2026-12-08)—a hard gate. This means specs by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01), framework/below-threshold orders by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), and all tenders closed by Month 2 (2026-12-08). For home kits and transport, delivery windows are extremely tight: first-tranche kits must arrive by Month 4 (2027-02-08) and be 80% installed by Month 5 (2027-03-08) to enable May–June deployment. If any supplier slips 4–6 weeks (normal for EU industrial supply), kits arrive in June–July after the first heat event. The plan notes the supply-chain risk but does not allocate enough schedule or budget buffer to absorb it.

8.5.B Tags

  • procurement-schedule-risk
  • supply-chain-buffer-insufficient
  • delivery-window-tight
  • contingency-not-pre-committed

8.5.C Mitigation

Replan procurement timeline: (1) Issue detailed specs to suppliers by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), 5 days earlier than planned; request quotes + lead-time confirmation by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01). (2) Pre-qualify all backup suppliers and negotiate 'emergency activation' agreements by Month 1 (2026-11-08) specifying that 20–30% of first-tranche stock can be ordered at 7-day notice with expedited freight. (3) Place the first-tranche kit order (600–800 units) by Month 1 (2026-11-08), not Month 1.2 (2026-11-14), to gain one week of buffer. (4) Arrange interim storage (≥200 units) at a municipal facility by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) so kits can be received and staged early if primary supplier delivers ahead of schedule. (5) Include in the retainer contract a 10% buffer-stock allowance (100–200 extra units) so if one tranche is lost in transit, a backup exists. Commit the €200k expedite premium immediately; do not hold it contingent.

8.5.D Consequence

If procurement slips 4–6 weeks, 60–80% of home kits will not be installed until July–August, missing the May–June peak-risk season entirely. The program will then have claimed a 2,000-home intervention on paper but delivered it after the first major heat event has already occurred. This breaks the enrollment promise ('your home will be cooler by May') and undermines trust for Year 2. Alternatively, the city cuts home kits from 2,000 to 1,000–1,500 to fit the revised timeline, which reduces coverage and the program's flagship tangible benefit.

8.5.E Root Cause

The procurement timeline was planned optimistically without realistic EU supplier lead times (6–8 weeks for mass-production items) or buffer for specification changes, supplier price renegotiation, or first-article inspections. No pre-commitment of backup suppliers or interim storage was made early enough. The €200k expedite budget was not actively deployed; it remained a contingency line instead of an active risk-mitigation lever.

8.6.A Issue - Outreach Reach Severely Constrained: 3,000 Enrolled ≈9% of 65+, Misses Most Isolated Residents

The outreach model targets 3,000 enrolled high-risk residents by Month 7 (2027-05-08), approximately 9% of the estimated 34,000 residents aged 65+. The plan uses intermediary-held lists (housing associations, social services, NGOs, pharmacies), which are GDPR-safe but depend on existing service contact. Residents who are isolated, living outside formal housing, mistrustful of services, or recently arrived will not appear on any list and will not be contacted unless a 'no wrong door' heat-line call reaches them. The 60% contact-success gate (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) measures reach only for enrolled residents; it says nothing about the 91% not enrolled. This is a coverage failure disguised as an operational gate.

8.6.B Tags

  • outreach-coverage-gap
  • isolated-residents-missed
  • enrollment-rate-9-percent
  • gate-measures-wrong-denominator
  • equity-goal-not-met

8.6.C Mitigation

Redefine success metric and expand enrollment strategy: (1) Set an absolute outreach goal of 5,000–6,000 contact attempts (not 3,000 enrolled), aiming for 50% enrollment = 2,500–3,000 signed up, plus 1,500–2,500 people reached once via heat-line or street teams (even if not formally enrolled). (2) Add a targeted door-knock phase in Month 5–6 (2027-03-08 to 2027-04-08) for top-floor and social-housing blocks with low intermediary reach (neighborhoods with <50% coverage). Use the 6 outreach FTE and hire 3 temporary door-knock staff (Months 5–7 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-05-08) to cover ≤1,000 additional households in priority blocks. This finds isolated residents who avoid formal services. (3) Require intermediary partners to report their outreach attempt rate and their base (how many residents do they have access to per organization?), so gaps are visible. (4) Measure equity: track enrollment by neighborhood deprivation index and housing type. Report what percentage of the 65+ population in each neighborhood was ever reached, not just what percentage was enrolled.

8.6.D Consequence

Without expanded outreach, the program will have reached only the 'easy' 9% of residents who were already known to services. When a heat event occurs, the 91% unreached will not have transport pre-arranged, will not be enrolled in the phone-check-in list, and will not know about cooling centers. Mortality and morbidity will be concentrated in the unreached group. A post-event analysis will reveal that the program helped its enrollees but missed its most isolated targets, undermining the 'equity' claim and the pilot's credibility for scaling. The playbook will be seen as a service for already-registered residents, not as a program for vulnerable populations.

8.6.E Root Cause

The plan conflated 'operationally safe and GDPR-compliant' (intermediary-held lists) with 'equitable reach.' It set a gate (60% contact success among enrolled residents) that measures operational fidelity for the people already enrolled, not coverage of the hardest-to-reach. The plan rejected building-level canvassing as too labor-intensive but did not cost a hybrid model: intermediary reach + targeted door-knock for low-reach neighborhoods. The root cause is a design bias toward legal safety and operational simplicity over equity and population reach.
