Review 1: Critical Issues

  1. Cool-season gate evidence creates unfalsifiable release cliff risk. The Month 4 (2027-02-08) gates (80% center hours, 60% outreach contact, <45-min transport) must be tested via drill alone because real heat events will not occur until June. If the funder rejects drill evidence, the €1.5M tranche-2 release is withheld, creating a €200–400k cash gap (€40–240k above the €160k available tranche-1 contingency). This forces mid-season service cuts to home kits, transport or outreach during peak summer heat, directly harming enrolled residents and destroying program credibility with funders and peer cities. No written funder pre-agreement on drill acceptance exists; this must be obtained by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) before procurement begins.

  2. Supply-chain compression leaves 4–8 week slippage exposure on home kits. Kits must be ordered by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14) and 40–50% delivered by Month 4 (2027-02-08) to enable installation by Month 7.3 (2027-05-17) during peak-risk May–June. EU supplier lead times are 6–8 weeks; a 4-week slip delays 60–80% of kits past the first heat events, rendering the 2,000-kit intervention ineffective for the highest-risk season. This forces either cuts to kit targets (500–1,000 homes lost) or an expedite premium (€50–100k, estimate) funded within the €800k kit category, which already holds the ≈€200k bundle for expedite premium, storage, buffer stock, QA and hydration; contingency is drawn only if costs exceed that category. Backup suppliers by Month 1 (2026-11-08) and the first call-off at Month 1.2 (2026-11-14) are critical but not yet pre-committed.

  3. Intermediary-list outreach model reaches only 9% of high-risk 65+ population, leaving 91% unreached. The plan targets 3,000 enrolled residents from an estimated 34,000 seniors aged 65+, using housing associations, social services, NGOs and pharmacies that systematically exclude isolated, mistrustful and offline residents—exactly the highest-mortality group. The 60% contact-success gate measures fidelity among enrolled residents, not coverage of the unreached majority. When a multi-day heat event occurs in July–August, the 31,000 unreached seniors (before expansion) will depend on passive messaging (flyers, radio) proven ineffective for isolated populations, leading to preventable excess mortality and media exposure that the program claims to serve but abandons the most vulnerable. Adding door-knock and sentinel outreach for 1,500–2,500 additional contacts by Month 5–7 (2027-03-08 to 2027-05-08) would cost €50–80k and is not budgeted.

Review 2: Implementation Consequences

  1. Successful Year 1 operationalization establishes foundation for scaled Year 2 replication at €2.3M/year recurring cost, but funding source and interagency coordination remain unidentified. If Month 4 (2027-02-08) gates pass and the pilot delivers measurable outcomes (operational KPIs: 80% center hours, 60% contact success, <45 min transport), the municipality gains credibility to scale from 3,000 enrolled to 8,000–12,000 by Year 2, extending coverage from 9% to 25–35% of high-risk 65+ population. This unlocks EU peer-city interest and strengthens the playbook's transferability. However, Year 2 requires €2.3M/year recurring (unidentified funding source) plus an estimated €50–100k for playbook refinement and cross-city training. Without pre-identified Year 2 funding by Month 9 (2027-07-08), scaling discussions will stall, leaving pilot infrastructure stranded, and the €400k spent on governance/PMO will yield no institutional continuity or policy change.

  2. Successful home-kit installation by Month 7.3 (2027-05-17) creates visible, tangible benefit to enrolled residents and drives sustained enrollment and retention through peak-mortality July–August, multiplying the program's equity reach and harm-reduction effectiveness. If 2,000 homes receive kits (shading, fans, thermometers) by May, residents perceive real protection and word-of-mouth referrals accelerate street and intermediary enrollment by 20–30% (estimated 500–1,000 additional contacts). This also validates the home-kit model for scaling and strengthens the business case for Year 2 expansion. However, supply-chain delays of 4+ weeks (4–8 week exposure at Month 1 = 2026-11-08) push 1,200–1,600 kits into June–July, missing the enrollment-leverage window and reducing installed coverage to 400–800 homes by peak season. This forces either an expedite premium (€50–100k, estimate) funded within the €800k kit category or a kit-scope cut to 1,000–1,500 homes, undermining equity claims and the visible program credibility that drives Year 2 political support.

  3. Intermediary-held-list outreach model preserves GDPR compliance and avoids municipal data-holding liability (legal exposure <€50k if designed correctly), but underfunding of door-knock and sentinel capacity leaves 80–90% of isolated high-risk residents unreached, resulting in preventable excess mortality during the July–August peak heat season. The GDPR-compliant design (€30k legal work + partner MOUs) removes the risk of a €2–4% regulatory fine and reputational damage from unauthorized health-data collection. However, the 3,000-enrolled-9%-reach model misses about 31,000 seniors aged 65+ (about 29,000 after door-knock expansion) living alone or in disconnected housing, who will suffer the highest heat-related mortality. A targeted door-knock phase for high-deprivation blocks (Months 5–7 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-05-17) costs €50–80k (11–18% of the €450k outreach budget) and could add 1,500–2,500 additional contact attempts and 500–750 enrollments from the unreached population. Without this investment, post-event analysis will reveal excess mortality concentrated in unreached neighborhoods, triggering media scrutiny ('program helped the connected and abandoned the isolated') that destroys municipal credibility and Year 2 political support.

Review 3: Recommended Actions

  1. Secure written funder pre-agreement on drill-based gate evidence and partial-release rule by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); high priority, risk reduction €200–400k. Cool-season gates depend entirely on drills; if funder rejects evidence, the €1.5M tranche-2 release is withheld, creating a €200–400k unfunded gap that exceeds the €160k available tranche-1 contingency. Written confirmation by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23)—before any procurement—eliminates this ambiguity and unlocks contingency-funding negotiation if needed. Immediate action: incident commander and PMO lead schedule a synchronous funder briefing, present the partial-release rule (€750k at Month 4 = 2027-02-08 if unmeasurable, remainder after Month 5 = 2027-03-08 re-test), and obtain written sign-off within 48 hours.

  2. Issue detailed procurement specifications and place first-tranche kit orders (600–800 units) by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14); critical priority, cost exposure €50–100k expedite premium. Cooling kits have 6–8 week EU supplier lead times; any 4-week slip pushes 60–80% of stock into June–July, after peak-risk May season and first heat events. Pre-qualifying 2–3 backup suppliers and placing orders 7 days earlier (Month 1.2 = 2026-11-14 vs. Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23) provides one-week buffer. Immediate action: procurement lead finalizes specs by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01) (a supplier market sounding may run at Month 0.3 (2026-10-17)), selects primary and backup by Month 1 (2026-11-08), and places the first call-off by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14), with the expedite premium (€50–100k, estimate) held within the €800k kit category.

  3. Add 1,500–2,500 contact attempts via targeted door-knock and sentinel outreach to high-deprivation neighborhoods Months 5–7 (2027-03-08 to 2027-05-17); medium priority, equity cost €50–80k (~11–18% of the €450k outreach budget), reach +500–750 enrollments from unreached population. Intermediary-held lists reach only 3,000 enrolled (≈9% of 34,000 high-risk 65+), leaving about 31,000 isolated, mistrustful residents unreached before expansion (about 29,000 after) and at highest mortality risk. Allocating 2–3 temporary outreach staff (Months 5–7 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-05-17) to canvass top-floor and social-housing blocks identified via deprivation index adds 1,500–2,500 contact attempts with an estimated 30–50% conversion to enrollment. Immediate action: outreach lead designs canvassing rubric and site-selection methodology by Month 1 (2026-11-08), secures budget reallocation from the €450k outreach category by Month 2 (2026-12-08), and launches recruitment of 2–3 temporary door-knock staff by Month 4 (2027-02-08).

Review 4: Showstopper Risks

  1. Volunteer driver recruitment and retention pipeline may collapse mid-season, forcing taxi-only fallback (+€150–250k unbudgeted cost). Likelihood: Medium. Vetting timeline (4–8 weeks per person) is compressed into 8 weeks (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) to achieve ≥20 recruits by Month 2 (2026-12-08) gate. Attrition during multi-day July–August heat waves is projected 15–25%, requiring 50–52 recruits at Month 0 (2026-10-08) to sustain 40 active by Month 11 (2027-09-08). If fewer than 20 recruits are in the pipeline at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), the taxi retainer scales up proportionally, capped at €80k; anything above that is the taxi-only fallback (+€150–250k), which needs an approval decision and would draw 54–89% of the €280k contingency (only €160k available before Month 4 = 2027-02-08) or cut kits. Compounding: if procurement also slips (+€50–100k expedite premium, held within the kit category), the combined exposure with the taxi-only fallback reaches €200–350k, exceeding all free contingency. Contingency: establish a standby volunteer reserve pool of 15–20 pre-vetted candidates (30–40% above active roster target) recruited and trained by Month 3 (2027-01-08), activated only on Level 3 alerts or if active roster falls below 20.

  2. Intermediary-held outreach model fails to reach isolated high-risk residents; coverage remains 9% of 65+ population, leaving about 31,000 people at peak mortality risk and exposing the program to media criticism and Year-2 funding loss. Likelihood: High. Housing associations, social services, NGOs and pharmacies predominantly contact residents already known to services, not isolated living-alone seniors or recent migrants who distrust official channels. The 3,000-enrolled target from 34,000 seniors represents inadequate reach; the 60% contact-success gate measures fidelity among enrolled only, not population-level coverage. If door-knock and sentinel outreach for high-deprivation neighborhoods (Months 5–7 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-05-17, estimated €50–80k cost) is not added, July–August excess mortality will concentrate in unreached populations, triggering post-event media investigation and political backlash that blocks Year-2 scaling. Compounding: equity gaps undermine the playbook's credibility for peer-city adoption and funder confidence. Contingency: Pre-identify and budget 2–3 temporary door-knock outreach staff (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) and execute neighborhood-level equity audit (coverage by deprivation index, housing type, language) by Month 9 (2027-07-08); if <20% of high-deprivation residents are reached by this date, add door-knock capacity for the final 6 weeks of season.

  3. Baseline heat-related EMS/ED data validation may reveal small-area counts insufficient for statistically credible evaluation, undermining Year-2 funding case and playbook transferability to peer cities. Likelihood: Medium. Provisional baseline estimates (80–120 EMS calls, 15–25 excess deaths per summer) are unverified pending data audit at Month 1 (2026-11-08). If actual baseline is 50% smaller (40–60 EMS calls, 8–12 deaths), statistical power to detect a realistic 10–15% program reduction collapses; the evaluation becomes underpowered and the final report must document this limitation explicitly, weakening the scaling cost model. Compounding: if procurement or staffing slips so that the program does not operationalize fully until June, real-season outcome data collection begins late, further reducing sample size and power. If Month 4 (2027-02-08) drill-based gates are passed but real-season data show no measurable harm reduction by Month 12 (2027-10-08), the playbook loses credibility and peer cities will reject the model as unproven. Contingency: Conduct baseline data audit by Month 1 (2026-11-08); if actual baseline is ≤50 EMS calls per summer, reframe evaluation focus to secondary outcomes (utilization, equity reach, partnership fidelity) instead of mortality attribution, and extend evaluation timeline to include Year 2 data (Months 13–24 = 2027-11-08 to 2028-10-08) to accumulate adequate sample size for credible analysis.

Review 5: Critical Assumptions

  1. Intermediary organizations possess adequate call-center capacity to execute ≥5,000 contact attempts per month at 60% success rate during alert season. Impact if incorrect: contact success drops to 40–50%, failing the Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate and withholding €1.5M tranche-2 release. Capacity shortfall of 20–30% forces either reduced enrollment targets (2,000 vs. 3,000) or emergency activation of €100–150k in municipal outreach staff, consuming 94% or more of the €160k tranche-1 contingency. Compounding: if transport also falters due to volunteer shortfall, both gates fail simultaneously and the city has no recovery path within budget. Validation: conduct rapid partner capacity survey (housing associations, social services, NGOs, pharmacies) by Month 1 (2026-11-08); model combined call attempts and success rate under multi-day fatigue; place written capacity commitments in partner MOUs by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); mock-call drill at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) so fixes can land before the Month 2 (2026-12-08) gate.

  2. EU kit suppliers deliver 40–50% of cooling-kit stock (600–800 units) by Month 4 (2027-02-08) and 100% by Month 6 (2027-04-08), enabling 100% installation by Month 7.3 (2027-05-17) before peak-risk May–June. Impact if incorrect: 4–8 week slip (realistic for EU industrial lead times) pushes 60–80% of kits into June–July, after first heat events and peak-risk season; 500–1,000 homes miss protected windows. Cost exposure: €50–100k expedite premium or €150–250k kit-scope reduction (from 2,000 to 1,000–1,500 homes). Compounding: if procurement slips AND volunteer recruitment fails, both transport and home-kit leverage vanish, eliminating the program's dual protective pathways. Validation: finalize specs by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01) (supplier market sounding at Month 0.3 (2026-10-17) only); pre-qualify 2–3 backup suppliers by Month 1 (2026-11-08); place binding first-tranche order (600 units) by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14)—one week earlier than planned—with signed delivery SLAs; confirm secondary stock arrives by Month 4 (2027-02-08) by Month 2 (2026-12-08) or activate backup supplier immediately.

  3. Funder accepts drill-based evidence (operational KPIs from full-system drill at Month 3.2 = 2027-01-14) as sufficient proof of gate success; partial-release rule (€750k at Month 4 = 2027-02-08 if unmeasurable, remainder post-May re-test) is documented in writing before Month 1 (2026-11-08). Impact if incorrect: funder withholds €1.5M at Month 4 (2027-02-08) citing insufficient real-event data; €200–400k cash gap emerges (€40–240k above available €160k tranche-1 contingency), forcing service cuts to home kits, transport or outreach during peak summer season, directly harming enrolled residents and destroying Year-2 credibility. Compounding: if cool May–July occurs naturally and no heat events test operations until August, gates become unmeasurable on any evidence (drill + real), triggering complete funding withhold. Validation: obtain written funder sign-off on partial-release rule and drill acceptance criteria by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23)—before procurement begins; document in signed funding amendment; brief incident commander and CFO monthly on funder alignment to flag ambiguity early.

Review 6: Key Performance Indicators

  1. Heat-related EMS call volume change (non-gating expectation of a 10–15% reduction, hypothesis only, reported with confidence ranges, by Month 12 = 2027-10-08; baseline 80–120 calls/summer, provisional). Success requires year-on-year comparison of aggregate heat-related EMS dispatch volumes during the season (Months 6.8–11.8 = 2027-04-23 to 2027-09-23) against the provisional 3-year baseline (80–120 calls estimated; audit pending Month 1 = 2026-11-08). Impact: A 10–15% reduction (8–18 fewer calls) validates the program's operational reach and protective effectiveness; <5% reduction signals outreach, home-kit or cooling-center underutilization requiring mid-season course correction. Interacts with: supply-chain delays (if kits slip past June, home-intervention effect is lost); intermediary-reach gaps (if 91% of 65+ remain unreached, EMS call reduction concentrates only in enrolled 9%, understating true population impact). Monitor: daily aggregate EMS count reporting (MOU by Month 1 = 2026-11-08); weekly trend analysis by incident commander; post-season epidemiologic attribution analysis by Month 12 (2027-10-08) with temperature adjustment and confidence ranges; recomputed against validated baseline after Month 1 (2026-11-08) audit.

  2. Outreach contact success rate ≥60% among enrolled high-risk residents (Month 4 = 2027-02-08 gate; tracked via drill + season Months 6.8–11.8 = 2027-04-23 to 2027-09-23). Success requires intermediary partners and city teams to reach ≥60% of enrolled residents (estimated 3,000 by Month 7 = 2027-05-08) within 4 hours of Level 2 alert declaration. Impact: 60% success = 1,800 residents contacted; <60% success fails the gate (65% (proposed threshold) is the early-warning level; results of 55–59% trigger corrective action within 48 hours and re-test before the gate), withholding €1.5M tranche-2 and forcing service cuts during peak heat. Interacts with: intermediary-capacity shortfall (if housing associations, social services lack call-center staffing, success drops to 40–50% mid-season); volunteer fatigue (if dispatch slows, residents cannot follow up on alerts with transport offers, reducing perceived reliability and future enrollment). Monitor: daily contact-attempt logs from all intermediary partners (shared spreadsheet, aggregate counts only); weekly success-rate calculation (contacts reached ÷ enrollment base); real-time escalation if weekly rate falls below 60% for ≥2 consecutive weeks; corrective action (additional staff, script revision, partner re-briefing) within 48 hours.

  3. Equity coverage: Year-1 expectation 13–16% overall of high-risk 65+ population (estimate); 20–25% (≈7,000–8,500 of 34,000 residents) is the Year-2 target, reached via enrollment + one-time contact; priority: ≥30% coverage in top-3 highest-deprivation neighborhoods. Success requires outreach expansion beyond intermediary lists to door-knock and sentinel pathways (Months 5–7 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-05-17, estimated €50–80k investment). Impact: 13–16% coverage in Year 1 validates population reach; <15% signals equity failure and leaves 85% unreached at peak mortality risk during July–August, triggering post-event media criticism and Year-2 funding loss (estimated €2.3M/year in jeopardy). Interacts with: intermediary-capacity gaps (if partner calls are 40–50% successful, baseline enrollment stalls at 1,500–1,800, floor coverage at 4–5%); kit-delivery slips (if homes lack visible protection by May, word-of-mouth enrollment growth stalls, depressing neighborhood-level reach). Monitor: monthly enrollment and contact audit by neighborhood deprivation index and housing type (top-floor, social housing, private rental, unhoused); disaggregate contact source (intermediary vs. door-knock vs. street) to identify gaps; Month 7 (2027-05-08) interim equity review; add door-knock capacity if high-deprivation coverage <20% by Month 9 (2027-07-08).

Review 7: Report Objectives

  1. Primary objectives: operationalize a gate-driven, replicable heat-response pilot in Castellón de la Plana (Month 0–12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08) that demonstrates measurable harm reduction and generates a transferable playbook for other EU cities. The report documents strategic decisions (11 primary, 12 secondary), operational plans, risk registers, and staff/procurement requirements to meet four scale gates at Month 4 (2027-02-08): ≥80% refuge hours, ≥60% outreach contact success, <45-min transport, after-action closure. Key deliverables: Heat Response Playbook with SOPs; scaling cost model (≈€2.3M/year estimated); evaluation report with temperature-adjusted baselines and attribution limits; Year-2 roadmap with funding recommendations.

  2. **Intended audience: municipal leadership (mayor, health officer, CFO) deciding immediate approval and resource commitment by Month 1 (2026-11-08); funder requiring written confirmation of drill-based gate evidence and partial-release rule by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); peer EU cities (Barcelona, Valencia, Poznań, Modena) evaluating replicability post-Month 12 (2027-10-08). The report informs: (a) funder decision on cool-season gate acceptance (€200–400k cash-flow risk if rejected); (b) procurement and hiring timelines with supply-chain buffer validation; (c) Year-2 funding source identification (€2.3M/year unidentified).

  3. Version 2 should differ from Version 1 by: (1) documenting funder's written sign-off on drill evidence and partial-release rule (gate 0, pre-requisite before Month 1 = 2026-11-08); (2) replacing provisional baseline estimates (80–120 EMS calls, 15–25 deaths) with validated audit results from hospital/EMS (due Month 1 = 2026-11-08); (3) confirming supplier quotes and backup-supplier emergency-activation agreements for kits and transport (Month 1.2 = 2026-11-14 commitment); (4) adding granular equity coverage targets by neighborhood deprivation index (Year-2 target ≥20–25% of 65+ population, ≥30% in top-3 deprived areas; Year-1 expectation 13–16%); (5) pre-specifying drill protocol and gate measurement SLAs (final Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23).

Review 8: Data Quality Concerns

  1. Baseline heat-related EMS/ED coding and volume estimates remain provisional and unvalidated; audit deferred to Month 1 (2026-11-08). The provisional baseline (80–120 EMS calls, 15–25 excess deaths per summer) underpins the evaluation design and power calculation; if actual baseline is 50% smaller (40–60 calls), statistical power to detect a realistic 10–15% program reduction collapses, and the final report must document this limitation explicitly. Consequence: playbook credibility for peer-city adoption weakens; Year-2 funding case becomes harder to justify if outcomes appear inconclusive. Validation approach: request hospital/EMS administrative data (3-year history, heat-coded calls by date/hour/age) by Month 0 (2026-10-08); conduct manual chart review for 50–100 cases to validate clinician coding practice (which ICD-10 codes or symptom patterns count as heat-related); deliver audit and temperature-adjusted baseline model by Month 1 (2026-11-08); if baseline is materially different from provisional estimate, recompute evaluation power immediately and adjust attribution design.

  2. Intermediary partner call-center capacity and summer staffing availability are estimated but not surveyed; capacity survey deferred to Month 1 (2026-11-08). The outreach gate (60% contact success from ≥300 attempts) assumes housing associations, social services, NGOs and pharmacies can sustain ≥5,000 contact attempts/month during May–September season with 80–90% staffing availability (15–20% typical summer turnover). If actual capacity is 20–30% lower (inadequate call staffing, competing priorities mid-season), contact success drops to 40–50%, failing the Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate and withholding €1.5M tranche-2. Consequence: outreach reach collapses from 3,000 to 1,800–2,400 enrolled, and the program must either reduce targets or draw €100–150k in emergency municipal staff (63–94% of contingency). Validation approach: issue a brief partner survey by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01) asking each intermediary current staff count, typical call-center hours/person/day, summer turnover forecast; model combined capacity and stress-test it in a mock-call drill (50–100 simulated calls) at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); obtain written capacity commitments and staffing reserves in partner DPAs by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23).

  3. Cooling-kit supplier lead times and expedite-cost benchmarks are not quoted; supplier capacity is assumed at 6–8 weeks and expedite premium is capped at 10–15%, but actual offers remain unknown. Procurement of 2,000 kits (€800k total including expedite) requires first call-off placement by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14) and 40–50% delivery by Month 4 (2027-02-08); if suppliers report lead times ≥10 weeks or expedite premiums >15%, the €50–100k budget reserve is insufficient and kits slip into June–July, missing peak-risk May season and reducing home-intervention effectiveness by 30–50%. Consequence: if both kit delivery and volunteer recruitment slip simultaneously (compound risk), transport and home-kit leverage both degrade and the program loses dual protective pathways. Validation approach: issue detailed RFQs to 5–8 kit suppliers after specs at Month 0.8 (2026-11-01) (market sounding at Month 0.3 (2026-10-17) only) requesting firm quotes, standard and expedite lead times, and minimum-order requirements; pre-qualify 2–3 backup suppliers with written emergency-activation agreements (7-day notice, price cap, premium fee acceptance) by Month 1 (2026-11-08); lock in primary order with confirmed delivery SLAs by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14) and hold the expedite premium (€50–100k, estimate) within the €800k kit category.

Review 9: Stakeholder Feedback

  1. Funder's written acceptance of drill-based gate evidence and partial-release rule by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); critical for €1.5M release timing and contingency-funding strategy. The cool-season gates (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) depend entirely on drill performance (center hours, outreach contact, transport time from simulated alert scenarios). If funder rejects drill evidence and demands real heat-event validation, the €1.5M tranche-2 release is delayed to Months 5–6 (2027-03-08 to 2027-04-08), creating a €200–400k unfunded gap (€40–240k above the €160k available tranche-1 contingency). This forces mid-summer service cuts to home kits, transport or outreach during peak July–August heat season, directly harming enrolled residents and undermining Year-2 credibility. Obtain written confirmation of the partial-release rule (€750k at Month 4 = 2027-02-08 if unmeasurable, remainder after Month 5 = 2027-03-08 re-test) and drill-acceptance criteria in a signed funding amendment by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), before procurement begins.

  2. Validated baseline heat-related EMS/ED coding practice and volume confirmation by Month 1 (2026-11-08); necessary to assess evaluation power and playbook credibility for peer-city replication. Provisional baseline estimates (80–120 EMS calls, 15–25 excess deaths per summer) are unverified pending hospital and EMS data audit. If actual baseline is 50% smaller (40–60 calls), statistical power to detect a realistic 10–15% program reduction collapses; the final report must document this limitation, weakening the playbook's transferability and Year-2 funding case. Consequence: if peer cities adopt the model and see no measurable harm reduction in their own pilots, credibility cascades downward across EU networks. Request 3-year historical EMS and ED administrative data by Month 0 (2026-10-08); conduct manual chart review (50–100 cases) to validate clinician coding for heat-related presentations; deliver audit and temperature-adjusted baseline model by Month 1 (2026-11-08); if actual baseline differs >30% from provisional, recompute evaluation power and revise attribution design immediately.

  3. Intermediary partner capacity commitment and written staffing-reserve guarantee by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); essential to validate the 60% outreach contact-success gate (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) and prevent mid-season collapse. Housing associations, social services, NGOs and pharmacies are assumed to sustain ≥5,000 contact attempts per month at 60% success during May–September season with ≥80% staffing availability. If actual capacity is 20–30% lower (competing priorities, summer turnover ≥20%), contact success drops to 40–50%, failing the gate and withholding €1.5M tranche-2. This forces either reduced enrollment (1,500–2,000 vs. 3,000 target) or emergency activation of €100–150k municipal outreach staff (63–94% of tranche-1 contingency). Conduct partner capacity survey (email questionnaire) by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01) asking each intermediary current call-center FTE, call duration per resident, summer turnover forecast; model combined capacity and validate in a mock-call drill (50–100 simulated enrollment calls) at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); obtain written capacity commitments and minimum-staffing reserves in partner DPAs by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23).

Review 10: Changed Assumptions

  1. Pilot-city climate and heat-event frequency assumptions (Mediterranean 15–25 excess deaths/summer provisional baseline) may not match actual historical patterns; re-evaluation required by Month 1 (2026-11-08) data audit. Castellón de la Plana's baseline is provisionally estimated at 80–120 EMS calls and 15–25 excess deaths per summer, sourced from published literature and peer-city benchmarks, not from verified municipal records. If actual 3-year historical data reveals ≤40–50 EMS calls per summer (50% lower), the evaluation will be underpowered to detect a realistic 10–15% program reduction, requiring evaluation design revision and extended data collection to Month 24 (2028-10-08). This directly impacts playbook credibility for peer-city adoption and Year-2 funding case. Validate by requesting hospital and EMS administrative data by Month 0 (2026-10-08); conduct baseline audit and temperature-adjusted modeling by Month 1 (2026-11-08); if baseline differs >30% from provisional estimate, recompute statistical power immediately and adjust evaluation scope.

  2. Intermediary-partner staffing stability and call-center capacity during multi-day July–August heat surges assumed at 80–90% availability; actual summer turnover and fatigue patterns unvalidated. The outreach model assumes housing associations, social services, NGOs and pharmacies can sustain ≥5,000 contact attempts per month and 60% success rate under multi-day alert conditions (Months 9–11 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-09-08). Summer staff turnover and competing priorities (vacations, concurrent crises) are projected at 10–20% but not benchmarked against actual municipal-partner data. If real turnover reaches 25–30%, contact success drops to 40–50%, failing the Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate and forcing €100–150k emergency municipal outreach staffing (63–94% of tranche-1 contingency). Re-evaluate by issuing partner capacity survey (Month 0.8 = 2026-11-01) and stress-testing in mock-call drill (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23); lock written staffing reserves into partner DPAs (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23).

  3. Year-2 funding source (€2.3M estimated recurring cost) and political continuity assumed available; no identified source, no mayoral term guarantee, no guarantee of cross-party support post-election cycle. The playbook is intended for scaling to other EU cities and establishing a sustained municipal program beyond Month 12 (2027-10-08). However, Year-2 funding is entirely unfunded and municipal political continuity is not guaranteed (elections occur periodically, administration changes). If Year-2 funding is unavailable by Month 9 (2027-07-08), the municipality cannot sustain refuges, transport or outreach beyond Month 12 (2027-10-08), orphaning infrastructure and violating implicit commitments to enrolled residents. This undermines peer-city credibility ('pilot program abandoned after Year 1'). Identify and pre-commit Year-2 funding source by Month 9 (2027-07-08) via EU climate grants, national health budget co-financing or municipal budget mainstreaming; include a 'continuity of command' clause in the mayoral delegation (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) ensuring heat-response priorities persist across electoral transitions.

Review 11: Budget Clarifications

  1. Contingency reserve allocation and draw-down authority remain undefined; free contingency €280k (€160k tranche 1 + €120k tranche 2) may be consumed by a single risk (taxi-only fallback +€150–250k, or delayed-release cash gap €200–400k), leaving zero buffer for compound failures. Impact: if supply-chain expedite premium (€50–100k, estimate, inside the kit category) + volunteer recruitment shortfall (taxi scale-up +€40–80k) occur simultaneously, exposure is €90–180k; only the taxi-only fallback plus expedite reaches €200–350k, exceeding the €160k pre-Month-4 free contingency by €40–190k. This forces mid-season service cuts or reallocation between home kits, transport and outreach, reducing program effectiveness. Clarification needed: (1) approve explicit contingency-draw authority and approval workflow (who authorizes draws >€10k, >€50k?); (2) pre-identify contingency sources if free reserve is insufficient (e.g., credit line, clawback from tranche-2, reallocation between categories); (3) publish decision tree: if supply-chain slips +€80k AND volunteer recruitment lags +€60k, which services are deferred/cut first (kits to 1,500, refuges to 6 sites, or taxi-only operation).

  2. Year-2 recurring cost (€2.3M/year estimated) lacks a committed funding source; if not identified by Month 9 (2027-07-08), municipal leadership may not authorize continuation beyond Month 12 (2027-10-08), stranding infrastructure and enrolled residents. Impact: playbook transferability to peer cities is undermined (pilot abandoned after Year 1); political credibility for heat-health spending is damaged; accumulated staff and volunteer relationships are lost. Year-2 continuation is critical for the program to demonstrate sustained harm reduction and to validate scaling assumptions. Clarification needed: (1) identify and pre-commit ≥1 Year-2 funding source (EU climate grants, national health budget line, municipal mainstreaming) by Month 9 (2027-07-08); (2) quantify what components are viable under a reduced budget (€1.5M–€2.0M) if full €2.3M is unavailable (e.g., retain refuges + transport, defer home kits to Year 2); (3) document in funder correspondence and municipal strategic plan.

  3. Home-kit installation buffer and remediation/replacement costs not explicitly budgeted; €800k home-kit category includes a ≈€200k bundle (expedite premium of €50–100k (estimate), storage, buffer stock (10–15%), QA and hydration) but does not itemize rework, QA audit costs (0.5 FTE inspector, ~€25k annually), or warranty/returns reserve. Impact: if 10–20% of 2,000 installations fail safety checks or customers require rework, the QA and rework cost could consume €50–100k (6–12% of kit category), forcing either a cut to final installations (100–200 fewer homes) or a draw from contingency. Clarification needed: (1) approve and itemize QA, rework and warranty reserves within the €800k kit budget (recommend €25–40k QA + inspection + €30–50k warranty/returns = €55–90k explicit line item); (2) confirm installer safety-check protocol and QA audit sample rate (proposed 10–20% of 2,000 installs = 200–400 homes); (3) define rework SLA and budget for rapid corrective action (target <5 days if defects found) before homes enter the season.

Review 12: Role Definitions

  1. Incident Commander: single point of authority for alert declaration, spending authorization and cross-department coordination; currently named as 'mayor's office' role but lacks written delegation, backup chain, and decision authority limits. Why critical: unclear authority delays alert decisions by 6–12 hours (loss of response time during critical morning heat peaks), invites conflicting orders across departments (refuges, transport, health system), and creates accountability gaps if response fails under media scrutiny. Impact: €3.5M program credibility depends on demonstrable command clarity; without written delegation by Month 1 (2026-11-08), municipality faces legal challenge to alert validity and inter-agency disputes mid-season. Actionable steps: (1) draft mayoral delegation letter by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01) specifying incident commander name, role, spending limits per tier (PMO lead ≤€25k, incident commander plus CFO €25–50k, above €50k with funder notice), alert-declaration triggers, and backup authority chain if primary is unavailable >2 hours; (2) obtain mayor's signature by Month 1 (2026-11-08) and file with municipal legal; (3) brief all partner organizations (health, civil protection, transport, refuges) on the delegation to embed understanding independently of municipal staff turnover.

  2. Partner Liaison Officer: owns outreach-partner engagement, capacity monitoring, and performance tracking for 4–6 intermediary organizations (housing associations, social services, NGOs, pharmacies); currently assigned as a shared coordination role with no dedicated FTE or written accountability. Why critical: partner capacity is the sole gatekeeper for the 60% outreach contact-success gate (Month 4 = 2027-02-08); if partner call-center staffing is unclear or capacity agreements are informal, mid-season deterioration goes undetected until gates fail and €1.5M release is withheld. Impact: partner withdrawal or reduced staffing could drop contact success from 60% to 40–50%, failing the gate and forcing €100–150k emergency municipal outreach staff draw (63–94% of tranche-1 contingency). Actionable steps: (1) designate a dedicated Partner Liaison Officer (1 FTE, Months 0–12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08) reporting directly to incident commander; (2) by Month 1 (2026-11-08), conduct formal capacity survey of all 4–6 partners (staff count, call-center hours, summer turnover forecast) and obtain signed capacity commitments in partner DPAs by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); (3) establish weekly partner performance reporting (call volumes, contact success %, staff absences) and monthly liaison contact to flag emerging capacity gaps.

  3. Project Manager (PMO Lead): owns procurement timeline, staffing ramp, budget burn tracking, and gate-readiness attestation; currently fragmented across HR coordinator, procurement lead, and incident commander with no single owner or written decision authority. Why critical: the compressed 8-week procurement window (Month 0 = 2026-10-08 to Month 2 = 2026-12-08) and staggered hiring of 43 FTE across 6 months are the critical paths for both gates; delays compound exponentially (if kits slip by 4 weeks AND volunteers lag recruitment, both transport and home-kit leverage degrade). Impact: procurement-path mismanagement could cost €50–100k in expedite premiums or lose €1.5M tranche-2 if gates are unmet; hiring delays of 3+ weeks could leave centers and dispatch under-staffed by May, degrading service by 10–25%. Actionable steps: (1) designate a dedicated Project Manager (1 FTE, Months 0–12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08) reporting to incident commander; (2) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), build and maintain a critical-path Gantt chart tracking all procurement orders, hiring cohorts, and gate milestones; (3) issue weekly status reports to incident commander flagging any item >1 week behind plan and pre-authorize contingency drawdown (PMO lead up to €25k per draw; €25–50k needs incident commander plus CFO) if slippage is detected early.

Review 13: Timeline Dependencies

  1. GDPR compliance and partner DPA execution must occur by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) before intermediary outreach staff can begin enrollment; delay risks partner withdrawal and eliminates the sole outreach model. Impact: if DPA negotiation slips 4+ weeks (typical for multi-org legal review), partner recruitment and briefing cannot begin until Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), compressing training into 1 month. This delays enrollment start to Month 4 (2027-02-08), reducing the 5,000 contact-attempt target to 2,500–3,000 by Month 7 (2027-05-08) and dropping enrollment from 3,000 to 1,500–1,800 enrolled (50% shortfall). Interacts with: if intermediary reach collapses AND door-knock outreach is not added, coverage remains ≤5% and isolation equity fails. Action: engage GDPR counsel by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) with strict Month 1 (2026-11-08) legal-opinion deadline; pre-draft template DPAs by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01) to shorten negotiation cycle.

  2. Procurement spec finalization and first-tranche order placement compressed into 6 weeks (Month 0.8 = 2026-11-01 to Month 1.2 = 2026-11-14); spec delays of 2+ weeks cascade into kit-delivery slippage by Month 4 (2027-02-08) and force €50–100k expedite premium or kit-scope cut. Impact: EU suppliers require 6–8 week lead times; placing orders at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) instead of Month 1.2 (2026-11-14) shifts 40–50% kit delivery from February to March–April, reducing February buffer stock to <15% of planned 600–800 units. This creates pressure to install kits in June–July (post peak-risk May) and reduces home-intervention ROI by 20–30%. Interacts with: if procurement slips 4+ weeks AND volunteer recruitment underperforms, both transport and kit leverage degrade simultaneously. Action: issue detailed specs to suppliers by Month 0.8 (2026-11-01); place the first call-off by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14), with all tranche-1 orders by Month 2 (2026-12-08); commit the ≈€200k kit bundle (expedite premium €50–100k (estimate), storage, buffer, QA, hydration) within the €800k category upfront (not contingent).

  3. Month 3.2 (2027-01-14) full-system drill completion and Month 3.9 (2027-02-04) after-action closure must occur on schedule to support Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate decision; any delay >4 days compresses corrective-action time into <1 week, preventing remediation and forcing gate escalation to Month 5 (2027-03-08). Impact: if drill is delayed to Month 3.5 (2027-01-23) due to unavailable staff or facility access, after-action report slips to Month 3.8 (2027-02-01), leaving only 5 days to close corrective actions before the Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate decision. Critical gaps (transport time >50 min, contact success <55%) cannot be remediated in 5 days, forcing the funder to declare gates unmeasurable and trigger the partial-release rule (€750k at Month 4 = 2027-02-08, remainder after Month 5 = 2027-03-08 re-test), creating a €200–400k cash gap. Interacts with: drill delays compound if hiring is staggered (only 30–40% of staff in post by Month 3 = 2027-01-08), reducing drill realism and forcing re-test. Action: lock drill date at Month 3.2 (2027-01-14) by Month 2 (2026-12-08) in writing; schedule after-action closure cadence (draft Month 3.5 = 2027-01-23, actions closed Month 3.9 = 2027-02-04); identify parallel drill observation team (independent from operations) to detect and escalate gaps in real-time.

Review 14: Financial Strategy

  1. Year-2 funding source identification and budget sustainability model (€2.3M/year recurring, estimate) remain unfunded; absence of committed source by Month 9 (2027-07-08) risks municipal abandonment of infrastructure post-Month-12 and destroys peer-city credibility if pilot cannot demonstrate sustained operations. Financial impact: if Year-2 funding is unavailable, the municipality cannot maintain refuges, transport or outreach beyond Month 12 (2027-10-08), orphaning €3.5M in setup costs and €800k in home kits. Peer cities viewing Year-1-only operation will reject the model as unproven and unsustainable. Interacts with: playbook transferability (core deliverable, user constraint) depends entirely on demonstrable Year-2 continuity; delayed-release cash gap (€200–400k exposure if tranche-2 withheld) compounds if Year-2 funding is also unavailable, creating a €400–800k total funding cliff. Action: identify and pre-commit ≥1 Year-2 source (EU climate grants, national health budget, municipal mainstreaming) by Month 9 (2027-07-08); if unavailable, document scaled-back Year-2 scope (refuges only, defer kits; estimated €1.2–1.5M/year) and obtain mayoral commitment to that minimum by Month 11 (2027-09-08).

  2. Contingency reserve draw-down authority and priority-sequencing rules undefined; free €280k (€160k before Month 4 = 2027-02-08) may be consumed by a single risk (taxi-only fallback +€150–250k OR delayed-release cash gap €200–400k), leaving zero buffer and forcing mid-season service cuts with no decision pathway. Financial impact: if supply-chain expedite premium (€50–100k) + volunteer recruitment shortfall (€40–80k) + unplanned staffing gap (€50–80k) occur simultaneously, the expedite and volunteer items alone sum to €90–180k; with the taxi-only fallback plus expedite exposure reaches €200–350k, exceeding free contingency by €40–190k. This triggers unplanned cuts to home kits (€150–250k loss), refuges (scale to 6 sites, -€100k), or outreach reach (500–1,000 fewer households). Interacts with: procurement timeline (if orders slip by 4+ weeks, expedite premium consumes €50–100k immediately); volunteer pipeline (if recruitment lags, taxi retainer scale-up consumes €40–80k within weeks). Action: publish explicit contingency-draw decision tree by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23): authorize draws ≤€25k (PMO lead), €25–50k (incident commander + CFO), >€50k (incident commander + CFO + funder notification within 24 h); specify service-cut priority: maintain refuges + transport first (gates 1–3), defer home kits to Year 2 if budget exhausted.

  3. Procurement budget allocation across categories (€3.5M total) leaves no explicit reserve for cost escalation in specific line items (refuge fit-out €850k, home kits €800k, transport €380k); if a single category overruns by 15% (typical EU inflation), total cost exceeds €3.5M cap by €150–200k (estimate) with no reallocation path documented. Financial impact: refuge sites may require unexpected accessibility remediation (€50–100k overrun if >3 sites need structural work beyond the €10k per-site cap, proposed threshold); kit suppliers may raise prices mid-contract (€50–100k escalation on €600k hardware); transport retainer may increase if volunteer recruitment fails earlier than forecast (€40–80k scale-up at Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23 vs. Month 3 = 2027-01-08). Combined exposure: €150–280k. Interacts with: free contingency (only €160k available before Month 4 = 2027-02-08) is already at risk from transport fallback and delayed-release scenarios; any category overrun forces immediate cascading cuts to other services. Action: by Month 1 (2026-11-08), conduct a cost-sensitivity analysis for each budget category (refuge fit-out, kits, transport, staffing) identifying which items have locked-in pricing (procurement contracts by Month 1.2 = 2026-11-14) vs. which remain at risk; establish explicit reallocation rules: if refuge remediation exceeds €10k per site cap, reduce site count from 10 to 8–9 rather than dip into contingency; if kit price escalation >5%, accept delivery delay (shift from February to March–April) rather than pay premium.

Review 15: Motivation Factors

  1. Clear early operational wins and visible resident benefit (home-kit installation completion by Month 7.3 = 2027-05-17) sustain staff, volunteer and partner morale through peak-stress July–August heat season. If 2,000 kits are visibly installed in enrolled homes by May–June, residents perceive tangible protection, word-of-mouth referrals accelerate enrollment by 20–30% (500–1,000 additional contacts estimated), and street-contact and intermediary staff see immediate evidence their work matters. Loss of this motivation driver occurs if supply-chain slips >4 weeks: 60–80% of kits arrive post-May, installation is compressed into June–July during operational peak, staff encounter enrolled residents without promised protection, and volunteer/partner engagement erodes mid-season. Interacts with: procurement timeline (Month 1.2 = 2026-11-14 order critical) and staff fatigue (multi-day heat waves July–August will test commitment if home-kit promise is already broken). Action: lock kit order by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14) with delivery SLA; conduct installation ceremony or resident testimonial communications by Month 8 (2027-06-08) to reinforce staff-team impact narrative.

  2. Cross-departmental incident-command alignment and demonstrated inter-agency coordination eliminate silos and build operational trust, preventing mid-season command-structure collapse and morale breakdown. If the incident commander (mayor's office) and deputies (public health, civil protection, communications) establish and rehearse protocols together by Month 2 (2026-12-08), daily SITREPs at 08:30 become routine, decisions are delegated transparently, and partners know who to escalate to during alerts. Loss of alignment occurs if incident command remains unclear: delayed alert declarations (6–12 hour loss), conflicting cross-department orders (refuges vs. transport vs. health system), unclear accountability mid-season when fatigue sets in (Months 9–11 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-09-08). Interacts with: volunteer and staff fatigue (if command is fragmented, staff see mixed signals and morale fractures); partner capacity (NGO and intermediary teams lose confidence in city coordination). Action: draft and execute written mayoral delegation by Month 1 (2026-11-08); conduct joint inter-agency tabletop drill at Month 2.5 (2026-12-23); confirm daily SITREP cadence and backup-authority chain before Month 3.2 (2027-01-14) full-system drill.

  3. Concrete performance feedback from Month 3.2 (2027-01-14) full-system drill validated against gate criteria (80% center hours, 60% contact success, <45 min transport) provides staff and leadership confidence that Month 4 (2027-02-08) gates are achievable and motivates corrective action. If drill results show 85% center hours and 65% contact success, the team enters the real season with confidence and media framing shifts to 'pilot validated.' Erosion of motivation occurs if drill data are murky, incomplete or contested: after-action report slips (Month 3.5 = 2027-01-23 draft, Month 3.9 = 2027-02-04 closure compressed into 6 days), corrective actions are unclear, leadership questions whether gates are realistic, and staff enter May season with doubt. Interacts with: funder confidence (if gates are ambiguous, funder may withhold €1.5M tranche-2, creating €200–400k cash gap that forces service cuts and staff notice immediately); contingency exposure (if drill reveals major gaps—e.g., transport time 60+ min—corrective spend may exhaust €160k tranche-1 contingency, signaling organizational distress). Action: lock drill date at Month 3.2 (2027-01-14) by Month 2 (2026-12-08); assign independent observation team (not operations staff) to capture gate-metric data in real-time; deliver draft after-action report by Month 3.5 (2027-01-23) with clear pass/fail/remediation decisions before Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate evaluation.

Review 16: Automation Opportunities

  1. Automate outreach contact-attempt logging and success-rate tracking via shared real-time spreadsheet (accessible to all 4–6 intermediary partners and city) instead of manual daily reporting. Impact: reduces partner reporting overhead by ~5 hours/week per organization (€40–60k annual FTE cost savings estimate) and enables daily success-rate visibility (target ≥60%) instead of weekly delays, allowing incident commander to escalate shortfalls within 24 h instead of waiting until end-of-month gate measurement. Interacts with: outreach gate (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) depends on real-time contact tracking; automated logging eliminates reconciliation delays that compress Month 3.9 (2027-02-04) corrective-action window. Action: design shared spreadsheet template (partner ID, attempt date/time, resident name optional, contact outcome, language) by Month 1 (2026-11-08); pilot with 2 partners in Month 2 (2026-12-08) drill; deploy to all partners by Month 3 (2027-01-08).

  2. Automate cooling-center occupancy reporting and transport-dispatch routing via a simple shared real-time dashboard (centers log occupancy every 30 min during alerts) instead of manual phone updates. Impact: eliminates dispatch phone-tree delays (currently 10–15 min coordination lag per request) and enables transport to reroute residents to available sites within 5 min instead of 15–20 min. Estimated transport time improvement: 5–10 min per request, supporting the <45-min gate target with margin. Interacts with: transport-time gate (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) depends on fast center-dispatch integration; manual updates add 10–15 min of system latency per request, risking gate failure if volume peaks. Action: build simple secure spreadsheet or low-code platform (center occupancy, capacity, access restrictions) by Month 2 (2026-12-08); integrate with dispatch system during Month 3.2 (2027-01-14) drill; confirm <5-min update latency before season.

  3. Automate heat-illness escalation decision-making for outreach staff via a simple laminated checklist and pre-recorded phone protocols (e.g., 'if confused + hot skin → call EMS; if mild dehydration only → phone triage line') instead of ad-hoc staff judgment. Impact: reduces escalation errors and delays (estimated 5–10 min saved per ambiguous case), improves consistency across 25–35 outreach and street-contact staff, and reduces occupational-health incident risk (safer decisions, clearer liability). Interacts with: staff fatigue risk (Months 9–11 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-09-08) worsens decision-making under pressure; automated checklists reduce cognitive load and burnout. Action: co-design checklist with senior clinician by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); laminate and distribute to all outreach staff by Month 2 (2026-12-08); integrate into training and drill scenarios; measure escalation accuracy post-drill at Month 3.5 (2027-01-23).

Q1: What does the 'Alert Trigger Ladder' mean, and why is it critical to the program's success?

A1: The Alert Trigger Ladder is a three-tiered forecast-based system that defines when cooling centers and support services activate. Level 1 (Advisory): daytime high ≥33°C or night low ≥20°C for 2+ days triggers phone check-ins only. Level 2 (Alert): high ≥35°C and low ≥22°C activates centers 10:00–20:00. Level 3 (Emergency): same for 3+ days or national red warning extends to 24-hour operation. The thresholds balance 'alert fatigue' (too-frequent false alarms waste budget) against 'missed hot nights' (underestimating nights with high mortality risk). Success is measured by false-alarm rates and missed-event counts post-season.

Q2: What is the 'Cooling Refuge Network Shape,' and how does it affect who can access help?

A2: Decision 2 (Critical) specifies whether the city builds 10 small neighborhood refuges within walking distance (favored option) or fewer large anchor sites requiring transport. The chosen design prioritizes small refuges in libraries, community centers and parish halls so ≥70% of enrolled residents are within 800 meters (10-minute walk). This design trades staffing complexity for equity: residents who cannot travel far or lack transport can still reach shelter. Overnight cooling is offered at 3 fully accessible sites only during Level 3 emergencies. The document raises a core tension: many small sites are expensive to staff and secure; few large sites save money but depend entirely on transport working for frail and mobility-limited residents.

Q3: What is the 'Consent-Light Identification Routes,' and why does the city avoid holding personal health data?

A3: Decision 3 (Critical) uses intermediary-held contact lists to identify high-risk residents without the city holding personal health data. Housing associations, social services, NGOs and pharmacies call their own clients directly to enroll them, and only report aggregate results to the city (e.g., '100 residents contacted, 65 enrolled'). This design avoids GDPR exposure (no city-held health registry = lower regulatory fine risk) and reaches offline residents (older people who distrust digital channels). The trade-off: isolated residents not already known to these intermediaries—the highest-mortality group—are systematically missed. The document acknowledges this coverage gap and raises the equity cost of the GDPR-safe design.

Q4: What is the 'Mobility Support Delivery' and why is the 45-minute transport target difficult to meet?

A4: Decision 4 (Critical) chooses how residents reach cooling centers: 40 volunteer drivers coordinated by dispatch, with a taxi standby retainer (capped €80k) as backup. The under-45-minute mean pickup time gate is measured from request to vehicle arrival. The document raises that this is ambitious because volunteer availability varies (illness, fatigue, competing duties), wheelchair-accessible vehicles take longer to board, and peak-demand periods (early morning hot-day peaks) overwhelm dispatch. If volunteers fall short of 40 recruits, the taxi retainer must scale up to €100–120k, consuming 63–75% of the contingency and forcing home-kit scope cuts from 2,000 to 1,000–1,500 homes.

Q5: What are the four 'scale gates' at Month 4 (2027-02-08), and what happens if they fail?

A5: The Month 4 (2027-02-08) gates are user-mandated thresholds (user constraints): (1) ≥80% of planned cooling-center hours delivered (from a full-system drill); (2) ≥60% contact success among enrolled residents (from ≥300 outreach attempts); (3) mean request-to-transport time <45 minutes (from ≥30 requests including ≥5 wheelchair users); (4) 100% of after-action corrective items closed. If all four gates pass, €1.5M tranche-2 funding releases. If gates fail or are unmeasurable (cool June–July = no real heat events), only €750k (50%) releases at Month 4 (2027-02-08), and the remainder is deferred to Month 5 (2027-03-08) after a re-test. Gate failure creates a €200–400k cash gap (€40–240k above the €160k available tranche-1 contingency), forcing mid-summer cuts to home kits, transport or outreach—directly harming enrolled residents during peak-risk July–August.

Q6: What is the ethical trade-off between legal safety and equity reach in the intermediary-list outreach model, and what populations are systematically left out?

A6: The intermediary-held-list model (housing associations, social services, NGOs, pharmacies contact their own residents without personal data transferred to the city) avoids GDPR regulatory fines (€2–4% revenue, €500k–1M+ exposure) and reputational harm from unauthorized health-data collection. However, this legal-safety design systematically excludes high-mortality populations: isolated, living-alone seniors not known to any intermediary (~25,000–30,000 of 34,000 seniors aged 65+ are unreached); recent migrants distrustful of formal services; unhoused people absent from all lists; private-rental residents not tracked by housing associations. The 3,000-enrolled target (~9% of 65+) represents inadequate population reach. The equity cost: preventable excess mortality concentrated in unreached neighborhoods during July–August, exposed post-event in media investigation and local analysis.

Q7: What does the 'cool-season gate-testing cliff' mean, and why does it create a €200–400k financial risk if the funder rejects drill evidence?

A7: The Month 4 (2027-02-08) scale gates (≥80% center hours, ≥60% outreach contact, <45-min transport, after-action closure) fall entirely in the cool season (November–February), when real heat events will not occur in Castellón de la Plana. Gates must be tested via a full-system drill (Month 3.2 = 2027-01-14) using simulated alert scenarios, not real operational performance under thermal stress. If the funder rejects drill evidence as insufficient and demands real heat-event validation, the €1.5M tranche-2 release is withheld at Month 4 (2027-02-08). This creates a €200–400k unfunded gap (€40–240k above the €160k available tranche-1 contingency), forcing mid-season cuts to home kits (500–1,000 fewer homes), transport capacity (taxi-only fallback), or outreach staff (reduced contact attempts) during peak July–August heat season, directly harming enrolled residents. No written funder pre-agreement on drill acceptance exists; this must be obtained by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23).

Q8: How do volunteer driver recruitment shortfalls cascade into budget cuts to home kits, and what is the exposure if recruitment and kit supply both slip?

A8: If volunteer driver recruitment falls short of 40 vetted drivers (target ≥20 by Month 2 = 2026-12-08) and fewer than 15 are in the vetting pipeline by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), the taxi standby retainer must scale from €80k (capped) to €100–120k immediately to maintain transport capacity and protect the <45-minute gate. This consumes 63–75% of the €160k available tranche-1 contingency. Simultaneously, if kit suppliers slip delivery by 4+ weeks (6–8 week EU lead times are realistic), 60–80% of kits do not arrive until June–July, after peak-risk May–June, necessitating a €50–100k expedite premium (10–15% cost premium) or a kit-scope cut from 2,000 to 1,000–1,500 homes. If both risks occur—volunteer shortfall AND supply-chain slip—the combined exposure reaches €200–350k (€80k taxi scale + €100k expedite OR €250k kit reduction), consuming 125–219% of the €160k free contingency by Month 4 (2027-02-08). This forces a choice: accept transport-only fallback (no home kits, home-intervention equity goal abandoned) or defer home-kit installation to Year 2 and lose the visible program credibility that drives sustained enrollment and Year-2 political support.

Q9: What are the safeguarding and occupational-health risks for street-contact and outreach staff, and how are they managed?

A9: Outreach, street-contact and cooling-center staff will regularly encounter residents in acute heat distress, heat stroke, and vulnerable populations during multi-day heat waves (July–August). Risks include: (1) Delayed escalation of heat illness (outreach staff may misjudge severity, delaying EMS calls by 10–30 minutes); (2) Staff assault or threat during street contact (estimated medium likelihood, medium–high severity; potential injury, psychological harm, litigation); (3) Fatigue and burnout during multi-day surges (staff work 7+ consecutive alert days, increasing decision errors and emotional exhaustion); (4) Occupational-health incident response gaps (if safeguarding protocols are not clear, incident debriefing is delayed, or counseling access is slow, staff psychological harm cascades into turnover). Mitigation: heat-illness escalation checklist with nurse-triage-line access (ready by Month 2 = 2026-12-08); de-escalation and trauma-informed-care training for all street and outreach staff (3-hour module, test ≥80%, refresher in May); safeguarding incident-reporting protocol (same-day supervisor debrief, 24-hour occupational-health counseling access); mandatory peer-support group monthly during alert season; shift limits of ≤3–4 consecutive days then 1–2 rest days enforced; 20–30% staff reserve to absorb absences and surge capacity.

Q10: Why is there no identified funding source for Year 2 (€2.3M/year recurring estimated), and what does this mean for the program's sustainability and peer-city replicability?

A10: The plan delivers a 12-month pilot (Month 0–12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08) funded entirely by the €3.5M grant (€2.0M initial + €1.5M conditional at Month 4 = 2027-02-08). Year-2 continuation at the same footprint (10 refuges, 3,000+ enrolled residents, 40 volunteer drivers, 2,000-home kits deployed) requires an estimated €2.3M/year recurring cost (estimate, not inflation-adjusted). However, no Year-2 funding source is identified in the plan—no committed EU climate grants, national health budget line, municipal budget mainstreaming, or regional authority co-financing. If Year-2 funding is not secured by Month 9 (2027-07-08), the municipality has three options by Month 12 (2027-10-08): (1) Abandon infrastructure and enrolled residents after Year 1 (reputational catastrophe: 'pilot program abandoned'); (2) Scale back to a reduced footprint (e.g., refuges only, defer home kits; estimated €1.2–1.5M/year, partial coverage); (3) Negotiate a municipal budget mainstreaming without external funding (likely requires deprioritizing other health/social spending). For peer-city replication, sustainability beyond Year 1 is critical: if Castellón's pilot collapses after Month 12 (2027-10-08), other EU cities will view the model as unproven and unfundable at scale, destroying the playbook's transferability and funder confidence.

A premortem assumes the project has failed and works backward to identify the most likely causes.

Assumptions to Kill

These foundational assumptions represent the project's key uncertainties. If proven false, they could lead to failure. Validate them immediately using the specified methods.

A9 Public and media trust will hold: residents, including migrants and older people, will believe the program's messages, and a single refuge or outreach incident will not trigger a backlash that suppresses use. Run 3-4 focus groups with 65+ and migrant residents by Month 1 (2026-11-08). Test message credibility and a scripted incident scenario, and ask which messengers they trust. Fewer than 60% of participants (proposed threshold) say they would use a refuge or answer a partner call, or most name channels the plan does not use.

Each scenario below links to a root-cause assumption and includes a detailed failure story, early warning signs, measurable tripwires, a response playbook, and a stop rule to guide decision-making.

Failure Modes

FM1 - The Winter Gate Cliff

  • Archetype: Process/Financial
  • Root Cause: Assumption A1
  • Owner: Project Manager (PMO Lead)
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 15/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 5/5)
Failure Story
  • Gates fall in the cool season, so the evidence is a drill.
  • Funder acceptance was never obtained in writing.
  • At Month 4 (2027-02-08) the funder withholds the €1.5M and wants real heat data.
  • Cash gap of €200-400k (estimate) exceeds the €160k tranche-1 contingency.
  • Staff, transport and kits are cut before the summer peak.
  • Partners and volunteers disengage, and credibility is lost.
Early Warning Signs
  • No signed funding amendment by Month 1 (2026-11-08)
  • Funder asks for real-event data or a different drill scale
  • Drill protocol not shared with funder by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23)
  • Monthly burn above forecast by 10%
Tripwires
  • No written funder sign-off by Month 1 (2026-11-08)
  • Drill protocol not final by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23)
  • Forecast cash gap >= €160k at the Month 3.5 (2027-01-23) reforecast
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Freeze new commitments above €25k and defer discretionary hiring until funder position is confirmed in writing.
  • Assess: Reforecast cash to Month 12 (2027-10-08) with the CFO within 5 days, and quantify the gap against the €160k contingency.
  • Respond: Negotiate the €750k partial release or a municipal credit line, and re-scope services to the tranche-1 minimum if needed.

STOP RULE: If the funder gives no written acceptance of the drill or partial-release rule by Month 2 (2026-12-08) and no bridging line of at least €200k exists, restart or re-scope the project to the tranche-1 minimum.

FM2 - The Empty Crates and Idle Cars

  • Archetype: Technical/Logistical
  • Root Cause: Assumption A2
  • Owner: Home Interventions and Handyperson Coordinator
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 16/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Kit lead times prove longer than the 6-8 weeks assumed, with no pre-committed backup supplier.
  • 60-80% of kits arrive after May.
  • Volunteer vetting lags, so pickups stretch past 45 minutes and wheelchair users wait longest.
  • The taxi-only fallback (+€150-250k, estimate) collides with the expedite premium.
  • Kits are cut from 2,000 to 1,000-1,500.
  • The transport gate fails in the drill.
Early Warning Signs
  • Supplier quotes show lead time over 8 weeks
  • Supplier misses an interim milestone by over 7 days
  • Vetting cohort falls over 1 week behind
  • Drill pickup times trend above 45 minutes
Tripwires
  • First call-off not placed by Month 1.2 (2026-11-14)
  • Fewer than 20 volunteers in the pipeline at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23)
  • Less than 40% of kits delivered by Month 4 (2027-02-08)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Activate the pre-qualified backup supplier within 2 business days and scale the taxi retainer proportionally, capped at €80k; anything above is the taxi-only fallback (+€150-250k) and needs an approval decision.
  • Assess: Rerun the delivery and dispatch simulation with actual numbers within 5 days, and cost the kit versus transport trade-off.
  • Respond: Reduce the kit scope to 1,000-1,500 homes if needed, protect transport and refuges, and brief the funder.

STOP RULE: If fewer than 20 volunteers are vetted and no taxi retainer is signed by Month 2 (2026-12-08), pause scale-up and re-scope transport before any Month 4 (2027-02-08) release request.

FM3 - The Calls Nobody Answers

  • Archetype: Market/Human
  • Root Cause: Assumption A3
  • Owner: Outreach and Street Contact Lead
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 16/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Partners are short of staff or lack a clear lawful basis.
  • Contact success falls to 40-50%.
  • Enrolled residents are mostly people already known to services; enrollment is about 9% of 65+ (estimate).
  • Isolated, migrant and offline residents stay unreached.
  • A summer heat event shows deaths concentrated among the unreached.
  • Media coverage says the pilot served only the connected.
  • Partners withdraw and Year-2 support erodes.
Early Warning Signs
  • Partner capacity survey shows under 4,000 attempts/month
  • Mock-call success under 65% (proposed threshold; 55-59% triggers a defined corrective action, under 60% is a failure)
  • A partner delays or refuses to sign its DPA
  • Fewer than 5% of calls in non-official languages
Tripwires
  • Contact success <60% in the drill (Month 3.2, 2027-01-14)
  • Fewer than 4 partner DPAs signed by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23)
  • Enrollment below 1,500 by Month 5 (2027-03-08)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Reassign call targets from weak partners to backup partners and start daily contact logging.
  • Assess: Audit enrollment by neighborhood, housing type and language within 7 days, and sample 50-100 consents for validity.
  • Respond: Add door-knock teams and ambassador-led enrollment in high-deprivation blocks, and renegotiate partner targets and the gate.

STOP RULE: If contact success stays below 60% after the Month 5 (2027-03-08) re-test, or counsel finds no valid lawful basis, stop the intermediary model and redesign outreach.

FM4 - The Locked Doors

  • Archetype: Technical/Logistical
  • Root Cause: Assumption A4
  • Owner: Cooling Center Network Manager
  • Risk Level: HIGH 12/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Site owners decline or add conditions on hours, liability or insurance.
  • Audits find ramps, toilets or quiet rooms unusable at several sites.
  • Remediation exceeds the cap, so sites are dropped.
  • Network shrinks below 8 sites and accessible places fall under 50%.
  • Drill delivers under 80% of planned hours; wheelchair users concentrate at a few sites.
  • Transport demand and the Month 4 (2027-02-08) gate suffer.
Early Warning Signs
  • Site owners not responding to agreement drafts within 10 days
  • Audit rates 3 or more sites red
  • Insurance cover for refuge use not bound by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23)
  • Named site manager missing at any signed site
Tripwires
  • Fewer than 8 signed sites at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23)
  • Accessible places <50% of planned ~400 at Month 2 (2026-12-08)
  • More than 3 sites rated red in the audit
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Stop fit-out spending at red-rated sites and hold remediation orders above €10k per site.
  • Assess: Re-map walking distance coverage (800 m) with the remaining sites within 5 days and recompute planned site-hours.
  • Respond: Recruit replacement sites such as sports halls, or concentrate on accessible sites with transport support, and brief the funder.

STOP RULE: If fewer than 6 accessible, signed sites exist by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), re-scope the network design before the drill.

Failure Story
  • Municipal HR approvals and seasonal recruiting are slower than the plan.
  • Hiring cohorts slip, so the Month 3.2 (2027-01-14) drill runs with few staff.
  • Reserve is used up in the first heat wave.
  • Overtime and agency replacement push payroll above plan.
  • Burnout drives turnover mid-season.
  • Payroll overruns compete with the €280k contingency.
Early Warning Signs
  • Position codes not approved by Month 1 (2026-11-08)

  • Drill rota filled by fewer than 80% of planned staff

Tripwires
  • Less than 40% of staff hired by Month 3 (2027-01-08)
  • Staff in post <90% of plan at Month 6.7 (2027-04-29)
  • Payroll forecast >10% over budget at any monthly review
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Freeze non-essential roles and shift overtime approval to the PMO lead.
  • Assess: Compare hires, absences and cost to plan by role within 5 days and identify gate-critical gaps.
  • Respond: Use agency or part-time retirees for centers and phone line, cross-train staff, and trim lower-priority roles to protect gates.

STOP RULE: If staff in post are more than 4 weeks behind plan at Month 3 (2027-01-08), trigger the funder restart or re-scope review.

FM6 - The Silent Dashboard

STOP RULE: If no health data agreement exists by Month 3 (2027-01-08), drop mortality attribution claims and re-scope the evaluation.

FM7 - The Thermostat That Burned the Budget

  • Archetype: Process/Financial

  • Owner: Incident Commander (Mayor's Office)
  • Risk Level: HIGH 12/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Thresholds were set from national levels without local calibration.
  • Season triggers far more Level 2-3 days than the 25 planned.
  • Each extra full-activation day costs about €324 per planned site-hour across 10 sites (estimate).
  • Refuge and transport spending exceeds plan; contingency is drawn early.

Early Warning Signs
  • Back-test shows more than 30 Level 2-3 days per season
  • Spend per alert day above forecast for 2 reviews

Tripwires

  • Refuge spend >10% above forecast at any monthly review
  • More than 30 full-activation days declared by Month 10 (2027-08-08)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Freeze threshold changes and hold extra Level 3 extensions until the commander and CFO approve each one.
  • Assess: Rerun the back-test with local EMS data within 7 days and cost each alert tier per day.
  • Respond: Shift marginal days to the Level 1 advisory tier, reset thresholds with public-health sign-off, and brief the funder.

STOP RULE: If projected alert-driven spend exceeds the free contingency of €280k before Month 9 (2027-07-08), cut refuge hours to the tranche-minimum and reset the ladder.

Failure Story

  • Residents decline visits, citing mistrust or fear of landlords.

  • Handypeople install fewer homes per day than planned.

Tripwires
  • Consent rate <50% in the Month 1.2 (2026-11-14) pre-test
